#5405. How State Environmental Laws Are Being ‘Weaponized’ To Stall Housing and Drive Up Costs

Congress is fixated on cutting red tape that drives up the cost of housing—but state policies have a role to play, too, a study finds.

The Pacific Legal Foundation studied state-level policies and found that certain environmental review laws are being "weaponized" to stall developments, driving up the costs and reducing the affordability of housing. This comes as state lawmakers have proposed many new laws this year to curtail policies that stall building, with mixed success.

The study looks at lawsuits that use state environmental policy acts, as well as environmental rights amendments written into state laws. Both of these kinds of disputes are expensive and time-consuming. Developers have to examine and reexamine the environmental impact of developments they want to build, and courts must then determine what cities are required to do to ensure a clean environment for residents.

"A real cost is borne on the people who are renting and buying those homes and apartments," Kyle Sweetland, the study's author, tells Realtor.com®.

About a dozen states have pitched laws that would make it easier to build homes, many of them by reducing zoning or lot size requirements. But some proposals have also met with failure, like California's Proposition 45, which aimed to expedite project reviews through the California Environmental Quality Act.

The Realtor.com Housing Supply Gap research shows the U.S. faces a shortage of 4.03 million homes. Our Let America Build campaign has tracked how states have responded to this shortage, and which are tackling the problem.

California has a long history of slow development on account of environmental review. In one recent example, a 49-unit housing development was stalled for 4.5 years in environmental litigation, which the developer said had raised the cost of the project by $9 million. In another, a 34-home subdivision was stalled for nearly 40 years, in part because of neighbors' environmental concerns.

It's not just a California problem. Sweetland looked at 16 states and the District of Columbia that have environmental policy acts that affect developers, or amendments that affect municipalities. Wyoming, Minnesota, New York, Hawaii, and Massachusetts have both.

But other protections are also in place in California, Nevada, Washington, North Dakota, Illinois, Wyoming, Michigan, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Connecticut, Rhode Island, and the District of Columbia.

It's hard to track precisely how much this kind of litigation drives up the costs of housing. Realtor.com senior economist Joel Berner also notes that it's hard to tell how many housing projects didn't start in the first place because developers expected a lawsuit.

"The bigger costs come from what the lawsuit does to the project’s financing and schedule," Berner says. "Appeals typically add years, and in the meantime, most projects can’t secure construction or grant funding. Loans, taxes, and insurance keep accruing, and construction costs can rise while the project waits."

Change could come at the federal level. Last week, the Senate passed a controversial bill that would reduce some federal environmental regulations, like the National Environmental Policy Act, to speed up construction of big-energy projects. Environmental groups opposed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which next heads to the House.

In some instances, the environmental lawsuits don't actually produce better outcomes for the environment. Seattle found that just 16% of cases filed using environmental laws over the 2010s resulted in decisions requiring environmental remediation. In New York, about 22% of cases over 15 years resulted in more environmental reviews, an outside researcher found.

Berner says the balance is that environmental laws are sometimes the easiest avenue residents have to oppose a residential project. It's just a matter of not abusing the process.

"While challenging a project is a relatively cheap thing to do, being on the receiving end of a legal battle can derail a project even without going all the way through the litigation process," Berner says. "This uncertainty adds to the cost of capital for builders and squeezes out lower-margin projects like affordable and infill housing."

Pacific Legal Foundation says one solution for these issues is to narrow the scope of some environmental laws. For instance, Sweetland says legal challenges from outside environmental groups could be limited. That way, the people challenging housing developments have a real vested interest in their outcomes.

He also suggests requirements that groups that lose cases have to pay the legal fees. That isn't typical everywhere, even if developers pay the legal fees when they lose. That provides some incentive that those launching lawsuits have a legitimate claim, as opposed to using the courts as a stalling tactic.

"The law shouldn't just give anybody the ability to have a license to stop a building from moving forward," Sweetland says.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5403. New Haven Weighs Sweeping Ban on Non-Owner-Occupied Airbnb Rentals—Will It Actually Lower Rents?

Homeowners and short-term rental hosts in New Haven, CT, are watching closely as city lawmakers weigh a sweeping proposal that would largely prohibit short-term rentals in the city.

Alderpersons Leland Moore, Frank Douglas, and Mandy Martinelli proposed OR-2026-0039 this past October. The ordinance would bar rentals of 30 days or less in properties that are not a host’s primary residence starting on March 31, 2027. Hosts operating full-time vacation rentals or investor units would need to switch to long-term leases of more than 30 days.

Residents who live in their home could still host short-term stays in their primary residences as long as they obtained a city home-sharing license, remained in the home during the rental, and followed occupancy limits.

"The conversion of long-term residential housing into short-term rentals inflates rental prices, reduces housing inventory, and directly contributes to the displacement of long-term neighbors and residents from communities," the ordinance reads in part.

Supporters of the measure argue it will help free up units in the housing-strapped city. Opponents say it will do little to improve affordability and will hurt residents who make a living from renting out their properties.

At a Nov. 16 Board of Alders meeting where the board was to take a final vote on the measure, more than a hundred residents packed City Hall. Alderman Richard Furlow ultimately tabled the vote until Dec. 7, giving members more time to review proposed amendments to the initiative.

The measure has been supported by housing affordability advocates, hotel and hospitality labor unions, and the city's mayor, Justin Elicker.

"We want to make sure homeowners, if they have an extra room or extra apartment in their building, have the ability to rent," Elicker told NBC affiliate WVIT.  "But at the same time, we're in an affordability crisis right now, and housing affordability is something that's affecting so many New Haven residents. We have a lot of new construction in the city. A lot of that’s affordable, but a lot of that’s not."

The advocacy group New Haven Rising has argued that short-term rentals drive up housing costs for residents and cannibalize local rental stock, keeping locals locked out of homes.

A separate group, Put New Haven First, came out against the proposed ban, noting that the city had yet to complete an economic impact study of the ordinance.

For its part, Airbnb has argued that the proposed ban will hurt locals who make a living by renting out their properties and "puts corporate hotel interests ahead of everyday residents.”

“Airbnb listings make up just 0.5% of the city’s total housing stock," a company spokesperson tells Realtor.com®. "Restricting them won’t lower rents or improve housing availability, but it will take away income that helps local homeowners stay in their homes and supports the house cleaners, landscapers, and small businesses who serve guests.

"Short-term rentals also give visiting families, including those in town for the hospital or university, flexible and affordable places to stay that hotels often can't match," the statement continued. "Residents have asked the Board of Alders to study the impact before acting, and we urge them to look at the evidence before passing a bill that puts corporate hotel interests ahead of everyday residents.”

New Haven is home to Yale University, a world-class hospital system, more than 70 biotech companies, and a burgeoning pizza tourism industry. Locals love its walkability, proximity to nature, and food scene—but they don’t love the city’s struggling housing market.

Between 2020 and 2025, New Haven added 3,535 housing units—more than any other Connecticut city. Yet, the city is still considered one of the worst places in the country for renters. It ranked 138 out of 182 cities on WalletHub's 2026 list of the best places to rent. The city’s median rent is $2,000 a month—more expensive than median rents in 42 of the top 50 metros.

The Realtor.com 2026 Housing Mismatch Report found that New Haven lacks homes for middle-class homebuyers.

"The data makes clear that more inventory alone won’t be enough to unlock the housing market," Danielle Hale, chief economist of Realtor.com, previously said. "A true recovery requires homes at the right price points.”

There are currently 559 rental units available in the city, a 38% increase year over year. By comparison, New Haven has approximately 765 active short-term rental listings across Airbnb, Vrbo, and Booking.com—a 19.1% decrease in active supply compared to October 2025, according to short-term rental tracking site AirDNA.

Proponents of the short-term rental ban have argued that the short-term rentals have had a deleterious effect on the city’s affordability by taking up housing stock that might otherwise be available to locals.

But those 765 units make up just 2% of the city’s 38,621 rental units, according to U.S. Census Bureau data.

What’s more, in other communities where short-term rentals have been curbed or prohibited, the impact on rental prices has been debatable.

In September 2023, New York City implemented Local Law 18, which requires short-term rental hosts to live in the unit and be present during stays. That slashed short-term rental listings by more than 90%, from roughly 38,500 down to around 3,000 to 3,500 registered hosts, according to city reports and a 2026 study.

That study found that the crackdown on short-term rentals had no demonstrable impact on rents and that median monthly rents in Manhattan climbed to a record $4,700 during that period.

A 2024 study from researchers at the College of William & Mary, Purdue University, and Chinese University of Hong Kong examined a similar short-term rental ban in Irvine, CA. According to their research, the ban led to a 23.1% decrease in Airbnb listings and a 2.7% decrease in rental prices.  However, the period of study happened to coincide with the early years of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Residents are eager to hear what amendments to the proposed short-term rental ban the alders will propose at the Dec. 7 meeting.

Sun Queen, a co-founder of Black Lives Matter New Haven and an organizer with the Unhoused Activists Community Team, told the New Haven Independent that short-term rentals can be useful transitional housing for unhoused people.

"I think more time was needed to do more research," she said. "I get it from all angles. We are in a housing crisis.”

Realtor.com reached out to Martinelli, Moore, and Douglas for comment.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. #5402. Zoom’s conversations-to-completion strategy is starting to pay off

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala

Zoom Communications Inc. has spent the better part of the past few years building products to become more than just the video company everyone used during the pandemic. Its fiscal third-quarter results, posted Monday, showed the strategy is working, though more work remains.

Total revenue grew 4.9%, but enterprise revenue rose 8.6%, its fastest pace in 13 quarters. Zoom raised its full-year outlook and announced its first quarterly dividend of 25 cents per share.

The acceleration should be viewed not as a one-quarter anomaly but as a manifestation of the strategy the company outlined at Zoomtopia about a month ago – moving from “conversations to completion.” That strategy gives customers a reason to buy more of Zoom and builds a competitive moat wider than most investors realize.

The concept of conversations to completion has enough merit that Microsoft used those exact words at its recent Ignite 2026 event. In fact, it held an entire session on the topic. Though having an 800-pound gorilla like Microsoft jump on a trend might seem threatening, Zoom has a significant lead and can use Microsoft’s marketing to add momentum to its current tailwind.

Nearly all work starts with a conversation: a meeting, a call, a chat thread or a customer interaction. Then everyone leaves, and the real work begins: updating the customer record, writing the follow-up and scheduling the next step. Collaboration vendors have always owned the first step, leaving the second to someone else.

Zoom wants both. “We’d like to leverage AI to transform our business from a conversation-centric vendor to a system of completions,” Chief Executive Eric Yuan said on the earnings call. He later put it more plainly: “Conversation is step 1. Step 2, AI will take over.”

His proof point was Zoom’s own sales organization, which uses ZoomMate, the company’s agentic framework. Sellers, Yuan said, “no longer log into the backend CRM system.” The agent takes over after the call ends. In enterprise software, value is shifting from where work is recorded to where it originates.

AI agents are quickly becoming a commodity, and so are the models behind them. What is scarce is context, the knowledge of what was decided, by whom, and why. Zoom sits on the richest source of it in most companies: what people actually said to one another and to customers.

“Any agent without context really cannot get work done,” Yuan said. That’s why the unified context layer Zoom showcased at Zoomtopia is central to the story. It links conversations to chats, documents and third-party systems, ensuring people and agents work from the same information.

My Notes, the company’s AI note-taker, extends that reach to third-party and in-person conversations. Yuan said it is nearing 2 million monthly active users, with one financial services firm rolling it out to 80,000 wealth advisers. Chief Financial Officer Michelle Chang added that online customers using My Notes have been associated with a 50% reduction in churn.

That is what will create a deeper competitive moat for Zoom. The more context a customer stores with Zoom, the more useful its agents become and the harder it is to leave. Zoom’s moat is not the meeting. Think of it as the memory of the meeting.

A context layer is only as good as the number of conversations it ingests, and this is where Zoom’s breadth of platforms matters. Meetings, phone, chat, contact center and now sales intelligence all feed into the same foundation, and each product gets smarter from the others.

Customers are consolidating. DSI Systems is replacing five separate products with Zoom. SolarWinds expanded its Zoom licenses while “recalibrating its Microsoft package,” according to Yuan. Enterprise net dollar expansion returned to 100%, its highest level in 11 quarters. “Strong RPO growth reflects our continued success in landing larger, longer-term multiproduct platform deals, demonstrating growing demand for our AI-first platform,” Chang said.

Customer experience is where completion gets paid for. Zoom CX recurring revenue grew in the high double digits for the seventh straight quarter, and all 10 of its largest CX deals included paid AI. More telling, Zoom said at Zoomtopia that 90% of its top 100 CX deals in the first half were with customers new to Zoom. Contact center is no longer a cross-sell. It is a front door.

Chang described the differentiation as “the ability to think about customer experience in a whole and fresh new way.” Specifically, she said, “to be able to seamlessly hand off from virtual agents to agents assisted with AI is a big winner for us.” AI-native startups have the virtual agent but not the human side. Legacy contact center vendors have the humans but not the pace of innovation. Zoom has both on one platform.

There is also an economic moat. Zoom runs most of its AI workload on its own small models and saves the expensive frontier models for harder tasks. “I fundamentally believe no single model can satisfy everything,” Yuan said. Gross margin rose even as AI usage grew, a feat that a point product reselling another company’s tokens cannot easily match.

The quarter was strong, but analyst questions revealed several concerns.

Some will read the dividend as a sign of maturity. With more than $7 billion in cash and free cash flow margins above 40%, I see a company that can fund innovation and return capital at the same time.

Although these issues came up during the call, most of the investment community remains positive about Zoom. In his note, Arun Bhatia of William Blair wrote, “Churn and downsell rates are becoming more favorable, AI usage and monetization are increasing, and adoption of new products such as Phone and Zoom CX is strong. We are encouraged by these trends and see potential for a growth uptick in the future.”

Zoom’s headline growth resembles that of a mature software vendor, but the company is in transition, so it’s important to look beyond the numbers. The underlying enterprise business is built to be a platform that uses context to drive customers toward more products and longer commitments. Investors should watch enterprise growth, net expansion and CX AI attach rates rather than the top line.

For information technology and business leaders, the lesson extends beyond Zoom. Conversation data is a strategic asset, so decide deliberately where it lives and which agents can act on it. Insist on openness so that context can feed the tools you choose. Start where completion is easy to measure, in the contact center and in sales.

That is where Zoom is proving that the conversation was never the product. The outcome is.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5401. Eight Guidelines for Brokerage Growth

Above from left to right: Jackie Louh, Rob Cleapor, John Finn and Doug Smith, on stage at RISMedia’s 38th Annual CEO & Leadership Exchange in Washington, D.C. this past October. Not pictured, Amy Somerville.

Business owners are constantly on the look-out for the best ways to evolve and grow their firms, and real estate broker/owners are no different. However, in today’s unpredictable market environment, growth can be an elusive goal, and taking a brokerage to the next level requires clarity, commitment and creativity.

A group of brokerage leaders addressed the growth dilemma at RISMedia’s 2026 CEO & Leadership Exchange this past fall during the panel discussion “More Than One Way to Grow.” Here’s their top advice for achieving growth despite current challenges that can feel insurmountable.

1. Take a broad approach. According to Jackie Louh, chief operating officer of Lamacchia Realty, increasing business means diversifying your efforts to ensure you’re growing on a variety of fronts, such as: expanding the brokerage footprint, increasing agent productivity, increasing market share and growing agent count.

“To do that, we have different people focused on those different avenues,” said Louh “Anthony (Lamacchia, company CEO) and I, for instance, we focus primarily on what we call chunk growth—acquisition opportunities. And then we have our regional sales managers who are focused every day on organic growth. They work with recruiting in their markets. They work with helping the agents in their markets grow their business. It’s not just about being the biggest company. We want to be the best, and to do that and to grow, you have to hit all avenues of that growth.”

2. Support agents and franchisees. Rob Cleapor, CEO of the growing franchise Iron Valley Real Estate, admitted that early on, growth equated to agent count. He soon realized, however, that the number of agents was not as important as the quality of those agents.

“As we started growing rapidly, you start realizing that’s really not what’s important,” said Cleapor. “For us, the way we define growth is supporting our agents and our franchisees along the way. “Growth, like (Jackie) said, is agent count, it’s footprint. But more importantly for me, it’s the support that you give for franchisees and the agents, and making sure that we’re keeping that support at the top so that everybody can grow and grow the right way.”

Echoing Cleapor’s sentiments, Doug Smith, founder and CEO of Douglas Realty is zeroing in on productivity.

“Our growth this year from an agent headcount is about 12%,” he said. “Our transactions are up almost 45% in this crazy down market. So we focus a ton on training, a ton on bringing in good agents.”

3. Talk to teams…and tired brokers. As John Finn, CEO and senior managing broker of United Real Estate Richmond pointed out, the majority of brokerages in his market—and across the country—are small, many with 10 agents or less. That’s why his growth strategy has focused on bringing successful teams into the fold.

“We have people who had good teams and decided they wanted to be brokers, and then woke up one day and said, ‘Oh, I really don’t want to do this.’ We have had great success with that,” said Finn.

Finn also homes in on brokers that want to go back to being agents.

“We’ve had success with older agents who really want to get back to the business of actually selling real estate and not having to provide the back-office services, the payroll, the tech stack, AI…things they don’t want to deal with anymore,” he said.

4. Build the right infrastructure. As panel moderator Amy Somerville, COO of the Real REMAX Group noted, the definition of brokerage growth changes when you put the word “sustainable” in front of it.

“I want to talk about the internal infrastructure and what needs to be set up to support the growth that you plan for your business,” she said. “Technology systems, financial systems, general infrastructure.”

Finn discussed the benefit of tapping into the tech stack of a large parent company like United.

“I found that by the time I studied and researched state-of-the-art (technology) and developed state of the art and got the money together to buy state of the art and got the agents to use state of the art, it wouldn’t be state of the art anymore,” he explained. “When we’re out approaching other people about coming to join our team, I don’t have to worry about AI as many other smaller firms in my market do, because I’ve got United in my pocket.”

5. Work on your business, not in it. In the early days of Iron Valley, Cleapor quickly learned that sustainable growth meant putting the right team in place, then delegating accordingly.

“Early on, I was managing three offices. I was the director of marketing. I did all of our graphic design. I did our franchise sales,” he shared. “One of my favorite lines somebody said to me years ago was, ‘When you’re doing 10 things, 10 things are getting 10% of your effort. And when you only do one thing, it gets 100% of your effort.’ Putting the infrastructure in, the processes, and more importantly, the people on your team…you have to make that decision or everything that you’ve grown is going to collapse.”

6. Set acquisition criteria and stick to it. Growing a real estate brokerage by acquiring another brokerage can quickly expand a firm’s business—provided a specific strategy is in place and adhered to.

Louh, for example, says that focusing on firms located in contiguous states is usually the best path. She then targets legacy firms within those states.

“The (firms) that have been around a long time have really built a strong brand and they have agents that have been with them a long time,” she said. “That makes for a much smoother transition because the agents trust the owner. They’re going to do whatever the owner says. They’re going to go wherever the owner goes.”

When considering a firm to acquire, Louh also advised making sure the owner is focused on their agents, not themselves.

“If the owner is saying, ‘How is this going to benefit me? How much money am I going to make off of this?’ that is not a company we want to align with,” she said. “If the owner isn’t invested in their agents, if that acquisition does come together, the owner’s going to basically disappear. They’re going to collect their paycheck. They’re not going to work to retain the agents. They’re not going to work to recruit, and then we’re just going to end up losing those agents.”

7. Always be networking. Smith reminded everyone that real estate is a people business, and staying committed to building relationships with other brokers can lead to organic M&A opportunities when values align.

“Last year we acquired a 50-agent brokerage, and it kind of happened by accident,” he said. “The owner of that brokerage was president of our local Realtor board and he invited me to speak. We didn’t know each other, but it turns out we were very much in alignment on so many different things in business. And it just so happened that his franchise renewal was up and he pulled me to the side and said, ‘Hey, we should talk.’ So it started there.”

8. Grow horizontally. While firms traditionally want to grow vertically—more agents, more transactions—in the current market, brokerages need to take a closer look at growing horizontally by getting more out of the transaction through services such as title, escrow, mortgage, insurance and more.

“The customer is looking for an experience at one stop where they can get everything,” said Finn. “We as agents, we as brokers are going to have to start providing that for our people.”

“The future of our industry is you have to be involved in more than just one area of the transaction or else I think you will get shut out,” agreed Smith. “I think you have to have your hands in a little bit of everything. Provide a consumer experience, create that client for life, but even more and just as important, create that agent for life.”

Maria Patterson is RISMedia’s executive vice president.

#5400. Hawaii Beachfront Battle Turns Into Bitter Clash Over Burial Grounds and Wastewater

What was supposed to be a routine permit hearing for seven new homes on Oahu’s North Shore devolved into a bitter clash, with neighbors alleging unpermitted construction, threatened ancestral burial sites, and tainted runoff one blames for giving local children boils.

“It’s a disgrace to the community,” Carla Lenhoff, who lives on the same residential lane as the proposed development, told Honolulu planners. “It’s a disgrace to the ocean. It’s a disgrace to your neighbors.”

At the center of the Nov. 20 town hall was homeowner Linda Donoso and Malaekahana LLC’s application for a Special Management Area permit on Mālaekahana Bay—a quiet stretch of coastline lined with beachfront homes between Kahuku and Lāʻie.

According to the public hearing notice, the permit would cover construction of seven new homes on Condominium Property Regime (CPR) Units 2 through 8, with the existing home retained on CPR Unit 1. The request also includes installation of six individual wastewater systems and utility connections, plus driveways, walkways, fencing, rock walls, and other site improvements.

The property is divided into eight separately owned condominium units, but Honolulu treats them as a single lot for zoning purposes.

Donoso said she took on the cost of pursuing a coastal permit covering seven additional homes because the other owners were unwilling to pay.

Donoso, who has lived on Unit 1 since 2016, acquired Unit 6 two years later.

“I am not a developer, I am building a home for my family. In order for me to build on this property, a legal CPR, I have to apply for an SMA permit,” Donoso told Realtor.com® ahead of the hearing.

“It will benefit all the lot owners. But in order for me to build, I have to pay for this SMA because no one else is.”

Donoso, who lost her husband to COVID-19 and wants her family nearby, told Realtor.com that there was no existing home on that lot, but one of those homes was already standing, unfinished, on a unit owned by her son, Allen Graham.

Michael Marchak, the city planner reviewing the application, confirmed that an August citation for building without a permit remained open.

Neighbors weren't swayed by Donoso’s description of the project.

“Are we just going to short-term rent it out to as many people as possible?” Lenhoff asked.

While Kahuku remains mostly residential, it sits along Oahu’s popular North Shore tourism corridor, where an estimated 12,100 visitors were present on a typical day in 2024, according to Hawaii state tourism research.

For Naomi Fiatoa-Holani, who raised six children along the same lane and was baptized in the bay, the prospect of additional vacation rentals hit close to home.

“We purposely live there for the serenity and the culture of that area,” she told planners.

In fact, short-term vacation rentals are already prohibited in the area. City zoning rules bar owners from renting out the homes for stays of fewer than 30 consecutive days, regardless of the coastal permit.

And Donoso had previously been cited over short-term rental advertising.

The city cited her home on Unit 1 in December 2023 over an ad offering stays under 30 days. Donoso acknowledged renting to vacationers, but insists she stopped accepting bookings after that notice.

A second citation followed in April 2024 over a recurring ad. Both cases are now marked corrected and closed by the city, and at the hearing, Donoso disputed that she had resumed renting out her property.

She also rejected the suggestion that the proposed development would become an outpost for tourists. Her son owned Unit 2, she told planners, and her grandson had recently bought Unit 4.

“It isn’t going to be a vacation rental community,” she said.

But neighbors questioned whether they could trust the applicants to follow the rules when construction on Graham’s home on Unit 2 had already begun without a permit.

Honolulu's Aug. 13 violation notice documented the unpermitted construction of a two-story structure. Neighbors alleged that work continued even after crews were told to stop, though city officials did not establish whether that was the case at the hearing.

“They’re still building,” Lenhoff told planners, adding that she had submitted photographs.

That incident was particularly troubling to residents because of the significance of the ground on which the home stands.

“That’s precious to us,” Fiatoa-Holani said of the sand along the bay. “That’s where our kūpuna are buried.”

In Native Hawaiian tradition, ancestral remains, known as iwi kūpuna, are sacred, representing an enduring spiritual connection between the land, the deceased, and their living descendants.

And in 2018, human remains were discovered during construction of two homes in a neighboring three-home development, according to draft minutes of the Oahu Island Burial Council.

No one at the hearing reported finding remains on Graham's unit, nor had archaeologists found cultural resources during an earlier investigation of the property—but that investigation had its limits.

The archaeologists dug six test trenches in 2021, none on Graham's unit. The applicants' own filing acknowledges that the State Historic Preservation Division considered the findings insufficient to rule out impacts to buried cultural resources.

The agency requested on-site archaeological monitoring during ground-disturbing work, noting that the area's sandy soils are known to contain human remains.

Graham maintained that work on his house had involved little new excavation. He said sand used behind a retaining wall came from an earlier driveway excavation.

“We didn’t go deep below the surface,” he said.

But when public testimony ended, Marchak asked whether anyone had monitored construction on Unit 2 for archaeological finds.

Donoso said the family had tried to arrange it.

“We couldn’t get it done till January,” she said.

Neighbors also raised concerns about water quality, describing floodwater they feared was carrying contaminants from the property onto their shared lane.

Fiatoa-Holani described watching water and debris wash down the road her children walked to collect the mail. She believed the flooding had made local children sick, and that wading through the water had given them boils.

Other residents also complained about runoff, though Fiatoa-Holani was the only one who reported children developing boils.

"It was completely dry during the rain,” she said, adding that her grandchildren had never developed any symptoms.

The permit application likewise maintains that the property's permeable sandy soil would keep stormwater on-site, with dry wells proposed to help manage drainage.

But beyond the dispute over flooding was another question: Could the property accommodate wastewater from eight homes?

The plans call for six wastewater systems, with Units 3 and 4 sharing one and Units 7 and 8 sharing another. Donoso said her son had already replaced an old cesspool on Unit 2 with a septic system.

Lenhoff challenged whether the parcel had enough land for the six proposed systems; and in his final questions to the applicants, Marchak raised the same issue.

Under state rules, six systems would require 60,000 square feet of land. The property originally measured 64,033 square feet, but a 2015 certified shoreline survey documented 6,229 square feet lost to erosion.

That leaves 57,804 square feet in the application's calculations—2,196 square feet short of the stated requirement.

When Marchak asked whether the wastewater plans had been submitted to the state Department of Health, Roy Irei, the applicants' engineer, said he had discussed the proposal with officials but had yet to submit it for approval.

Kahuku resident Evelyn Lane had a more immediate request for the unfinished house already standing behind Donoso's home.

“They should tear down the unpermitted building that they built, and I don’t know why that wasn’t brought up in this discussion,” Lane told planners.

Three days later, Hawaii News Now was interviewing Lenhoff about the project when Donoso stepped in.

“So you guys want to fight, you guys will have a fight,” Donoso told the neighbors. The station reported that the argument lasted roughly 20 minutes and ended after police were called.

Donoso told the station her son hadn't known he needed a building permit and that the house was “already done by the time he was notified.”

The October application anticipates construction beginning in early 2027, with work on Donoso's own home scheduled for the fourth quarter of that year. The full project is expected to take approximately five years after permits are approved.

First, however, the City Council must decide whether to grant the coastal permit.

Under Honolulu law, planners have 45 days after the hearing to send their recommendation to the City Council, unless the applicant agrees to an extension. Residents will have another opportunity to testify when the City Council takes up the proposal, though no date has been announced.

#5399. Formal verification startup Sequent raises $2.2M to prove code obeys its safety rules

Formal verification startup Sequent Inc. today announced that it has raised $2.2 million in new funding to take its Alan proof platform out of early access.

Founded in London in January, Sequent offers a platform that uses artificial intelligence to find mathematical proofs that code obeys the safety rules its engineers set. Decentralized exchange Curve Finance is its first paying customer.

Curve also figures in how Sequent got started. Chief Executive Charles Cooper, who leads development of Vyper, one of the two main programming languages for Ethereum, inadvertently introduced a flaw into the Vyper compiler in 2021. Though the bug was fixed within months, programs already running on the blockchain could not be updated, leaving older Curve pools and other projects exposed when attackers used the flaw to take more than $50 million in July 2023.

Following the incident, Ramana Kumar, now Sequent’s chief technology officer and formerly an AI safety researcher at Google DeepMind, offered to help prove the Vyper compiler correct. Kumar co-created CakeML, a compiler proved correct all the way down to the instructions a computer runs.

Cooper believes the lesson reaches far beyond crypto, saying that “smart contracts taught us that anything that can be exploited will be.” Banks, governments and companies running older systems have relied on keeping their code private, according to Cooper, who said AI-powered cyberattacks are now eroding that protection.

Alan works today on Vyper smart contracts, with support for Solidity and Solana in development and general software in Rust, C, TypeScript and Python to follow.

For now, engineers using Alan write rules for their code such as “no user can withdraw more than their balance” in plain language, and the job of finding a mathematical proof is handed to AI. Nothing the AI comes up with is taken on trust, as each proof has to get through HOL4, a checker Kumar has helped build for more than a decade.

For two-coin StableSwap pools holding standard tokens, Alan was used to prove that no user can take more than a set limit from depositors, whatever they do and in whatever order. The work also found minor accounting and rounding errors, none of which breached the limit. The founders are now proving the Vyper compiler itself, since the Curve proof does not cover the compiler where the 2021 flaw sat.

Along with AI computing costs, the funding will pay for engineering, sales and marketing hires. Subscriptions to Alan start at $99 a month for individuals, with auditor plans priced at $200 a month and team plans starting at $500 a month.

Frachtis and Metaplanet Holdings OÜ co-led the pre-seed round. Metaplanet is the investment firm of Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn, who led Anthropic PBC’s Series A round in 2021. According to Frachtis founder Xavier Meegan, crypto is the right place to start, with “billions already at risk.”

#5398. Bellflower Rents Are Skyrocketing—but Is It Worth Trying to Buy in Los Angeles ?

According to the latest Realtor.com® Rent report, the rental market is showing signs of a shift. October 2026 marked the first month of year-over-year rent growth since June 2023, though the change was modest. The median national asking rent rose by just $1, a 0.1% increase from the previous year, to $1,692.

Additionally, the Housing Vacancy Survey revealed that the rental vacancy rate hit 7.6% in the last quarter, the highest it has been since early 2014. In the Los Angeles market, rents can vary dramatically, from the high $1000s to as much as $6000 in more exclusive neighborhoods.

Which brings us to Bellflower, a neighborhood where the cost of renting has its own unique story.

In Bellflower, the average rent has been on the rise. The average rent increased from $2,439 in the second quarter of 2026 to $2,551 in the third quarter. This represents an increase of $112 per month.

Furthermore, this monthly increase adds up over time, costing renters an additional $1,344 per year. Then again,  for those considering buying, the median listing price for a home in Bellflower was $699,500 in October 2026.

According to the latest L.A. Rental Report, the median asking rent for all properties in Los Angeles County was $2,554 in the third quarter of 2026, a decline of 3.6% from the previous year. Despite this county-wide dip, buying a home remains significantly more expensive. A median-priced home cost $4,716 more per month than renting, which is nearly 185% higher, making the decision to save money by renting a compelling one for many, even with a hefty down payment and a friendly landlord.

Renters may be catching a break, as homeownership in L.A. County remains out of reach for many. With mortgage rates still above 7%, higher borrowing costs could push the dream of buying even further away for those currently renting apartments. This situation may give tenants some leverage when it comes to their lease.

If you're looking to negotiate a rent decrease, consider asking your landlord what they might accept in exchange for a lower monthly payment. This could include offering to sign a longer lease, providing a higher security deposit, or prepaying a month or two of rent. Being a reliable and considerate tenant is also a strong bargaining chip.

"The best way I’ve seen renters negotiate rent is to be an amazing applicant," said Glenn Carter, a real estate investor at Condo Capital. Remind your landlord that you consistently pay on time, maintain the property well, and are considerate of your neighbors.

Moreover, landlords often value stability and may be willing to negotiate to keep a good tenant. "As a landlord, I would accept lower rent from a dependable source," said Steve Silberberg, a Boston -based landlord.

#5397. A $12K Amazon Tiny Home Actually Costs $68K. Here Is the Detailed Receipt.

With housing prices through the roof, many people are looking for a good deal on a home.

While the viral, cabin-inspired tiny home that was once sold on Amazon for $12,000 might seem like a deal, that price is only a fraction of what you’d have pay to make it livable.

That’s because Amazon doesn’t allow sellers to list habitable, code-compliant tiny homes, and many of these listings are actually uncertified storage sheds, prefab shells, or overseas flat-pack container kits.

“This is really deceptive and confusing for people looking for a legitimate, affordable living situation. In many cases, these projects become nothing more than a throwaway situation because buyers realize how much it costs to turn the ‘home’ into a functional, livable space,” says Dan Salinger, log cabin and luxury home specialist at Zook Cabins in Gap, PA.

Before you buy a “tiny home” that seems too good to be true, be sure to understand what it includes and how much it will cost to turn it into a livable property. Otherwise, you may end up with a $60,000-plus project you didn’t expect.

To turn a relatively inexpensive prefabricated tiny home into a space you could actually live in, you’ll need to account for the following:

Your home must get delivered by a freight carrier, hauled out on a trailer, and craned into position.

“I would estimate $2,000 to $7,000 more for a remote area. Many sites do not have adequate road widths to accommodate delivery on a flatbed or permit a crane due to wires, HOAs, etc. There may be an additional fee if it has to be redelivered,” explains Cameron Walker, real estate expert and manager of the Agent Network at Clever Real Estate in St. Louis.

Clearing, grading, drainage, and foundation work are usually performed as one service.

“I would expect costs ranging from $4,000 to $15,000, depending on conditions. Factors such as depth of frost line, flooding potential, and required footing depths would all affect this amount,” Walker explains.

Keep in mind that all houses require some form of foundation. Simply placing a structure on concrete blocks won’t meet residential code requirements.

Walker recommends reserving $1,000 to $5,000 for drawing preparation and all required permits, but this will be dependent on where you live.

“Many towns and cities require a minimum size of 600 to 1,000 square feet, making it impossible to build a tiny home. Others may allow it as an ADU. Always check applicable regulations prior to any purchase,” says Walker.

For a reputable contractor to assemble and frame the tiny house, you’ll likely pay between $10,000 and $25,000.

“Some might charge even more, as these are generally difficult kits to complete, due to lack of fit of parts and applicability to local building codes,” Walker explains.

Most imported tiny homes lack sufficient insulation. According to Walker, you could spend an additional $2,000 to $6,000 to ensure the insulation is compliant.

“There are local rules that specify minimum insulation levels, measured by R-value, for walls, floors, and roofs,” Walker adds.

Hooking up plumbing, septic/sewer, electrical, and HVAC systems is anything but cheap.

“If your utilities are in place, you can expect the connection costs to run a few thousand dollars. However, if you are on raw land with no utility connection, it can be tens of thousands of dollars to get your infrastructure in place,” explains Salinger.

If you’re still interested in a tiny home, even after doing the math and calculating the total cost, you may wonder what financing opportunities are available.

The reality is that it may be difficult if not impossible to obtain a loan on such a small home. That’s because appraisers will have difficulty finding appropriate comps.

“Depending on your situation, you may have to get a personal or construction loan and settle for higher interest rates. Or you might be forced to save up and pay cash,” says Walker.

#5396. A ‘Holiday Hangover’: How Black Friday and Holiday Shopping Can Delay Your Mortgage Next Year

The holiday season is finally here. And if you’re planning to close on a home in late 2026 or early 2027, you should be extra cautious of your holiday spending.

Otherwise, it could derail your approval for a mortgage and delay your homeownership goals.

While Black Friday sales, Cyber Monday deals, and holiday splurges may be tempting, making larger purchases or taking on additional debt could easily create unexpected issues with your mortgage.

Before loading up your shopping cart, consider what the data says about this year’s holiday spending. According to the National Retail Foundation, U.S. holiday retail sales will hit $1.013 trillion in November and December 2026—a 4.2% hike over 2025.

Furthermore, an estimated 182.7 million Americans plan to shop during Thanksgiving weekend alone, with Black Friday expected to attract an additional 126 million.

The high spending projections come at a time when credit card debt is already out of control. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that Americans carried approximately $1.285 trillion in credit card debt as of the third quarter of 2026, an increase of $52 billion compared with the same time last year.

“Be frugal now. Once you’ve moved into the house and have rebuilt a cash cushion, you can splurge on gifts. Or maybe you’ll realize you’d rather devote the extra cash to renovating the kitchen,” says Jeff Ostrowski, housing marketing analyst at Bankrate.

By being mindful of your purchases, you could enjoy the holiday season without jeopardizing your future home.

Before you close on a mortgage, all lenders will pull your credit history. By doing so, they can determine if you’ve opened any new accounts or initiated any new inquiries since you were initially approved.

“Simply opening a credit card at checkout for 20% savings will result in a new inquiry, account, and monthly payment. While this will only negatively affect your score slightly, the underwriter may require an explanation letter. It may also result in a higher rate if your score drops significantly,” explains Ali Zane, CEO and personal finance expert at IMAX Credit Repair in Los Angeles.

Zane points out that many buy now, pay later programs, which are popular during the holiday shopping season, also report to the credit bureaus.

“Each one you agree to will lead to another monthly payment. And unfortunately, purchasing an item you’ll pay off over four installments can significantly affect your debt-to-income (DTI) ratio, especially if you're already at the maximum amount, which is usually 45%, depending on the lender,” says Zane.

Credit card balances, which affect your DTI ratio, will likely have the most significant effect on your mortgage approval, particularly when increased spending raises your credit utilization and monthly debt obligations.

“If you go on a holiday spending spree and raise your utilization from 8% to 60%, you may see a significant decrease in your score as well as an increase in your DTI,” says Zane.

Cash reserves are also important to most lenders.

“An underwriter will want to verify you have sufficient amounts for the down payment, closing cost, and reserves. You don't want to spend this amount of money on furniture, appliances, and holiday gifts,” Zane cautions.

The holidays are a great time to score great deals, but these deals can easily put your home purchase at risk.

“Many stores, both online and in person, will offer incentives to get you to buy right there and now. Sometimes, it's a massive discount and other times it's a rebate they'll give back to you. In any case, if you’re in the middle of buying a home, think twice before pursuing them,” says Ray Hicks, home loan specialist at Churchill Mortgage in Brentwood, TN.

Hicks cites a sitution that he sees often: You’re in the middle of the mortgage process. Then, your car breaks down or the dealership has some crazy New Year’s deal on a car you can't refuse, so you go for it. Your monthly payment on the shiny new toy puts you over the maximum DTI and you eventually learn you can't buy a home after all.

Here’s the moral of the story: To be as safe as possible this holiday season and ensure your home purchase goes through as planned, make only those purchases you can cover with your debit card or cash on hand.

“Normal expenses like groceries and gifts that fit in your budget are fine. New lines of credit and debt are usually not,” explains Zane.

#5395. Small Business Owners Reluctant to Take Next Step in Home-Buying Journey: Report

Buying a home is a daunting task for most people, even without considering the latest mortgage rates averaging above 7%.

But how consumers earn an income can greatly affect their transition from homebuyer to homeowner.

A recent survey conducted by mortgage lender Newrez found that small business owners are reluctant to take the next step in their home-buying journeys, while loan officers say that small business owners can qualify for a home much sooner than they realize.

The report found that 77% of mortgage lenders identified tax write-offs/deductions reducing their client’s qualifying income as one of the biggest challenges their small business owner clients face when trying to obtain a mortgage.

“If you’re self-employed, trying to determine if you’ll be eligible for a mortgage isn’t always as simple as asking, ‘How much does my business make?’” the report states. “How your income is documented, the loan program you’re considering and other qualification requirements can all affect your eligibility.”

Have an opinion on this topic? Please submit a Letter to the Editor.

Inflation—exacerbated by rising energy costs—has left little breathing room for the average consumer. The latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) from the Bureau of Labor Statistics found that the all-items index grew 0.4%, a slight decrease from the previous report, but still a “hotter than expected” estimate.

The CPI report attributed the jump to the increases in shelter inflation (up 0.3%), which contributed to over 30% of the increase. Core inflation also grew 0.3% in October, and has been growing at a constant rate for the past few months.

Other challenges that mortgage lenders highlighted include documentation or requirement-related factors. But having an inconsistent/variable income on a monthly basis can make it difficult to lock in a reasonable monthly mortgage payment.

Businesses of any size can feel the squeeze of high prices and operating costs. As of late, homebuilders point to rising labor costs and ongoing inflation pressures as significant challenges, with National Association of Home Builders Chief Economist Robert Dietz highlighting the effect of tariffs on building material costs.

Another aspect the survey dives into is the information available to small business owners. According to the report, 84% of mortgage originators stated that small business owners could qualify for a mortgage sooner than they realize.

“Originators who work with small business owners said awareness is as big a hurdle as financial qualifications,” the report continues. “Sixty-five percent said the two were equally significant, and 75% said lack of awareness was at least as significant, if not more so.”

In the same vein, 71% of mortgage lenders agreed that small business owners tended to be more anxious about the mortgage process than their W-2 counterparts. A significant majority (73%) of mortgage lenders also agree that small business owners assume they won’t qualify for a mortgage, even before speaking with a broker or lender.

“Small business owners have income that isn’t always fully captured by traditional documentation,” Bob Johnson, Newrez head of origination, stated. “Giving our broker partners and loan officers a variety of ways to meet borrowers’ needs helps us make home happen for more small business owners across the country.”

Rising operating costs are not the only issue small business owners face. The New York Times reported that Etsy—an online marketplace geared toward independent creators who sell handmade items and custom products—is facing a significant amount of backlash over a new policy change.

The policy in question reserves Etsy—and its third-party vendors—the right to use sellers’ content to develop and train AI models. Following the company’s new terms, many independent sellers withdrew from the platform, citing anger and dissatisfaction with the company’s turn toward AI, with one creator saying he won’t let his content “be stolen.”

Rather, the platform states that it is using AI actions such as “translating your listing descriptions so buyers around the world can discover your items, or featuring your listing photos in Etsy marketing campaigns to showcase your creative work.”

It’s unclear whether small business owners will flock back to Etsy’s platform, but the situation does shed light on hurdles small businesses may face.

“Mortgage lenders and originators can play an important role in helping these borrowers understand the available options and feel confident navigating the homebuying process,” Johnson added. “Building a business of your own should help you buy a home, not stand in your way.”

Desirae Sin is an assistant editor for RISMedia. She graduated from the University of Connecticut in 2025 with a double major in Journalism and Political Science. Prior to joining RISMedia, Desirae wrote stories geared toward policy issues for the Connecticut Mirror. She also worked as a staff writer for The Daily Campus, UConn's student-run newspaper.

Homebuyers are gaining leverage across much of the country, but assuming every seller is ready to accept a discount could leave them misreading their local market. Read more.

#5394. Open-weight models are the hottest thing in AI. Are they right for you?

For the first three years of the generative artificial intelligence boom, enterprise technology strategy relied on a simple rule: Select the premier frontier foundation model, route every prompt through its commercial application programming interface and pay the subscription premium for access to cutting-edge technology.

That monolithic approach is now collapsing under the weight of operational reality. Open-weight models, AI models whose trained parameters, or “weights,” are publicly available for others to download, run, customize and fine-tune, are the overnight sensation in an industry already moving at light speed.

These models don’t necessarily provide access to their training data, source code or training methods. They also carry a variety of license types that may restrict how they can be used commercially. But they offer choice, flexibility and cost advantages that the leading-edge “frontier” models such as OpenAI Group PBC’s ChatGPT and Anthropic PBC’s Claude don’t. For information technology organizations, they can be a respite from spiraling token costs.

The popularity of these models has soared as AI has matured and organizations have realized that not every use case demands the biggest and best solution. They come in various shapes and sizes, ranging from less than 1 billion to nearly 3 trillion parameters. Many are tuned for specific tasks, such as recognizing images or writing software. That gives organizations the flexibility to match the model to the job.

“Frontier intelligence is priced for the hardest problems, and most agent work isn’t hard,” said Dhruv Amin, co-founder of Anything, the business name of Create Inc. and developer of an AI-powered platform for building mobile and web applications. “Companies are chartering a jet to cross the street.”

“There are lots of tasks in customer self-service and employee self-service that need a smaller model,” said Dheeraj Pandey, chief executive officer of DevRev Inc., maker of a unified customer support, software development and engineering platform.

DevRev created an open, vendor-neutral benchmark to measure how reliably enterprise AI agents perform in realistic organizational environments. “We get almost the same accuracy and precision on enterprise tasks, whether you use the open-weight models or the frontier models,” he said.

The ascendancy of open-weight models has been breathtaking. Vercel Inc.’s monthly AI Gateway report found that their share of observed token traffic surged from 7% last December to 56% in August and that the models held eight of the 10 busiest spots on OpenRouter Inc.’s large language model ranking in August by token volume.

Three-year-old OpenRouter itself turned heads in August when it sold to Stripe Inc. for an eye-popping $7.5 billion. The firm’s technology connects developers and users with hundreds of AI models from dozens of providers through a single interface.

In September, Nvidia Corp. paid nearly $13 billion for Hugging Face Inc., which hosts more than 3 million models. “For most enterprises, the practical path to an open-weight model — evaluate, fine-tune, quantize, deploy — runs through that hub,” wrote Zeus Kerravala, principal analyst at ZK Research, referring to Hugging Face.

Enterprises aren’t abandoning frontier models. Rather, they’re learning to fit the model to the problem. None of the experts SiliconANGLE contacted believes open-weight models are a threat to the big players.

“All players can win because the market is growing and the number of places where it makes sense to deploy AI increases,” Amin said.

Cost is currently the principal driver of open-weight adoption. As AI use has evolved from question-and-response generative models to sophisticated multistep agentic workflows, inference costs have soared. Gartner Inc. predicts inference costs per agentic workflow will increase more than fivefold through 2028.

“They are quickly starting to rival even payroll expenses,” Amin said.

By most accounts, frontier models still offer the greatest power and range of usage options. But the gap is closing. Mozilla’s September State of Open-Source AI report put the capability gap between leading open-weight models and proprietary frontier models at roughly four months, down from 18 months just two years ago.

“The differences in quality are starting to be outweighed by the differences in cost,” wrote Ioana Hreninciuc, co-founder of inference platform Runware Ltd. She noted that though proprietary models still lead on top-tier reasoning, “you probably don’t need a frontier model for 80% of what you do.”

The pivot to open weights isn’t a zero-sum proposition. Low token prices can mask integration overhead, tool failures and operational risk. “Tokenomics,” or measuring, attributing and managing the cost of tokens, has become an essential information technology discipline.

In a Hyper Labs Inc. survey conducted by The Harris Poll, 86% of AI leaders said managing token expenses is as critical as containing cloud costs. More than three-quarters said they are directing routine tasks to smaller models to protect budgets, while 89% have redesigned AI initiatives after getting token shock.

“The whole world is trying to solve for tokenomics,” said Armando Franco, senior director of cloud and platform modernization at IT services provider TEKsystems Inc.

Experts say open-weight models are well-suited for repetitive, routine workloads. “Basically, they work best when the task is clear and it’s easy enough to check if the work was done correctly,” said Louis Amira, CEO of Circuit & Chisel Inc., an AI infrastructure and agentic commerce startup.

Karen Panetta, an IEEE Fellow and dean of graduate education at Tufts University School of Engineering, said open models are flourishing as technology leaders learn to match the engine to the task.

“If a bicycle will get you there, don’t pick the expensive sports car,” she said. “You have to ask: What problem you are trying to solve?” She asserted that for applications that don’t require 99.9% precision, organizations can achieve massive savings with compact models.

They’re also an attractive option when protecting customer data is a priority, since sensitive information never needs to leave the organization. “Customer data never, never goes into a frontier,” Scott Wallace, senior global director of solutions architecture at Digital Realty Inc., said in an interview with the Financial Times.

Sovereignty, or the ability to control and govern digital assets in line with local laws, security needs, and strategic interests, is a growing issue for organizations. A Linux Foundation survey last year found that 79% of AI leaders — and 86% in the U.S. — rate sovereignty as a strategic priority.

“What began as a specialized concern for highly regulated industries is rapidly becoming a strategic consideration for nearly every enterprise,” Paul Nashawaty, a principal analyst at theCUBE Research, wrote in a recent analysis.

Some early adopters are demonstrating impressive returns.

Advocates point to a shrinking capability gap, too, with some open-weight models nipping at the heels of the frontier alternatives. Beijing Moonshot AI Technology Co., Ltd.’s 2.8 trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.’s 2.4 trillion-parameter Qwen3.8-Max nearly match closed models on coding benchmarks, according to Stanford University’s Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Institute.

An agent built by Tenzai Inc. recently captured the top spot on HackerOne’s leaderboard using Z.ai Inc.’s GLM 5.2, generating 30% more findings per unit of computing power than a previous baseline using a proprietary model.

“What was the frontier 18 months ago is now well-mapped territory, and open-source models are closing the gap at a fraction of the cost” wrote Runware’s Hreninciuc.

Though such metrics explain open models’ ascendancy, the decision to use them isn’t open-and-shut. Experts cite four common myths that can mitigate the cost efficiencies.

One is the mistaken belief that open-weight models conflate with traditional open-source software and its permissive licenses. “This is a misnomer among many enterprises,” said Dr. Dorotea Baljević, EMEA Lead for AI Advisory at technology research and advisory firm Information Services Group. “There is licensing for these models in most cases, particularly for commercial usage.”

Although some, such as Qwen3, Mistral 3, Gemma 4 and DeepSeek V4, are covered by standard Apache or MIT licenses, terms and conditions vary. For example, Liquid AI Inc.’s open-weight models are free for commercial use only to organizations with less than $10 million in annual revenue.

“Other licenses require attribution, restrict certain application categories, or impose acceptable use policies, none of which carry a direct fee but all of which create legal exposure if ignored,” noted Bumu Technologies Inc., which does business as Nanobase.

Baljević said two hidden liabilities are data distribution rights for public training datasets used upstream and the evaluation, stability and legal audit costs that shift directly to the enterprise. “When using open-weight models, you need to lean in on understanding data distribution rights, copyright, contractual restrictions and consent,” she said. “In most cases, this carries costs.”

Evaluating models for accuracy, stability and explainability also falls to the user. With thousands of open-weight models available, the costs of a bake-off between multiple candidates can add up.

Baljević suggests organizations consider whether the model will be used internally or externally, the organization’s tolerance for accuracy, strategic fit and switching costs as evaluation criteria. Performance on public benchmarks also doesn’t guarantee a model will work well with an organization’s data, workflows and language.

Finance leaders may look at the 80% to 90% cost advantage of open-weight tokens and assume operational expenditures will drop proportionally. But tokens are only one part of the cost equation and not necessarily even the biggest one.

Organizations that plan to deploy models on their own infrastructure must bear the costs of integration, API development, IT infrastructure and human labor required for auditing and verification. A fraction of a cent saved on an inference call can be wiped out by the cost of a human expert spending a half-hour re-entering flawed database transactions.

Lack of visibility into how the model is operating can also produce sticker shock. A retry loop, in which an agent tries repeatedly to complete a failed task, can go on for hours or even days. The Wall Street Journal recently reported on a case in which an AI-generated out-of-office message at a San Francisco-based software company went into a loop that ultimately burned $10,000 a day in token costs.

If a cheap open-weight model fails a multi-system query or generates invalid JSON, it triggers automated retries that can consume millions of secondary tokens. The human expertise required to repair the transaction manually can erase months of token savings.

“The core software engineering required to test and integrate new models into the software stack is often the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities, APIs and such,” said Alex Bakker, an ISG distinguished analyst. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”

Using private graphics processing unit clusters eliminates external API fees, but self-hosting economics hinge on high, sustained utilization. Models that sit idle or at low usage levels consume power, create processing inefficiencies and incur costs if restarts are required.

Cast AI Group Inc. reported last spring that the average GPU utilization was 5% across thousands of clusters it monitored. Frontier models are usually a better option in that case. “Open models can be dramatically cheaper at high utilization, while frontier APIs remain cheaper for intermittent workloads because you aren’t paying for idle capacity,” said Arun Chandrasekaran, distinguished VP analyst at Gartner.

For intermittent workloads such as batch payroll processing or seasonal financial reporting, the organization pays 100% of capital expenses, power, cooling and depreciation while hardware idles.

“On-premises hosting wins when there is high, predictable 24/7 traffic where servers are constantly busy,” said Debojyoti Dutta, chief AI officer at Nutanix Inc. A hosted frontier model is a better choice “with spiky or lower traffic, where paying per token with zero setup cost is cheaper than renting idle hardware.”

When AI agents fail, the default reaction is to switch to a newer model, but benchmark data shows that approach is usually a dead end.

Most evaluation tests give agents relatively simple tasks and judge them mainly on whether they get the right answer. But real business environments are much more complicated. Agents must gather information from different systems, connect it correctly, handle growing amounts of data, and work within security rules.

This interface complexity is what usually breaks AI agents. DevRev estimates that moving an agent from clean test tools to real-world corporate use causes an 18% to 19% drop in accuracy. Upgrading the model improves performance by less than 1%.

“Every time a new model comes out, you need to re-evaluate your benchmarks, your models and your fine-tuning processes,” said Steven Yang, senior director of product management at Tanium Inc. That means better data integration is a more effective strategy than buying new models.

Though the open-weight option is viable for any company, experts say the best use cases are those where control, accountability and performance are paramount. The following three factors are at least as important as cost.

Compliance: Regulated industries have been held back from adopting AI over data residency and confidentiality concerns. Deploying open weights within enterprise data centers or virtual private clouds reduces the need for external data egress, ensures zero training data retention and allows for total physical isolation. The models also allow inspection of internal mechanics such as log-probabilities, token confidence scores and loss landscapes.

Training datasets, model weights and inference prompts never cross borders or leave the organization’s physical perimeter. That makes it easier to comply with strict data localization laws such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act in the U.S. and the General Data Protection Regulation in Europe. Local auditing and observability also aid in compliance with regulatory frameworks like the EU AI Act, which requires detailed logging, risk assessments and explainability.

But deploying on private infrastructure isn’t a cure-all. “You still have to maintain an aggressive data security posture around your processes because even open-weight models sometimes will take action trying to accomplish their tasks that could potentially violate some type of compliance rule,” said TEKSystems’ Franco.

Transparency: Understanding how models arrive at an answer is critical in many scenarios, particularly those involving safety, law and finance. “Open-weight models expose the math behind their answers,” said Brian Weiss, chief technology officer at document processing platform maker Hyperscience, the business name of Hyper Labs Inc. “You can use that to hold the model accountable for accuracy.”

In contrast, frontier APIs often obscure the equations used to generate probabilities, which are critical to assessing accuracy. Asking a model how confident it is in its answer may yield a subjective response. Open weights allow confidence scores to be scored against ground-truth outcomes for better reliability.

“People can take these models inside their organization, do some post-training and fine-tuning and have a customized model where they know the costs, where it’s sitting and what data is being sent to it,” said David DeSanto, CEO of Anaconda Inc., maker of an AI development platform.

“The future is an orchestrated ensemble of bounded, transparent, governed, cost-effective models,” Weiss said. “If I find a better model for a particular task, I can swap it out because I have the framework to do that.”

Performance: As organizations move from the relatively simple generative AI question-and-response metaphor to sophisticated multi-agent frameworks, latency issues can compound exponentially. For example, a 500-millisecond API delay across 50 sequential reasoning steps creates 25 seconds of cumulative latency, which would render many applications useless.

Executing open-weight models directly alongside operational databases or within containerized edge pods minimizes routing hops and rate limits. Distillation, which trains smaller, specialized open models from frontier “teacher” models, is faster.

Hyperscience reported that distillation delivers up to 97% cost reduction and four times faster inference, while retaining over 95% of the original model’s performance on designated tasks. Small models are faster and considerably cheaper than frontier LLMs.

Experts say constructing a business case for open-weight models requires understanding three major sources of hidden expense.

Complexity tax: Reasoning can break down when open-weight models interact with complex enterprise data at scale. The “Cartesian Shortcut” refers to a phenomenon in which AI models rely on workarounds learned during training rather than demonstrating a flexible understanding of the problem they’re trying to solve.

Google LLC researchers found that the models struggled with visual reasoning problems, such as solving mazes, when the data was presented in a circular rather than a grid layout. Leading models answered 69% to 83% of the square-grid problems correctly, but their accuracy fell to below 40% when the problems appeared in circular layouts.

The corollary to a business scenario is a multihop join across multiple systems. Models may “cheat” by collapsing field-level relationships into hierarchical groupings, generating massive data fabrications.

Human oversight remains critical: “For validation and rework, humans in the loop need to be taken into account on top of all the tokens you’re paying for already,” said TekSystems’ Franco.

Poor data quality: Foundation models can’t fix bad data, a fact that’s holding back AI adoption across the board. The Hyperscience/Harris Poll study found that 86% of IT leaders said dirty internal data is actively crippling GenAI performance.

Feeding error-strewn or outdated information into probabilistic models creates “context pollution,” the accumulation of irrelevant, redundant, outdated or contradictory information. When agents execute multistep database joins, system workflows or automated tool calls based on flawed data or ambiguous schemas, cascading errors can occur.

Sauce Labs Inc. Chief Technology Officer Anoop Tripathi recommends creating validated “golden datasets” for fine-tuning and evaluation. He also cautions architects against misapplying probabilistic AI to structured business logic. In other words, use models only where they add value and apply conventional (and cheaper) data processing to everything else.

Continuous evaluation: Selecting the right model out of thousands of open-weight alternatives requires ongoing evaluation against internal workloads rather than public leaderboards. That demands expensive MLOps, site reliability engineering and platform engineering skills.

Because new models are constantly being introduced and revised, Circuit & Chisel’s Amira recommends building custom testing harnesses that can quickly evaluate candidate models against business-relevant tasks.

Rather than treating open-weight adoption as an all-or-nothing choice, enterprise architects should bucket organizational tasks into distinct operational tiers. Don’t feed every problem into a token-hungry trillion-parameter model if a smaller, specialized one will do the trick.

“Organizations don’t give a heavyweight reasoning model a lightweight sorting job,” said Nutanix’s Dutta. “They divide their business workloads into tiers based on cost, speed and hardware footprint.”

Lower-tier workloads such as search, embeddings and document classification work well with inexpensive, compact open-weight and small language models. Sophisticated tasks such as autonomous reasoning and restructuring large, deeply entangled legacy software systems are better suited to commercial alternatives.

ISG’s Bakker believes the need for constant evaluation is the biggest impediment to open-weight adoption. “The core software engineering required to test and integrate new models into the software stack will likely be the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities and APIs,” he said. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”

Enterprise IT organizations must develop expertise in local model execution, containerized execution sandboxes and agent harness orchestration. Managing AI and agents safely “is, in the near future, going to be as important an indigenous knowledge as how to upgrade Windows,” said Gordon Allott, founder and CEO of private infrastructure provider nFOX Lab.

The shift toward open-weight models represents a permanent maturation of enterprise IT from experimentation to disciplined financial and architectural management. Success is no longer about raw model parameter size or benchmark ranking, but matching the model to the task. That’s a discipline that was barely on the roadmap a year ago.

At the start of the year, there was no way enterprises were going to touch open-weight models, Brad Maltz, head of AI factory solutions at Dell Technologies Inc., said in a November interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE’s streaming media platform. “People were pretty wrong about that. I think the open-weight movement is the future.”
