#5392. EXCLUSIVE: Watch Chip and Joanna Gaines Turn a Stressful Mansion Demo Into an ‘SNL’ Skit in Exclusive New Clip

When Chip and Joanna Gaines started “sweating” over their massive remodel being documented on “Fixer Upper: Chip Bought a Mansion,” they both leaned into the laughs to turn a challenging moment into a scene out of “a "Saturday Night Live" skit.”

The six-episode spinoff series, which is due to premiere on Dec. 27 on Magnolia Network and HGTV, sees the husband and wife team take on what they deem “the biggest fixer we’ve ever done”: a 15,000-square-foot mansion that sits on a 5.7-acre lot in their hometown of Waco, TX.

Chip had unilaterally decided to purchase the outdated manse three years ago. Once he realized the palatial investment property had more issues than anticipated, he turned to Joanna for help transforming the space. Adding to the pressure was a three-month timeline to transform the place.

In an exclusive clip shared with Realtor.com from the back-to-back premiere episodes, the Gainses hold a pre-renovation open house with two of their designer friends to get a fresh perspective and some professional guidance on what changes are necessary.

The four experts gather in the mansion’s oversized living room that Jo previously described as something out of “Beauty and the Beast” due to the high ceiling, multiple decorative columns, and golden paint covering the walls. The room is anchored by honey-toned hardwood floors and adorned with elaborate trim, molding, and millwork throughout.

Standing in front of a cream-colored fireplace with a sprawling floral arrangement on its mantel, Chip asks the women what task they want him to tackle.

“What curtains would you like me to demo?” he inquires.

When one of the designers comments that Chip “needs a man job” to do, he signals he’s totally up for the challenge.

Joanna explains that “they really want to see the room without curtains,” so Chip makes his way toward a wall of windows and French doors that are concealed by a peachy-orange, grid-patterned window covering lined with pom-poms and tassels.

As the impromptu demo day begins to unfold, Jo nervously places her hands on her head while Chip confidently tugs on one side of the curtain.

“This is turning into a ‘Saturday Night Live’ skit,” Joanna says. “I’m sweating.”

“I feel like this is going to be totally doable,” Chips responds.

Chip’s prediction is correct. The curtain comes down easily, so Joanna praises her husband and directs him to continue.

“My hero! OK, do the other thing,” she says.

Chip proceeds, but he quickly discovers the second side requires a bigger effort to bring down the drapery due to the metal track that held up the coverings in the first place.

“Oh, God. There was a little more to that one,” admits Chip.

Jo and the designer guests are pleased with what’s exposed. Natural light pours into the large living space from the glass doors and windows that now clearly have a view of the property’s mature trees and a covered patio built with beautiful red brick.

“Yes, I’m feeling it. Pretty awesome,” the designers say.

Typically, it’s Chip who often displays his silly side on work sites, while Jo plays the part of his professional-minded foil. However, pleased with the results of the curtain reveal, a noticeably relieved Joanna momentarily pivots from interior design to fashion design.

“Style me. I want a dress,” she says as she wraps herself up in the downed curtains with an assist from Chip.

“Well, twist. Turn, turn, turn. There you go. Now that’s it. Yeah, just that. Wow,” he comments when he sees the finished frock on his wife.

“Very Italian. That’s cool. Pretty awesome,” notes the admiring group.

After Jo models her new look, more of the mansion’s ground floor is visible. Just past the double glass door entrance of the home, a staircase with an ornate wrought-iron railing leads to the second floor, and a black table fills space in the grand foyer.

Behind Jo, a rendering of her vision for the room shows the area styled with an oversized mirror above the fireplace and several comfy chairs placed opposite a couch. With that plan in place, she lays out the next steps for the rest of the residence.

“So I think at this point, it’s mainly the kitchen, and then it’s just a refresh,” states Joanna.

The pair of experts agree and reassure the Gainses that a less is more approach is the way to go.

“You don’t need to add any panelling. You don’t need to add anything. This is just, paint it. Simplify. Just, like, slow the roll, relax. Yeah, you got this,” they say.

As the action begins on “Fixer Upper: Chip Bought a Mansion,” the upgraded Waco Lake estate is currently listed on the market by Amanda Nesbitt of Magnolia Realty. While one qualified buyer was reportedly turned off by the new renovations, the $7.39 million price tag will hopefully make the rollercoaster of emotions Chip and Joanna have experienced throughout the process well worth the ride.

“Fixer Upper: Chip Bought a Mansion” premieres Sunday, Dec. 27 at 9 p.m. on Magnolia Network and HGTV and streams the next day on discovery+ and HBO Max.

#5391. Bronwyn Newport Gives Estranged Husband Todd Bradley a Tour of Her New Salt Lake City Home: ‘It’s Time To Move On’

Bronwyn Newport has a new Utah home—and she just gave fans and her estranged husband a tour of the dwelling.

On the Nov. 25 episode of “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City,” the fashion blogger received a visit from Todd Bradley, her estranged husband. The couple announced their separation in December 2025 after nine years of marriage.

The tech investor initially said he “just wanted to come by and see” Newport and her new home, but soon admitted that he had stopped by to apologize after an explosive conversation the pair had shared over dinner in the previous episode.

In a confessional interview, Newport admitted that Bradley had reached out to smooth things over after their last dramatic conversation, but that she had not yet been ready to talk.

Instead, she extended an invitation to her new property.

“I invited him to the house because it’s a smaller, nicer way for me to say, ‘This is what I’m doing, and this is the direction I’m going,’ without saying things that are hard for him to hear,” she explained.

Bradley had not yet seen the home in person, although he said it looked nice in the photographs he had looked at. Newport offered him a tour of “some of it.”

“The whole basement is going to be Gwen and Logan’s domain,” she explained, referring to her 20-year-old daughter and her daughter’s boyfriend.

The ground level of the home—which was empty at the time of the impromptu tour—featured hardwood flooring, an open-concept plan, a fireplace, and plenty of windows. There were also recessed lights and a glass sliding door, which led to an outdoor space.

“Upstairs is really Muzzy’s space,” Newport said as she walked up the steps of the yet-to-be-furnished home with Bradley.

She said that the upstairs space—in which her mother, who goes by Muzzy, will reside in—includes a kitchen and essentially functions as an apartment.

Finally, Newport brought Bradley into her primary squite, a light-filled space lined with expansive windows. The room features an en suite bathroom with a walk-in shower and tub, which she said she’s very excited about, as she and Bradley had previously discussed a remodel of the home they shared, which would have included a lavish bathtub.

There’s also a well-organized walk-in closet, though fans of the show will understand that it’s likely not going to be enough space for Newport’s massive wardrobe.

In a Sept. 30 interview with Vulture, she did a photo shoot in a storage unit she has in the nearby suburb of Millcreek, UT, which serves the sole purpose of storing all of her clothes and accessories.

“It’s very weird to give Todd a tour of a house that’s going to be mine and not his,” she said during the episode. “There is a part of me that feels I need to be totally free and separate of Todd, but there’s a part of me that is scared to death to not have Todd be a part of my life at all.”

Newport and Bradley had moved into a sprawling Salt Lake City home not long before she joined the cast. In a September 2024 tour of the previous abode, she said they had been living there for a year and a half after moving from nearby Park City.

In the video, Newport revealed she came across the home in a viral listing. It had originally featured a sunken floor with a "psychedelic carpet,” which she said she “liked and really wanted to keep.”

Per Bradley’s wishes, they upgraded the space to have sleek hardwood floors.

“I love a project, so I wanted this old, haunted house in Salt Lake that we could remodel,” she said. “When we first came in, I was obsessed with this living room, the view of Salt Lake and the mountains, all the light, and a big space for me to have tons of parties all of the time.”

The home was boldly decorated, with a royal blue kitchen, rainbow couches in the living room, and a color-drenched lavender office space, with built-in shelving filled with art and designer accessories.

After their separation, Newport and Bradley sold the home for an undisclosed amount in an off-market deal.

The transaction has become a storyline this season of “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City,” with friend of the cast Britani Bateman flexing her real estate expertise to suggest that the home was priced too high when it was on the market, and that Newport must not have received the 50-50 split from the sale that she had claimed to get.

#5390. Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Fully Connected event

AI infrastructure economics are increasingly defined by the cost of producing intelligence rather than acquiring computing capacity.

As inference demand outpaces training growth, infrastructure providers and their customers must increase productive computing time without a corresponding rise in operating costs. The emergence of continuously learning agents and physical AI applications is further complicating that equation. For CoreWeave Inc., the changing workload mix is altering the economics of infrastructure delivery, according to theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and John Furrier.

“What you’re seeing CoreWeave do strategically is they’re expanding out beyond compute,” Vellante said. “They’ve got networking; they’ve got storage. They’ve got this software layer, which is observability. They’ve got security in there. They’ve got this closed-loop system between evaluation, observation [and] runtime curating … that’s sort of how they’re saying their software layer is now intact.”

During the Fully Connected event, Vellante and Furrier spoke with CoreWeave executives, technology partners and customers about the technical and economic realities of running artificial intelligence at production scale. (* Disclosure below.)

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video analysis with Dave Vellante and John Furrier:

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s exclusive coverage of this event:

The commercial value of inference depends on both token volume and delivery speed. Nvidia Corp.’s Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator, which works with its Vera Rubin platform, is attracting interest in financial technology and other sectors that require real-time processing, according to Ian Buck, vice president and general manager of hyperscale and HPC at Nvidia.

“Data centers have a natural cap, and that cap is actually their power,” he told theCUBE. “With every generation of GPU, we make sure that our tokens per watt is upwards of 10 times more efficient. In fact, we saw that with Blackwell — we got, in the end, a 30x improvement in tokens per watt.”

Memory management adds another dimension to AI infrastructure economics as agents engage in increasingly lengthy interactions. A single session involving 500,000 tokens can consume between 5% and 10% of a graphics processing unit’s memory. Retaining session context in persistent storage can reduce costly recalculations, according to Alon Horev, co-founder and chief technology officer of Vast Data Inc.

“You can move a session from one busy GPU to one less busy GPU and move KV cache either over the network or read it from Vast,” he told theCUBE. “Once you look at inference as a distributed problem where you have the opportunity to use GPU memory, CPU memory and Vast across a fleet of machines, you have more optionality and you have more optimized scheduling.”

For AI-native startups, specialized cloud providers offer an alternative to owning capital-intensive infrastructure. LlamaIndex Inc. processes millions of document pages daily for customers in finance, legal services and insurance. Inference accounts for about 75% of its workloads, with training accounting for the remainder, according to Jerry Liu, co-founder and chief executive officer of LlamaIndex.

“We serve a lot of different customers at extremely persistent and also spiky workloads,” he told theCUBE. “We really, really need to make sure that we have the right capacity to serve our customers without getting throttled.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Ian Buck:

Protecting AI infrastructure investments starts on the factory floor. Dell Technologies Inc. has developed modular rack designs to accommodate different power and cooling configurations. Its collaboration with CoreWeave includes integrating the cloud provider’s Racky management software into factory testing and improving liquid-cooling leak detection, according to Sarat Krishnan, director of PowerEdge AI architecture and systems development engineering at Dell.

“It becomes increasingly expensive to remediate and fix something as you go later on in the manufacturing process; [it] becomes extremely expensive if you have to replace something in the data center,” he told theCUBE. “What we have done over the last two years is shift our most complex diagnostics — the ones that are going to capture true hardware failures — further and further left.”

At Cognition AI Inc., continuous model improvement involves training across data centers in multiple countries. The company’s Devin software engineering agent now handles tasks ranging from code development to resolving production issues, according to Chen Goldberg (pictured, left), executive vice president of product and engineering at CoreWeave, and Silas Alberti (right), head of research and founding team at Cognition. To support these learning systems, CoreWeave introduced Forge, a platform that connects inference, evaluation and model refinement and incorporates Agent Lens to trace agent activity.

“If you run a big training run, you’re not just looking at the GPUs, but you also want uptime,” Alberti said during the event. “If just one replica goes down, the whole training run goes down. I think a very important metric is getting to this 99.99% reliability.”

For International Business Machines Corp., the power and cooling demands of newer hardware helped drive its decision to work with CoreWeave. The relationship has since expanded to include joint engineering around identity management and workload isolation through CoreWeave Sandboxes. IBM also benchmarks the performance impact of security controls to inform architectural decisions, according to Brian Belgodere, senior technical staff member at IBM.

“This is a supply chain problem, top to bottom,” Belgodere told theCUBE. “It’s not just the hardware: it’s the firmware, kernel levels, code, your data provenance. Then you get into the whole world of agents, your images. It is an absolute provenance problem.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Brian Belgodere:

For organizations deploying physical AI, implementation time is a key consideration in AI infrastructure economics. Aston Martin F1, whose race cars generate a million data points per second each, operates under strict budget constraints and development deadlines. CoreWeave’s forward-deployed engineering approach brings specialized expertise to those operations, according to Richard Ahlfeld, senior vice president of physical AI at CoreWeave, and Eric Ernst, commercial technology ambassador of AMR GP Ltd., trading as Aston Martin F1.

“We really need people that can be outside of the car development phase and come in with the fresh knowledge of what’s happening in this industry that is moving extremely quickly,” Ernst said during the event. “You can build as many processes as you want, call it agile, whatever you want. You cannot stop that process. You got to hit a deadline.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Richard Ahlfeld and Eric Ernst:

Walden Robotics Inc. uses large-scale virtual simulation to prepare robots for physical deployment. Its robots have been working full production shifts alongside humans since May, performing tasks such as machine tending, parts kitting and subassembly, according to Adrien Gaidon, co-founder and chief strategy officer of Walden Robotics, and John Mancuso, vice president of field engineering at CoreWeave Inc.

“If you’re changing things and you have machines that cannot change and continuously learn in deployment, then you become a burden,” Gaidon told theCUBE. “We do machines that continuously learn from deployment and adapt so customers can change their mind and improve the process and give them the superpower to change even more and faster.”

Here’s theCUBE’s full video discussion with John Mancuso and Adrien Gaidon:

#5389. FHFA Increases Conforming Loan Limit by $22k for 2027

The Federal Housing and Finance Authority (FHFA) has announced a new conforming loan limit (the maximum dollar amount for a conventional mortgage) for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac mortgages in 2027. The new limit for one-unit properties will be $855,400, up $22,650 from 2026’s limit.

The Housing and Economic Recovery Act (HERA) requires FHFA to adjust the Enterprises’ baseline conforming loan limit each year to reflect the change in the average U.S. home price, according to a release. As the organization’s research found that home prices were up 2.72% on average from Q3 2025 to Q3 2026, the FHFA said that the conforming loan limit has increased on the same baseline.

In addition, high cost areas (where 115% of the local median home value exceeds the baseline conforming loan limit) have a higher limit due to HERA, according to a release. The high cost area limit sits at a ceiling of 150% the baseline limit, which in 2027 will be $1,283,100.

The FHFA also noted special statutory provisions establishing different loan limits for Alaska, Hawaii, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands. In these areas, the baseline loan limit and the ceiling loan limit for one-unit properties will be $1,283,100 and $1,924,650, respectively.

Due to rising home values, the FHFA stated that the conforming loan limit will be higher in all but 24 U.S. counties or county equivalents.

#5388. After Seeing Her Neighbor Priced Out, She Wrote a Novel Where Zoning Codes Are ‘the Villain’

Author Rachel Pastan tackles housing affordability in her latest novel, “We’re So Lucky To Live Here,” which she wrote after her neighbor was priced out of town.

The novelist drew on her experience chairing a housing affordability task force in Swarthmore, PA, to write the book, which follows a late-20s woman who challenges zoning laws and so-called NIMBY neighbors in a fight to remain in her childhood home.

The novel addresses housing issues in a fictional Philadelphia suburb based on Swarthmore, the town where Pastan has lived since 2000. A quaint borough of some 6,000 residents that is centered on the college of the same name, Swarthmore features a housing stock consisting mainly of single-family homes on tree-lined streets.

Pastan and her husband bought a modest single-family house there on the combined salaries of an author and professor, which she acknowledges they couldn’t do if they moved there in the 2020s. As of October, the median listing price in Swarthmore was $499,000, according to Realtor.com® data.

Pastan’s longtime friend lived with her husband and four kids in an apartment while saving up to buy a house in town, she recalls.

When her friend began looking to buy, she realized her family’s goal of owning a home locally wasn’t attainable. This was during the COVID-19 pandemic, when houses in small towns and suburbs rose to a premium.

Pastan’s friend and her family relocated to North Carolina to realize their dreams of homeownership.

Pastan says she regrets when friends are forced to leave due to a lack of affordable housing. Not only does she lose a neighbor, but her community also loses socioeconomic diversity, which she sees as necessary to a healthy and well-rounded community.

Pastan knew her next novel needed to take on housing affordability. That’s when Gwen’s story in “We’re So Lucky To Live Here” came to her.

Pastan’s novel focuses on the ways in which young people in particular are affected by and adapt to housing affordability.

After inheriting her mother’s home, Gwen needs to figure out how to afford her new housing situation on the small salary she earns from her career in the arts.

“I’m interested in the way people from younger generations seem interested in making family and bringing people together under one roof,” Pastan tells Realtor.com, explaining her decision to make the protagonist a woman in her late 20s.

Pastan believes that housing affordability issues aren’t exclusive to young people trying to become homeowners.

“It’s a problem for people in their 30s, people with kids, older people who are retired and trying to stay in their homes. The affordability crisis in housing affects everybody at all levels,” she says.

Pastan says she sees “zoning codes as the villain in the novel.”

The protagonist Gwen enacts different plans to afford the home she inherited. She invites roommates to share expenses and attempts to build an accessory dwelling unit in the backyard. Each attempt is thwarted by local codes.

Pastan has campaigned for five years to legalize ADUs in Swarthmore, as part of her work on the housing task force. She sees ADUs and the conversion of single-family homes into multiunit buildings as paths to make Swarthmore affordable to more people.

In Swarthmore, zoning code limits who is allowed to live together in a single-family home, requiring residents be related by marriage, birth, or adoption, with the addition of no more than two unrelated tenants.

At a point, Gwen’s elderly neighbors lash out at her for having too many roommates, stating that local ordinances prohibit it. But Gwen sees her friends as a kind of family, showing differing attitudes among generations and how necessity challenges zoning.

“Housing policy touches on so many aspects of our lives,” Pastan says, and her novel shows how housing affordability and policy affects a community at all levels.

#5387. EXCLUSIVE: This Miami Condo Tower Will Offer a Concierge That Can Find a Sitter, Stock Your Fridge, and Arrange Dinner for You

Imagine coming home to a stocked fridge and a chef already making dinner. At Cipriani Residences Miami, an 85-story luxury condo tower under construction in Brickell, that’s how a busy weeknight could look.

Residents will be able to ask the building’s concierge to find a sitter for their kids for an evening meeting, arrange to have dinner served in their apartment, or line up someone to look after the dog.

For developer Mast Capital, the appeal lies in how many items residents could cross off their to-do lists with a call to someone downstairs.

Michael Patrizio, the company’s managing director, tells Realtor.com® that the team considered who would be buying a home in the tower before deciding what services to offer.

“When we started planning Cipriani Residences Miami, we really thought about how people live today and what would genuinely make their lives easier,” Patrizio says. “Our buyers are busy. Many are running businesses, raising families, traveling frequently, or balancing all three.”

For someone who splits time between homes, one of the most appealing services might be the easiest to overlook on a tour of a luxury building. A buyer who spends weeks away can ask the concierge to find someone to keep the plants alive until they return.

“They don’t necessarily want more amenities just for the sake of having them. They want to know that when they get home, things are taken care of,” Patrizio says. “That could mean having someone look after their plants while they’re away, arranging childcare, coordinating housekeeping, or having dinner prepared and served in their own residence.”

A dedicated director of residences and a Cipriani residential concierge will help coordinate those requests. Owners getting ready for a business trip, for instance, could arrange to have a suit altered, shoes shined, and transportation booked through the building.

“It’s those everyday conveniences that can make a tremendous difference,” Patrizio adds. “We’ve seen particular interest in services that give residents more flexibility and allow them to spend less time managing their homes and more time enjoying them. That’s really what we wanted to accomplish.”

Cipriani will bring its hospitality experience to the dinner table, too. Plans call for a private restaurant where residents can head downstairs for a meal, along with in-residence dining for nights when the kids are already in bed.

Owners hosting a party can arrange catering, right down to having fresh flowers delivered and arranged before guests arrive.

The Miami tower has counterparts in other cities. Waldorf Astoria Residences New York and Aman New York bring hotel-style service to residential addresses in Manhattan. In Boston, buyers can find a similar approach at Four Seasons Private Residences One Dalton.

“I think the definition of luxury has changed quite a bit, especially in Miami,” Patrizio says. “We’re seeing more people move here from places like New York and California who are accustomed to having services and conveniences readily available.”

In his view, what buyers expect from a Miami condo depends in part on how much of the year they plan to spend there.

“Miami isn’t just a place where people come for the weekend or spend a few months out of the year anymore,” he says. “They’re moving their families here, building businesses and establishing their primary homes. That changes what they expect from a residential building.”

For a family settling into Brickell full time, the service menu covers everything from laundry and personal shopping to car detailing and tech support. Residents can also arrange personal training sessions and in-home salon or spa treatments. The plans even include access to on-call emergency medical care.

“Having a beautiful apartment and great amenities is important, but being able to get help with childcare, have your groceries stocked before you arrive home, or arrange dinner without leaving your residence is a different level of convenience,” Patrizio says.

“Time has become one of the biggest luxuries, and I think developers who recognize that are going to have a real advantage,” he adds. “At Cipriani Residences Miami, we wanted to create a place where residents can enjoy the best parts of living in Miami without having to worry about all the little things that come with managing a busy household.”

#5386. AI infrastructure stocks continue their slide, but Anthropic closes higher

Investors continued to offload artificial intelligence infrastructure stocks today, but Anthropic PBC recouped some of its losses from earlier this week.

The AI selloff reportedly began in August. It accelerated on Nov. 17, the day Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang resigned over his affair with a former executive of Megaspeed, a cloud provider under investigation over alleged export control violations. Huang returned to the helm of the chipmaker Monday.

Nvidia closed at $173.73 the day before Huang’s resignation. It dropped as low as $125 during the executive’s two-week hiatus and surged 30% on Monday, the day he returned. Nvidia lost some of its recent gains in today’s trading session: Its share price closed 3.8% lower.

Other AI chip stocks have also taken a hit. Broadcom Inc. closed a small fraction of a percent lower than yesterday, while Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Intel Corp. fell 1.6% and 0.6%, respectively.

The semiconductor stock that logged the biggest drop today is Ambarella Inc., a relatively low-profile maker of AI image analysis chips. Its accelerators are used by edge devices to process footage from their cameras. Ambarella dropped 19.8% today after closing 19% lower yesterday.

The stock’s decline was driven not so much by the broader AI selloff, but rather the weak earnings that Ambarella posted on Tuesday. The company missed expectations across the board. Ambarella said that some customers had canceled or delayed orders to mitigate the financial impact of soaring memory prices.

Micron Inc., one of the world’s top memory chip suppliers, saw its market capitalization drop more than 4.5% today. That’s despite CEO Sanjay Mehrotra’s recent disclosure that the company has already sold out 75% of its 2027 manufacturing capacity. According to the executive, the gap between memory demand and supply is only set to increase next year.

Companies downstream from chipmakers in the AI data center supply chain fared better. Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. ended the trading session 1.8% higher after dipping into the red earlier today, while Dell Technologies Inc. gained 0.64%.

In contrast, the major cloud providers weren’t left out of today’s selloff. Amazon.com Inc., the cloud market’s largest player, closed 3% lower. Microsoft Corp. and Google LLC dropped 1.25% and 2%, respectively. Oracle Corp., which trails the three companies in market share but has emerged as an important AI infrastructure provider, took the biggest hit: It’s down 5% from yesterday.

Anthropic ended the trading session with a 1% gain. The company thereby recouped some of yesterday’s losses, which pushed its stock below its $80 debut price. Anthropic went public last week through a record-setting offering that raised more than $93 billion.

Overall, the tech-heavy Nasdaq lost 0.6% while the S&P 500 slid 0.25%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 0.33%.

#5385. Why is Crypto Down Today? BTC Under $60K: How Low Will It Go?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Why is crypto down again? The cryptocurrency market is firmly in the red on Wednesday, November 25, 2026. Total market capitalization has slipped to around $2.02 trillion, down roughly 1.8–2% over the past 24 hours, while the Fear & Greed Index sits deep in Extreme Fear territory near 13/100.

Traders are growing disillusioned with the crypto market after weeks of downside sell pressure that has seen Bitcoin crash nearly -30% to under $60,000. Many are left wondering what could reverse the market’s course as we head toward 2027.

Bitcoin (BTC) is trading near $58,000–$58,400, down approximately 3% on the day and struggling to regain the $60,000 level after briefly testing higher earlier in the week.

Ethereum (ETH) sits around $1,630–$1,640, off about 3.3–3.5%. Solana (SOL) is softer still at roughly $66.80–$67.30, down around 4%. XRP is near $0.89–$0.90 (down ~2.5%), and BNB trades around $533–$536 (down ~2.5%).

Most other large-cap altcoins are also lower, reflecting weak market breadth. These levels follow Bitcoin’s failure to hold gains sparked by the recent Nvidia-related rebound, leaving the market on the back foot heading into month-end.

🚨 THE MARKET IS CRASHINGThe Nasdaq is down over 3%, the S&P 500 over 2% and Nvidia about 8%, all within minutes of the open. The VIX is back above 30.Here's why:1. New tariffsThe Trump administration just announced 20% tariffs on China, the EU and 12 other countries.… pic.twitter.com/JeWavoJwQC

The primary driver remains persistent institutional selling through U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs. November has already set a record for monthly outflows, with figures ranging from about $4.71Bn to nearly $5Bn depending on the data provider.

BlackRock’s IBIT has led the redemptions on multiple sessions, including large single-day withdrawals exceeding $500M earlier in the week and continued outflows of roughly $230M more recently. What was once a reliable source of demand has flipped into a consistent headwind.

Broader risk-off sentiment is amplifying the pressure. A sharp sell-off in Asian markets, including a roughly 6% drop in South Korea’s KOSPI and heavy losses for SoftBank, spilled into global risk assets. Technology and AI-related stocks, which had briefly rallied on news of Jensen Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia, quickly faded.

Crypto continues to trade as a high-beta risk asset, moving closely with equities as investor risk appetite contracts. Macro factors are also weighing heavily. Markets are pricing in high odds of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December, with elevated Treasury yields reducing the relative appeal of non-yielding assets like Bitcoin.

Reports of potential new U.S. tariffs targeting multiple trading partners have added another layer of uncertainty. Thin liquidity around the Thanksgiving holiday period may also be magnifying moves.

In short, the market faces a classic mix of sustained ETF outflows, cooling equity momentum, tighter monetary-policy expectations, and residual geopolitical/trade noise. Sentiment has deteriorated to the point where any bounce is being sold rather than chased.

Despite the heavy atmosphere, several catalysts could stabilize or reverse the decline. Today’s U.S. economic data, particularly PCE inflation and GDP figures, will be closely watched.

Softer-than-expected readings that reduce the probability of aggressive Fed tightening could quickly improve risk appetite across stocks and crypto. A slowdown or reversal in ETF outflows would be an important positive signal.

Even a return to modest net inflows would suggest institutional selling is exhausting and that larger players are beginning to accumulate at these lower levels.

On-chain data has already shown some large-wallet accumulation in recent weeks even as ETF products bled, hinting that longer-term holders may be positioning ahead of a potential recovery.

Bitcoin and Ethereum look deeply oversold on shorter timeframes, with RSI readings in the low-to-mid 20s in some analyses. Extreme fear readings have historically preceded relief rallies, especially when price approaches prior support zones.

Any constructive regulatory development, clearer institutional adoption news, or a rebound in technology stocks could also help shift momentum. Thinner holiday liquidity means volatility is likely to remain elevated in either direction.

While the near-term setup remains cautious and further downside is possible if risk assets continue to weaken, extreme sentiment, oversold technical conditions, and potential macro relief provide a plausible path to stabilization once the current wave of selling pressure eases.

Crypto markets have repeatedly demonstrated resilience after periods of heavy institutional outflows and macro headwinds; whether that pattern reasserts itself in the coming sessions will depend heavily on the data and a shift in broader risk appetite.

#5384. What Next-Gen Real Estate Leaders Are Leaving Behind and Embracing Instead

Above, from left, Eric Fite, Jack Markham, Marisela Harper, Lori Muller and Adrian Provost

“All the technology in the world doesn’t matter unless it makes a fundamental impact on the relationship with the client, the way we serve them. That’s our true north.”

That was the sentiment summed up by Eric Fite, COO of CENTURY 21 Judge Fite Company in Dallas/Fort Worth, when moderating a recent panel of up-and-coming brokerage leaders about what old ways they are leaving behind and what innovative new approaches they are bringing to the fore.

AI and technology and how they can best be used dominated the discussion, but panelists also shared some of the ways they are reimagining traditional business practices to support their agents in the session titled, “Next-Gen Leaders and Their Powerful New Approach to Business,” held this past October at RISMedia’s CEO Exchange in Washington, D.C.

In addition to Fite, the panel included Marisela Harper, broker/owner of ClearView Realty; Adrian Provost, CEO of ONE Terminus & LEVEL; Lori Muller, president of Fathom Realty; and Jack Markham, chief marketing officer at Inside Real Estate.

The group also shared insights into how they are positioning their tech stacks and CRMs, how they are viewing their data and data ownership and control,as well as the future of AI and how it can assist agents through automation.

“I think everybody’s realizing that the CRM is not necessarily your tech stack,” said Markham when asked what old beliefs most forward-thinking brokerages have already abandoned. “Traditionally, you would pick a CRM, and that’s where your data is; that’s who owns the workflows. But quite honestly, the smartest brokers are realizing that the tech stack is way more than your CRM.

“Most teams are running two to three CRMs. And that’s not because everybody loves using multiple CRMs. They do it because it’s a fear of loss. They do it because if I drop a tech stack, if I drop a tool, I don’t want to lose my data. And so they’re doing it as insurance. So I think most of the smart brokers today are realizing they don’t need more tools in the tech stack. They don’t need another tool, another app. What they need is something to absorb the tech stack, something that’s going to empower their data so their agents think less about where they log in and more about how to drive conversations.”

Provost said he views the “tech stack,” or the set of software tools, apps and technologies a company uses, as more of a folder, and a platform as more of an operating system.

“Ultimately, what I look for is how (tech) helps close certain loops that lead to that appointment-to-close loop, and then to that close-to-repeat-and-referral-business. I think that if it’s something that isn’t touching one of those or enhancing the agent’s ability to perform, then it probably doesn’t really belong in the tech or in the platform.”

Fite then turned the conversation to AI, asking panelists how they are using it and consumer behavior data to identify when and how an agent should engage a consumer.

“With consumer behavior data, that data is your opportunity,” Muller said. “It’s your opportunity to be strategic with what you’re going to do with it, how you’re going to utilize it. And then AI is the actual action step. It’s how you take action with that data to create a result.”

Markham said it’s all about control over data.

“The uncomfortable question for most brokers is, if you decided to leave your tools or your tech stack, could you take your data with you? And the answer most likely for most brokers in the industry is no,” he said. “They find out far too late that they can’t take it with them. Real ownership of data means you control that data no matter what CRM or tech tool you’re using.”

On a question about what work AI should be doing for a human, Provost said:

“I look at it from an operational standpoint. How can AI assist me and my agents in enhancing our service to our clients? And in my case, my clients being the agent. And so I think that humans need to always be in the loop. There should never be one point where they’re disconnected, but it should be streamlined, and we should be able to have AI connect components that don’t normally talk to one another so we can perform better and elevate that entire experience for whoever’s on the opposite end of it.”

Muller added that AI can help with automating transaction management, marketing solutions, social media, communication or “B- and C-level” operational tasks, while leaving more time for the most important aspect of the business—client relationships.

“No matter who tries to destroy the real estate industry, you can’t take the relational side away from the Realtor® and the consumer. AI is not going to do it. Technology’s not going to do it. That’s the most important thing we have to look at,” she said.

How does the next generation of real estate business leaders view traditional ways of supporting agents, or “loving on them,” as the panel discussed?

“We really do everything so strategically to love on the agent, down to when we built our office four years ago,” said Harper. “We built this big hub and we put our offices right where people that come in can see us. And that’s done on purpose. We have our staff completely trained to love on the agent. We also train our mentors to love on the agents. And when I say love, that’s really being intentionally present with them, spending the time to go to their weddings, go to the baby showers, attend the funerals because that’s a time when they really need just someone to be there for them.”

She added, “And one of the most important things on that contact card is the agent’s birthday. And that might seem so silly, but when I open my calendar for the day, I see whose birthday it is and that’s the first phone call I make just to call them and wish them a happy birthday. Of course, we do the birthday cards and the gift card and all of that, but the call just to wish them happy birthday, see how they’re doing, it goes over so well. They absolutely love it.”

Here are some more notable quotes from the session:

What’s most important when an agent leaves the brokerage?

Lori Muller: When an agent leaves, sometimes they leave because they think the grass is greener on the other side, and they get over there and it’s not. So I think it’s super important to have some type of exit strategy when an agent leaves and have a conversation to say, “Hey, what could we have done better? What was the situation that caused you to leave?” And it’s a teaching moment for both people. We also just recently did a comeback campaign where we called agents that have left over the last two years, and we have had almost a 25% return rate.

Are we heading toward a world where technology becomes table stakes and culture, service and execution become the real differentiators?

Jack Markham: I think you could take two people and give them the same tech stack, and what’s really going to separate them is not necessarily the tools that you’re using. It’s once you plug in your data, right? Once you plug in those relationships, once you plug in the trust, once you plug in the consumer behaviors that you’ve been tracking and the history behind that, it becomes your thumbprint. What’s unique and can’t be copied is all the history there. It’s all the relationships, it’s all the trust that becomes your thumbprint. And so that can never really be duplicated.

What’s the one move you would make over the next 12 months to better position your brokerage and your agents for where the industry is going?

Jack Markham: Figure out if you own your data. Meaning if you left today, some of your tools, could you take them with you? And if the answer is no, then I would fix that.

Marisela Harper: I would say just be super, super present because (agents) need that from you, and just show the love. And when I say show the love, I really mean truly say, “I love you.” Sometimes people might know that you love them, but they need to hear it too.

Lori Muller: Embrace your relationship with not only your technology, but your people. Longevity is in the relationship with the people; tech stack and your technology is constantly changing.

Adrian Provost: Move away from tech stacks completely and create platforms. The old days are completely over. Whatever you need, you can literally build it. And so I would move away from being so reliant on a tech stack and subscriptions and actually figure out what it is that your agents need and provide that to them.

Beth McGuire is RISMedia’s vice president of online editorial.

#5383. The World’s Lowest-Priced Frank Lloyd Wright Home Is Listed for $975K—Complete With Original Furniture and a Fireplace Designed for Goldfish

Homes designed by Frank Lloyd Wright are special—but the new-to-the-market Eric V. Brown House in Kalamazoo, MI, boasts additional amenities that make it noteworthy.

Completed in 1951, the home listed for $975,000 is one of four Usonian-style homes in the Parkwyn Village, a residential community created for Upjohn Company scientists and their families. It's on the National Register of Historic Places.

“There are homes, and then there are works of architectural art. The Eric V. Brown House is one of the latter,” states the listing for the 2,800-square-foot home.

Like all Usonians, there are walls of windows, built-ins, a floor-to-ceiling fireplace, concrete-block construction, and an open-concept layout for the living room and dining room. This one has five bedrooms and 3.5 baths. Anne and Eric Brown commissioned the design.

“This home has the most original Frank Lloyd Wright-designed furniture of the homes that I have seen,” says listing agent Fred Taber of Chuck Jaqua, Realtor, Inc.

Taber has sold six Wright-designed homes in Michigan, including the Eric and Pat Pratt House in Galesburg, MI, twice. The most recent sale was in 2024, for $1,800,000.

This home’s collection of original furniture features all of the living room pieces, plus the dining table and chairs and about a dozen footstools. They are included in the listing price.

“When Anne gave piano lessons, the kids sat on the footstools, which is why there are a lot of them,” says Taber. “Because she taught piano lessons at home, it has the largest living room of the Wright homes in Parkwyn Village.

“One thing that sets the home apart from the others is that the floors are not painted or stained ... like the others,” says Taber. “Personally, I like the look, and it is my favorite home.”

As one of three homes on Little Asylum Lake, he says, this one affords the best view.

Another unique feature is the 6-foot-wide fireplace, “recessed to allow it to hold water for goldfish,” says Taber. “There is a photo somewhere that actually shows goldfish swimming in the fireplace.”

“For the discerning buyer, this is an opportunity that extends well beyond acquiring a residence ... to become the steward of an important piece of American architectural history—a home conceived by one of the most influential architects of the twentieth century and a lasting expression of his vision for how we live," the listing states.

"The Eric V. Brown House is not simply a place to live. It is a piece of architectural history to experience, appreciate, and preserve for generations to come."

The sellers are the third family to own the home and invested in updates such as building stables that were part of Wright’s original plan.

Today it is used as a storage shed. Previous owners also embarked on restorations when they replaced most of the roof and added steel beams for the carport.

“This is the lowest-priced Frank Lloyd Wright home in the entire world and is move-in ready,” says Taber.

Based in Milwaukee, Kristine Hansen writes for TravelandLeisure.com, ArchitecturalDigest.com, Vogue.com, and other outlets. She’s also the author of “Frank Lloyd Wright’s Wisconsin: How America’s Most Famous Architect Found Inspiration in His Home State.” She lives in a 1924 bungalow.

#5382. A $535K Lake Superior Property Comes With Two Homes—and Four Rented-Out Teepees

An unusual investment opportunity has just become available on Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, overlooking Lake Superior—and it's listed for $535,000.

Located on 1.86 acres in Marquette, MI, the waterfront lot features two homes and four teepees, with six bedrooms and 2,898 square feet in total, offering the chance to live in one of the dwellings and rent out the others for additional income.

“The highest and best use would be as a single-family property,” said listing agent Terry Huffman of RE/MAX 1st Realty. “It has been an investment property for many years, so you could live there and rent the other structures out.”

Al of the teepees are currently rented out on a month-to-month basis, according to Huffman.

The listing says every unit on the property is rented the same way, so a buyer would inherit existing tenants and rental income while keeping the flexibility to change course.

“It’s a rather unique property with all the options,” he said. “It has such a beautiful beach and is just minutes from downtown Marquette.”

Huffman noted that the property originally had five teepees, but one was torn down.

“You could probably rebuild a structure there because the foundation is still there,” he said. “The home that is closest to the water could also be rebuilt, if you wanted to look into that.”

With lake views and waterfront access, and shopping, dining, and other Marquette amenities close by, the property is ideally set up for both residents and tenants.

“Marquette is a wonderful place,” Huffman said. “It is the largest community on the upper peninsula with about 22,000 people that is a real playground.

"Northern Michigan University is the crown jewel to Marquette. It’s a real gathering place that hosts everything from car and boat shows to indoor tournaments in a climate-controlled building. If you visit the area, you will fall in love with the place.”

The listing also warns that entering the property without an appointment is trespassing.

#5381. Attacker used 1Password employee’s GitHub account to copy customer records

Identity security company 1Password today disclosed a security incident in which an attacker, working through an employee’s corporate GitHub account, copied account records belonging to a subset of its customers.

According to the company, the incident came to light on Nov. 19, when 1Password began investigating signs that the GitHub account had been compromised. Using the account, the attacker is said to have pushed malicious code to 1Password’s backend services, which then downloaded what the company describes as “administrative data pertaining to our customers.”

The records taken include names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters and other non-secret account metadata. Rounding out the list are tokens found in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery.

Customer vaults, the items stored in them and the keys that protect them were not affected, according to 1Password. “At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker,” the company said in its disclosure. Account passwords and Secret Keys are not stored by the company. Also left untouched, the company says, were account recovery keys and the 1Password apps and browser extensions.

Beyond the customer records, the attacker is said to have copied source code from private repositories. Access was also gained to 1Password’s continuous integration and continuous delivery system, which contains infrastructure-related secrets needed for its product to work. According to 1Password, the source code contains no user secrets. Having triggered a rotation of all credentials that may have been exposed, the company claims there has been no impact to its services, availability or product security.

The tokens taken from emailed links cannot be used on their own to access an account, since completing an invitation or recovery also requires a sign-in through single sign-on or a six-digit code sent to the user’s registered email address. Users with provisioning invites or recovery requests pending at the time of the incident, said to be a small number, have been notified directly.

As a precaution, the emailed codes have now been lengthened from six numeric digits to 10 alphanumeric characters. 1Password says it has found no internal evidence of account takeovers using the exposed tokens. Other steps taken in response include disabling the affected GitHub account, revoking the stolen token, tightening internal controls and bringing in independent cybersecurity experts to validate its containment and remediation work.

Customers do not need to change anything in their 1Password accounts. The company is instead warning users to be cautious of phishing attempts, such as unexpected emails, texts or calls about invitations or account recovery requests they did not start. “1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key,” the company noted.

1Password, which claims to serve more than 200,000 businesses, did not say how many customers had records downloaded. How the employee’s GitHub account was compromised was also left unexplained.

This is not the first intrusion 1Password has disclosed. In October 2023, the company said that an attacker had accessed its Okta tenant using session data stolen in the breach of Okta Inc.’s customer support system. No user data was found to have been compromised in that case.

Today’s disclosure comes nearly four years after rival password manager LastPass US LP revealed that a hacker had copied encrypted customer password vaults, using information taken in an earlier breach of its development environment.

1Password says it will update its post if the investigation turns up anything that changes what it has disclosed so far.

#5380. Chip and Joanna Gaines Reflect on ‘Drowning in Debt’ Early in Their Careers—And Why They’re Glad They Didn’t Find Major Success Until Later

Chip and Joanna Gaines are at the top of their game, but there was a time when the Magnolia co-founders didn't know if they'd make it.

The "Fixer Upper" stars took a trip down memory lane when they joined "Shark Tank" investor Daniel Lubetzky for the Nov. 24 episode of his podcast, "Build or Break."

The successful couple—who began their empire with a decor shop they opened in their hometown of Waco, TX in 2003—admitted that although the early days of their career were filled with lots of fun, they began to feel some serious pressure around the housing crash in 2008 and 2009.

"We started feeling the pressing where it was just like, 'Oh. This is really hard,'" Joanna recalled. "It just felt so hard. I remember there was days I was just on my face, on the floor going, 'I can't even see up.' We were kind of drowning in debt, drowning in projects, and couldn't see up or out."

During that challenging time—which Joanna referred to as their "hardest season"—Chip made a risky bet and purchased a six-acre plot of land where he planned to develop a whopping 28 homes.

"We'd always done homes kind of onesie twosie, where we would do a renovation for you or we would flip a house," she said. "Chip bought six acres and saw in his mind we could build 38 homes in this little area of town. And that was our first big move, not just like, we have three renovations. Now it's, 'We're going to build 38 homes in the heart of Waco, Texas and during the housing crisis,' which for us was like 2009."

Now that enough time has passed, Chip joked, "I missed the timing by a minute," to which Joanna replied, "Yeah, a little off on the timing."

The couple had different opinions on how to tackle the development. Chip was strong-willed towards doing 38 homes, while Joana suggested doing just a few to get started.

"Our strength, our yin and yang is Chip has this knack to have these instincts about the future. He has a vision for big. My vision is never really big. It's like, my vision is what's manageable," she said.

Eventually, Joanna came around to Chip's vision.

"Did we finish the development? Yes. Was there some hard learnings along the way in that development? The hardest times in our life was when we said yes to that development," she admitted.

Although the Gainses had "no money left" at that time, they continued working towards the vision and pulled it off.

Despite the struggles in their early days, it sounds as though Chip and Joanna understand the importance of every step of the journey.

"When 'Fixer' really started taking off in 2014 and 15, no one knew about what was happening from 2003 to 2015 to really pave the way," Joanna explained.

She noted that even though there may be a faster path to success, a longer, more "authentic" track may help sustain success longer.

"I've always felt nervous for folks who find success early because either you're satisfied with less success than you would've been had it been a little bit deferred, or it's sort of that flash in the pan, early success, but you don't have the staying power to sustain it," Chip continued.

He added that the couple often talks about "how thankful" they are that their careers took off after some tough years of growth in their career, as well as their marriage and family's evolution.

"We were very, very stable and then success sort of sat on that foundation as opposed to it sort of being part of the foundation itself," he said.

Despite the stability they feel in their business, Chip and Joanna aren't immune from having to make challenging decisions.

During a recent appearance on the "Joy 101 with Hoda Kotb" podcast, the mom-of-five explained that she still battles imposter syndrome, and revealed she has reimagined her role within Magnolia.

After a brief, three-month hiatus from the business to reconnect with her vision, as well as a productive conversation with Chip and a spiritual experience, Joanna changed her title from "CEO and founder" to "president."

She realized that after spending years focusing on the creative side of the business, she had lost her connection to the more analytical work. These days, she's focusing on a role that balances both.

“Now, I’m like, on fire,” she said. “The very thing I was avoiding was the very thing I needed to see the full picture.”

#5378. New-Home Sales See Welcome Shift, but Not an Overall Improvement

With housing construction continuing to face supply chain and affordability challenges, the latest data from the U.S. Census Bureau and the Department of Housing and Urban Development saw new-home sales experience a welcome shift upward.

New-home sales jumped 14.2% in October to a rate of 701,000, up from a revised rate of 614,000 in September (originally 676,000). This was also up 7.5% year-over-year.

While a positive shift for the construction industry, the shift is notably due entirely to growth in the South. While all three other regions were down both month-over-month and year-over-year to varying degrees, the South was up 36.2% month-over-month and 24.7% year-over-year.

Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington, National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) assistant vice president for forecasting and analysis, noted that while any increase in new-home sales is “encouraging,” it is “too early to interpret the gain as a sustained recovery in housing demand.”

“Elevated mortgage rates and high home prices continue to limit purchasing power, and the outlook for new home sales remains sensitive to financing costs and broader economic conditions,” she continued.

Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant noted that as mortgage rates remain near a three-year high, “the new home industry is experiencing the same pullback in demand that we are seeing on the resale side.”

“While home builders can help offset some of the pain of higher rates by offering buyers rate buydowns and favorable financing, prospective buyers are cautious as we head into the end of 2026,” she continued. “Some buyers have been priced out of the market, while others are simply waiting until 2027, hoping for more favorable conditions.”

Inventory remained on the downslope, falling 1.5% month-over-month and 4.1% year-over-year to 477,000. At the current sales rate, this clocked in at an eight-month supply, down 14% from last month and 11.1% year-over-year.

Builder activity has been significantly diminished due to aforementioned market challenges, with builder confidence recently tanking to a 14-year low.

“Builders are responding with incentives and pricing adjustments, but a more sustained improvement in affordability will be important for strengthening housing demand,” noted NAHB Chairman Bill Owens.

In line with this trend, the median price for a new home slipped 0.3% month-over-month and 3.2 year-over-year to $391,300. Sturtevant noted that this was near a “five year low.”

“Traditionally, new homes command a premium over existing homes, but in October, the median price of a new home was 6% lower than the median price of an existing home,” she continued.”

Sturtevant concluded that with incentives and lower pricing on the table, “new homes continue to be an attractive option for buyers who remain in the market, particularly when builders can offer a discounted interest rate.”

She noted, though, that the issue at hand is “that there are simply fewer buyers in the market as we head into the last few weeks of the year.”

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5377. FCC clears SpaceX to put up to 1 million Starmind data centers in space

Elon Musk’s Space Exploration Technologies Corp. today received approval from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission to deploy up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to operate as data centers in orbit.

Issued by the FCC’s Space Bureau under delegated authority, the order is described by the agency as “the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space.”

“By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said. “This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home.”

Replying to Carr on X, Musk wrote that Starmind “will be a great asset to America and the world.”

Under the terms of the approval, the Starmind satellites are to sit in six orbital shells, or altitude bands, between 500 and 1,002 kilometers, below the 2,000-kilometer ceiling in SpaceX’s original application. Most communications will run over optical links to other satellites, including those in the Starlink network. The license itself covers a backup Ka-band radio system for emergency telemetry, tracking and command.

The approval does come with conditions. SpaceX’s orbital debris plan was found to comply with the agency’s rules only for satellites below 600 kilometers, and four of the six shells sit above that line. Before deploying anything higher, SpaceX is required to file a modification application containing a final debris plan.

A request from the company to retire some of those higher satellites into disposal orbits around Earth or the sun, rather than having them re-enter the atmosphere within five years, was deferred for lack of information.

To keep the authorization, SpaceX has to have its first Starmind satellite in operation by Nov. 25, 2033. The schedule then calls for 100,000 satellites by 2035, 500,000 by 2038 and the full 1 million by 2040. Missing any of the deadlines would void the license.

Petitions to deny the application from Amazon.com Inc.’s Amazon Leo satellite business, Viasat Inc. and the American Astronomical Society were all rejected. In a March filing, Amazon had described the plan as “a lofty ambition rather than a real plan.”

According to the bureau, nothing in the FCC’s rules limits how many satellites a single constellation can include. Astronomers’ concerns about the satellites’ brightness in infrared were ruled to fall outside the scope of a radio license.

SpaceX first applied for the system in January, shortly before it acquired Musk’s artificial intelligence company xAI Corp. Orbital data centers then featured in SpaceX’s pitch to investors ahead of its record initial public offering in June. Built around a space-optimized version of Nvidia Corp.’s Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale system, the first-generation Starmind satellite, known as AI1, could reach orbit as early as the third quarter of next year, according to Musk.

The competitors Carr referred to include Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin LLC, which applied in March for Project Sunrise, a planned network of up to 51,600 data center satellites. Starcloud Inc., a startup developing AI data centers in orbit, raised $250 million at a $2.3 billion valuation in August.

#5376. Engel & Völkers sets sights on Aruba as brokerages add agents

Engel & Völkers announced an Aruba shop, Realty of America entered San Diego, and eXp Realty added a Tampa Bay brokerage and an Ohio team.

Brokerage expansion stretched from the Caribbean to the West Coast in recent days, as firms moved into new markets and picked up agents and teams from other companies. Engel & Völkers is headed to Aruba, where it plans to open a shop in April 2027, and Realty of America reached California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 of her Team Z Realty agents in San Diego.

eXp Realty picked up a Tampa Bay brokerage and a Cincinnati-area team that spent 20 years with REMAX. Baird & Warner brought on Oak Park, Illinois, boutique Beyond Properties, and Dane Briggs teamed up with Phil Sexton at HomeSmart’s NEXT team. IRES MLS welcomed back a former staffer to run operations, and Howard Hanna Portside added an agent in Massachusetts.

Engel & Völkers expanded into Aruba with license partners Zobaida Akkari and Richard Franken, Aruba-based entrepreneurs with backgrounds in real estate, luxury sales, hospitality and tourism. The shop is projected to open in April 2027 at L.G. Smith Blvd. 330 in Palm Beach and will serve clients across the island, according to the company.

“Aruba is a compelling addition to the network’s growing presence in the Caribbean,” Stuart Siegel, president and CEO of Engel & Völkers Americas, said in a statement.

Realty of America entered California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 Team Z Realty agent partners in San Diego. Ulloa has generated more than $4.2 billion in sales volume over her 13-year career, and Team Z peaked at 72 agents and $589 million in annual volume, according to the company. Agent-owned ROA, founded in September 2024, says it has more than 3,900 agents across 26 markets.

“People around me may see what I am giving up, but I see what I am making room for,” Ulloa said in a statement.

Rene Carpena and Dana Carpena moved Florida’s 1st Choice Realty, their independent Greater Tampa Bay brokerage, to eXp Realty, where it now operates as 1st Choice Collective. The group brings more than 70 agents and support staff and recorded more than 325 transactions and $60 million in sales volume in 2025, according to the company.

Jon Bowling also brought his 17-person team in Mason, Ohio, to eXp after 20 years with RE/MAX. eXp Realty is the core subsidiary of AGNT Inc.

Baird & Warner added Beyond Properties, a boutique brokerage in Oak Park, Illinois, whose dozen agents will operate as Beyond Properties Group. Owner and designated managing broker Erica Cuneen, who founded the firm almost 20 years ago, will co-lead the group with team leader Cynthia Howe Gajewski. The group joins Baird & Warner’s Oak Park office and keeps its Marion Street location.

“This partnership will allow me to simplify the operational side of the business and spend more time doing what I love, which is focusing on our agents and clients,” Cuneen said in a statement.

Dane Briggs, an Arizona real estate veteran, partnered with Phil Sexton, founder of HomeSmart’s NEXT team, in a leadership role focused on agent workflows and AI integrations. Briggs has worked as a designated broker and title executive, founded referral brokerage Roosted and led expansion initiatives at Homie. He has also served as an Inman Ambassador.

“Before long, we weren’t just talking about what Phil was building. We were talking about what we could build together,” Briggs said in a statement.

IRES MLS, which serves Northern Colorado and parts of the Front Range, rehired Samantha Ewing as director of operations. Ewing spent 13 years at IRES as a projects manager and quality assurance tester before leaving in 2018, and she has more than 20 years of experience in MLS operations and real estate technology.

“Having Samantha return to IRES is an exciting opportunity for our team and the local industry we serve,” CEO Julie Dahl said in a statement.

Howard Hanna Portside Real Estate Group added Melissa Winter, an agent with nearly 15 years of experience who focuses on first-time homebuyers, to its Massachusetts team in Amesbury. Portside, which has more than 200 agents, entered a strategic partnership with Howard Hanna in 2026, according to the company.

“What drew me to Portside was the energy, the people, and the opportunity for growth,” Winter said in a statement.
