#5358. Mortgage Rates Dip Ahead of Holiday, Application Activity Increases as Rates Fluctuate

Real estate housing market decline concept. Wooden house model standing next to falling red arrow on floor with window blind shadows. Decreasing property value and mortgage rate.

Even while lingering above 7%, slight dips in the average mortgage rate were enough to spur home-buyer activity this past week.

The latest Market Composite Index from the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA)—its measure of mortgage loan activity volume and includes purchases and refinances—shows mortgage application activity increasing 6.1% on a seasonally adjusted basis, a notable increase from last week’s 2.3% decrease. On an unadjusted basis, the Index increased 3% compared to a 5% decrease the previous week.

This week’s increase follows weeks of fluctuations as the 30-year fixed mortgage rate still remains over 7%–this past week decreasing to 7.21% from 7.28% the previous week, according to Freddie Mac and currently sits at 7.29%, according to Mortgage News Daily.

“Mortgage rates moved higher, with the 30-year fixed rate rising to 7.28 percent (last week),” said Joel Kan, CMB, MBA’s vice president and deputy chief economist. “While mortgage rates increased slightly on a weekly average basis, rates declined over the course of the week, which likely spurred purchase application activity.”

“Purchase applications reached their strongest weekly pace since September but remained well behind last year’s pace,” he added.

The latest Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey® released Wednesday ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, also shows the 30-year FRM is still up year-over-year more than a full percentage point from 6.23% last year. The 15-year FRM averaged 6.66%, up from last week’s 6.45%. A year ago at this time, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.51%.

“Mortgage rates currently are about a percentage point higher than a year ago, while home prices are also still rising in many local markets,” said Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant. Affordability is the biggest constraint on housing market activity, and until affordability eases, the pace of home sales transactions is going to be far below average. Existing home sales are on pace to come in below 4 million for 2026, which will be the first time sales have tracked below that level since the mid-1990s.

“Inflation continues to exceed the Fed’s target raising expectations for a December Fed rate hike, placing a floor under interest rates, including mortgage rates,” said Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale. “Despite this week’s decline, mortgage rates remain roughly a percentage point above where they were at this point in 2025, adding another headwind for buyers contending with high home prices.”

Kan pointed to a rise in adjustable rate mortgages (ARMs) as most notable this week.

“A larger share of borrowers relied on ARM loans for lower monthly payments, which accounted for 11.5 percent of applications, the highest share in more than a year,” he said. “At 6.39 percent, the ARM mortgage rate was nearly a full percentage lower than the 30-year fixed rate last week.”

#5357. New York bans AI toys amid concern after stuffed animals going rogue

New York Governor Kathy Hochul today signed legislation that will impose a five-year ban on children’s toys powered by artificial intelligence chatbots, amid fears that dolls, robots and stuffed animals might be leading children astray or discussing X-rated themes.

“This is a warning that there are toys out there that could be harmful to your children,” the governor said. “When tech companies and unregulated AI pose a threat to our kids and our babies, you bet I’m going to have something to say about it.”

Though dangerous dolls manipulating innocent children may sound like the plot of Hollywood movie, recent tests of certain chatbot-powered toys have become a real cause for concern. When journalists at NBC News tested the Pixie Paw, an AI-powered plush cat toy marketed to children aged three and older, it reportedly shared stories of massacres, gang rape and firing squads in what was described as graphic detail.

Other tests have shown some of the toys can become very convincing when trying to persuade the young user that they are human. “Parents have enough to worry about,” said Hochul, who was also aware some of the smart toys have encouraged kids to jump out of windows.

State senator Andrew Gounardes applauded the move, saying that modern life seems to be mimicking science fiction of days gone by. He invoked an episode of the “Twilight Zone that featured the Talky Tina doll, an insidious, possessed toy that tried to persuade a young girl to murder her strict stepfather.

New York Attorney General Letitia James explained that the toys being put on the market is reckless when they clearly expose “young people to inappropriate content and put “their mental health at risk.” She added, “We won’t allow our children’s health to become the collateral damage of big tech.”

Hochul has been vocal about the dangers of AI for some time, recently imposing the first statewide moratorium on new data centers and last month signing a bill titled “AI Chatbot Restrictions for Minors,” which will prohibit firms from developing chatbots that feature elements that could be harmful to minors.

#5356. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

Want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

A sold comp tells us where a buyer said yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

One of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”

When I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

This is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”

Twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:

We’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

#5355. Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont said in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon said in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

“Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan said in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an important step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

“I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said. “I think it’s important to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

“A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really important component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”

#5353. What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

Taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in New York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He said he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”

His co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be said for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

“I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan said. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”

Jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

“Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he said. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

Daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she said, but it showed cold.

“By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova said. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”

For mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

“If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova said. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney said.

She leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he says, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

He also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

“In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer said. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea says she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”

Marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

His Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein said.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

“Every week, I share new songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he said. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”

On setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she said.

As for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova said she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

So the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova said, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”

#5352. NAR’s latest data, must-have AI tools, Compass’ 15 new lawsuits

Congratulations, you’ve made it to Friday again this week. But before you head out for the weekend, we’re bringing you a quick catch-up on the biggest headlines and the most helpful how-tos for your business. So, Take 5 and peruse our top editor picks for this week and why they matter to your business.

P.S. Don’t miss The Download, our weekly column that breaks down one of the week’s top stories and equips you with what you’ll need to meet next Monday head-on.

Homeownership is slipping further out of reach for young Americans, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. The report, released on Thursday, revealed that the share of first-time homebuyers rose 1 percent year over year to 22 percent. Despite the small gain, first-time buyer activity remains near historic lows (21 percent) and 18 percentage points below pre-2008 trends (40 percent). Same as last year, the median age of a first-time homebuyer was 40 — roughly a decade older than the typical median age in the 1980s.

Why it matters: This annual report gives you a pulse on national real estate trends and how you might want to pivot your strategies. For example, as noted above, the median age of the first-time homebuyer is 40, and the share of single women homeowners has risen to 20 percent. A longer nurture campaign might be in order (ahem, see below), and if you’re not already marketing toward single women, perhaps you should. Read the full report for more.

EXTRA: The buyer who can’t close for a year is your best asset in 2026

AI has been the topic of conversation for the past couple of years. And there’s a lot of talk. So how do you suss through the noise and find what works for your business? Jimmy Burgess has created a no-nonsense list of seven AI tools that are actually worth your time.

Why it matters: Burgess shares not only his top tools but also how to use them. These tools will help you turn prompts into better questions, find the questions your future clients are asking, remember the details that matter, evaluate your AI search visibility, turn one video into multiple pieces of content, make video editing easier and use AI as a strategist rather than a writing assistant. Don’t feel overwhelmed. You don’t have to use all of them at once.

Krystopher Benyamein recently sold a property in San Pedro where his team hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. They found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and they had to start again.

They eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when they shared the case study on Instagram, they didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing they’d done. They opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”

That opening puts the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, they explained how they responded, got the property back in front of buyers and ultimately closed.

Why it matters: In today’s market, there are many stories of buyers backing out of deals. This approach allows you to create content that keeps you top of mind, show sellers exactly how you work and reach a wider audience. Benyamein shows you how to do it and shares a FREE Canva template to help get the job done.

VA loans often get passed over for conventional loans. Inman’s Nick Pipitone spoke with Fathom Realty’s Lindsey Schmidt, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, about why VA financing still carries a stigma among sellers and listing agents, how she gets around it and why VA assumptions remain one of the most misunderstood tools in the market.

Why it matters: Military members often have to move. Understanding and busting myths about VA loans can help you get ahead of objections before making an offer, which will help you get more deals across the finish line and get more service members into homes.

Compass has been busy, creating and formalizing policy around employees in association leadership positions and how Compass brokerage agents cooperate on private listings.

The company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

#5351. Your AI agents can be fully authorized and still do damage

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

For as long as we’ve had enterprise security, it’s been organized around one question: Who is allowed to do what?

Identity, zero trust and least privilege all exist to answer that question. The internet and mobile disrupted the landscape by bringing more people and devices onto the network, but the underlying problem remained.

Artificial intelligence agents expose the limits of that question. An agent can hold only the permissions it was given and still email a customer list to a stranger because it read an instruction buried on a web page or in a support ticket and treated it as a legitimate order. That is the problem Cato Networks Ltd. is trying to solve with its recent launch of AgentSense, a runtime capability built into its secure access service edge platform.

AgentSense monitors an agent as it works and traces each proposed action back to its instruction source. Its first component, Untrusted Influence Detection, separates what the user asked for from content the agent encounters along the way, such as emails, documents and tool responses. If that external content steers the agent toward a risky step, the action is blocked before it runs. A second component, Drift Detection, is planned to check whether an agent’s steps still serve its original task.

With agentic agents, they can have the right permissions and still take harmful actions. The first release covers coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and GitHub Copilot. These are included at no extra charge in Cato AI Usage licenses, and Cato is offering $10,000 to each of the first three researchers who can beat it. This has clear value for security leaders. As organizations give AI more responsibility, they need visibility into what it is doing and when human intervention is required.

Language models read instructions and data in the same stream, and no patch will change that. Filters that look for known attack phrases catch poorly formed attempts, but a well-written injection will be interpreted as a valid business request. The control therefore must sit at the moment of action and ask where the instruction came from.

Permissions alone won’t close the gap because multiple actions, when executed individually, can still combine to produce an unauthorized outcome. Adoption is far ahead of control. A Gartner survey cited by Fierce Network found that 71% of organizations expect to deploy agentic AI within 12 months, while only 21% have governance in place.

AgentSense is a single product from a single vendor, and it will take time and independent testing to prove itself. The more important point is the shift it represents. Zero trust taught us to verify who is asking. Agents also require us to verify why an action is happening and whose instruction is behind it.

The companies that get value from agents will be the ones that can let them run without watching every step, and that only happens when the controls are in place first. Start the inventory and the permission cleanup now. The tools to enforce the rest are arriving quickly, and they will work far better for the teams that did the groundwork.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5350. NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO says

License under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license.

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents said.

Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint said he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”

White also allegedly said that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton said it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or plan.”

Pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also said the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

“NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears said the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

“John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” said David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”

“Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”

#5349. Crypto News Today: Is Bitcoin Bottoming Out? BTC Bounces Back After PCE Shock

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin bounced back toward $60,000 this morning after news on hotter-than-expected US inflation broke and sent the crypto tumbling to $57,300, its lowest level in more than two years. The rebound has brought back speculation that Bitcoin may finally be approaching a bottom, but ETF outflows and bearish signals continue to cloud the outlook.

October’s Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation came in at 3.8% annually, while core PCE reached 3.3%, above the 3.2% expected by economists. These figures strengthened concerns that the Federal Reserve could keep monetary policy restrictive for longer, which then adds pressure to risk assets like Bitcoin.

Bitcoin nevertheless recovered after briefly dipping below $58,000, as we gauge and predict its next move.

Bitcoin remains down 23% this November, putting it on track for its worst monthly performance since June 2022. Spot Bitcoin ETFs have also suffered nearly $5 billion in net outflows this month through November 24, adding another source of selling pressure.

BlackRock’s IBIT has accounted for more than $4 billion in redemptions during the month, showing how quickly institutional demand has reversed.

However, not all investors are moving in the same direction. Data cited by Nansen shows wallets that rarely move Bitcoin received a net 10,000 BTC from exchanges over the past month, while ETFs collectively sold 70,000 BTC during November.

Nansen data shows large, infrequently moving wallets absorbed a net 10,000 BTC from exchanges over the past month.Meanwhile, spot Bitcoin ETFs sold 70,000 BTC in November.The imbalance is stark. Long term cold wallets are still accumulating, but nowhere near enough to offset…

Bitcoin’s rebound also comes after an arguably huge derivatives-market reset, with leveraged positions being flushed out during the recent slide. That could reduce some immediate selling pressure.

Holders have realized $8.4 billion in net losses over the past 30 days, according to CryptoQuant data, as investors are increasingly capitulating during the selloff. But the figure remains well below the $30 billion recorded during February’s bottom and $18.4 billion during June’s low. Selling pressure has intensified, but the scale of realized losses has yet to match previous capitulation events.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Some analysts believe Bitcoin’s recovery could be running ahead of the underlying market conditions. CoinMarketCap research head Alice Liu warned that the rebound may largely reflect short sellers covering positions, and not fresh demand, leaving prices vulnerable once that buying subsides.

Meanwhile, 10x Research’s bearish signal issued in October correctly anticipated Bitcoin’s decline toward $57,300. The firm has cautioned that oversold conditions can trigger short-term rebounds without necessarily signaling a reversal in the wider trend.

“Bitcoin has reached our $57,300 target. Short-term indicators were oversold for much of the decline, and tactical bounces were always possible. Our market structure work, however, kept pointing to a bearish primary trend.” – 10X Research

Bitcoin faces a difficult combination of persistent ETF withdrawals, uncertain news from Federal Reserve policy, and weakened market sentiment. The selloff has removed substantial leverage, but convincing evidence of renewed demand remains limited.

The $57,300 low is now a key level to defend. Holding that support while ETF outflows begin slowing will likely strengthen the case that Bitcoin is forming a bottom.

#5346. Report sheds light on China ties of some US-based Nvidia partners

An investigation has shed light on links between some Nvidia Corp. partners and companies that are based in China or are accused of breaching export controls.

The analysis was carried out by C4ADS, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit, at the request of CBS News. The outlet published the findings Wednesday evening.

The first focus of the investigation was a San Jose, California-based company called RiCloud AI Inc. It’s an Nvidia preferred partner, which means that it can buy the chipmaker’s high-end graphics processing units. Companies with that partner destination also have access to Nvidia’s GPU software and technical support services.

The investigation determined that RiCloud AI is a unit of Shenzen-based Yuxing InfoTech Investment Holdings Ltd. The latter company’s chief executive reportedly has a degree from a university run by China’s military. Yuxing’s chair, in turn, previously worked at a Chinese tech firm that drew national security scrutiny in Australia.

RiCloud AI recently signed a $120 million deal to lease Nvidia-powered servers to a Taiwanese whiskey company. The latter firm generated just $609,000 in profits last year.

The investigation also looked into a company called Topmost Corp. It’s reportedly linked to a California businessman who was recently indicted for allegedly smuggling GPUs to China.

According to CBS News, Topmost’s website states that it’s an authorized reseller of Nvidia partner 2CRSi Inc. The latter company makes servers powered by the chipmaker’s GPUs. Last month, it disclosed that it received a grand jury subpoena in connection with a client “we ourselves had reported to the authorities.”

The report also noted that California-based Aivres Inc. has exported $3 billion worth of Nvidia-powered servers to Southeast Asia since 2024. It’s a subsidiary of Inspur, a Chinese tech firm that is on the U.S. Commerce Department’s Entity List. Organizations on the list are subject to trade restrictions.

U.S. regulations prohibit companies from exporting Nvidia’s most advanced GPUs to China. Earlier this month, the Commerce Department closed a loophole that Chinese tech firms used to bypass those restrictions. The tech firms in questions rented access to Nvidia GPUs deployed in data centers outside China.

Some of the data centers used by Chinese companies are in Southeast Asia. On Wednesday, the Financial Times reported that Nvidia had instructed manufacturing partners to stop shipping GPU-equipped servers to four countries in the region. It’s reportedly unclear whether the move is temporary.

Separately, CNBC reported that companies have put an “unusually high” number of Nvidia GPUs up for sale since the Commerce Department announced the new restrictions. It’s believed the chips were intended for data centers that are used by Chinese firms. According to the report, thousands of high-end B300 GPUs are among the processors that were put up for sale.

#5344. The 4 best online real estate schools for 2026

Our editors independently review the products we recommend. When you buy through our links, we may earn a commission. Learn more

Are you aspiring to become a real estate agent and don’t know where to start? Well, you’ve come to the right place. The first big decision you’ll make is deciding where you’ll complete your licensing education. Finding the right program will give you the confidence and tools to pass the exam and hit the ground running.

There are so many online real estate schools that claim to be the best, but it’s not easy to know which programs are really worth it. That’s where we come in. We’ve reviewed the best online real estate schools based on what future real estate agents really care about – flexibility, pricing, pass rates and student support. Let’s take a look at your options to see which one is the right fit for you.

Before you review the school information below, here are the features you should pay attention to when deciding on which online real estate school is best for you.

Now that you’re armed with a checklist of items to keep your eye on, continue reading to choose the best school for your needs.

The CE Shop offers real estate courses in all 50 states, plus the District of Columbia, and boasts a 96% student satisfaction rate. Students attribute this to its engaging course features, student support and a proprietary online learning platform called LEAP.

You can complete your online real estate prelicensing coursework in as little as two weeks if your schedule permits. The CE Shop regularly updates course content, and every topic covered is based on commonly faced, real-life scenarios. It can be tough to stay consistent with self-paced courses, but The CE Shop makes it easier with interactive content with built-in progress tracking to keep you engaged and motivated.

If you’re concerned about investing in a course you’re not sure will be a good fit for you, The CE Shop offers a free five-day trial with unlimited access for all prelicensing courses. What’s more, they offer a money-back guarantee within 30 days of purchase, as long as your course is less than 50% complete.

The CE Shop’s product offerings include prelicensing, post-licensing, continuing education and exam prep courses, depending on your state. In most states, The CE Shop offers exam prep and continuing education courses that can be bundled with prelicensing courses for convenience and significant savings. As an added bonus, they offer a pass guarantee with any Exam Prep Edge purchase for prelicensing. If you don’t pass, they will refund the cost of your initial licensing exam.

The CE Shop’s courses can be accessed through your tablet, computer or smartphone 24/7 for on-the-go learning that is flexible and convenient. On the downside, the course can be heavy on text and light on video lessons. With certain packages, you get unlimited attempts at passing the course’s final exam.

Colibri offers real estate courses in 40 states plus Washington, D.C. More than 1.5 million students have enrolled in Colibri Real Estate’s courses to complete their education requirements and prepare for the license exam, and students give the school a rating of 4.5 out of 5 stars.

Prelicensing course upgrades include Exam Prep Plus for instructor engagement and study tools, and Ultimate Learning for access to the school’s Career Booster. If you’re balancing completing your education requirements with work and family demands, you’ll appreciate being able to move through the online course at your own pace with the next-generation student dashboard.

Students enjoy Colibri’s clear course format, real-world examples and practice exams that simulate live tests and include assessments. Colibri offers a Pass or Don’t Pay Guarantee. If you don’t pass the licensing exam within 30 days of completing your course, Colibri will reimburse the cost of the purchased package, unless state laws or regulations prohibit qualification for the guarantee.

Colibri’s product offering includes post-licensing courses, exam prep and continuing education courses in most states listed above, in addition to prelicensing courses. They also offera pass or don’t pay guarantee.

Colibri’s self-paced and livestream courses are designed to allow you to study on any device with internet access and a browser, including your smartphone or tablet. With 24/7 access to the dashboard, you can stop and start your course anytime without losing track of your progress.

While it doesn’t operate in all 50 states, Aceable Agents offers prelicensing courses in 15 states, including Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Michigan, New York, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia and Washington.

Built by learning science experts, Aceable Agent’s workshops, practice tests and other study tools are designed to help you pass your exam on the first try. The school offers a first-of-its-kind mobile app from which students can complete their studies, anytime from any device.

The hands-free audio narration lets you tune in as you would to your favorite podcast. We also love the Mastery Tracking algorithm. As you progress through your course, it learns where you need improvement and provides personalized exam prep. Students can switch between their browser and Aceable Agent’s mobile app, both of which track and save progress, so you can stop and resume your studies when it’s convenient for you across devices.

Aceable Agent is so confident that you’ll love their courses, they offer a 30-day money-back guarantee. If you did not complete the course and don’t feel their program is right for you – you can request a full refund. The school also has an Ace or Don’t Pay Guarantee, so students who take one of AceableAgent’s prelicensing courses and don’t pass the licensing exam are eligible for a refund.

AceableAgent’s product offering includes post-licensing courses, exam prep and continuing education courses in most states, in addition to prelicensing courses. Course availability varies by state, so be sure to check if the course you are looking for is available in your area.

Students have access to self-paced, online courses from a mobile device or computer at any time of day. Aceable Agent’s courses feature interactive games, videos and bite-sized lessons to help students successfully meet prelicensing coursework requirements and pass the state and national exams. While most students appreciate that course content is presented in a highly engaging way to help with retention, interactive courses may not be best for visual learners who prefer to read or see pictures.

Kaplan offers real estate pre-licensing courses in 33 states including Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Virginia, Washington and Wisconsin.

While Kaplan does not publish pass rates, the school is committed to your success. They offer the Kaplan Commitment which promises that they will continue to support your studies for the same state exam at no cost to you. With over 50 years of experience, Kaplan has helped thousands of students begin and advance their real estate careers every year.

Kaplan’s real estate course uses interactive content that combines industry fundamentals with the latest state-specific information needed to pass your state’s licensing exam. Video-based courses make complex topics easier to understand and feel more like a real classroom experience. Even better, the courses are created by real estate experts to mirror licensing exam topics to give you a greater chance to pass the exam on your first try.

Kaplan’s self-paced, online prelicensing offerings let you start, stop and resume your course when it’s convenient for you. In addition to prelicensing courses, the school offers continuing education packages and exam prep courses in most states. Full tuition refunds are available within 30 days of purchase for web-based courses and online classes that have not been completed.

Kaplan’s product offering includes prelicensing courses in over 30 states, post-licensing courses, exam prep and continuing education courses in many of those states. Exam prep is included in most packages and backed by some of the best educators in the business.

You can access your courses online and the courses are mobile-friendly. Access your courses anywhere, anytime from your laptop, tablet or mobile device. Kaplan’s online video courses complement text-based course content to reinforce key concepts, even on the go.

To find the best online real estate school, we have evaluated dozens of real estate schools, reviewing both online and in-person programs. We’ve chosen schools with interactive content, hands-free audio, mobile learning and other convenient formats that will help you fit your studies into your busy schedule. Our real estate experts possess in-depth knowledge of real estate licensing and online courses and evaluate real estate licensing programs based on pricing, course packages, course materials, teaching styles, online user experience, exam success rates, customer reviews and more.

The best online real estate schools on our list are not only widely available — they offer economies of scale that make their course packages affordable — using tech that makes their online courses way more convenient than having to commute to attend in-person classes at a brick-and-mortar location. Unlike your local school, they have the scale to invest in leading-edge technology that makes getting prepped for your state real estate exam a snap.

Don’t believe us? Check out our real estate education page for more information about getting licensed and the best real estate schools available in your state. We recommend the schools on this list for their convenience, value for money, excellence in course materials and thoughtful user experience.

Each state has its own license reciprocity and portability rules, and many have license reciprocity agreements with other states. If you have your real estate license in one state and want to conduct business in another, check with the state you are not licensed in to see if they will waive your prelicensing education requirements based on a license reciprocity agreement.

The schools featured in this guide make it easy to sign up for your online real estate classes. Just click the website of the school of your choice below, select the package you want from the school’s catalog, add it to your cart, check out and wait for the school to deliver your course (typically as a link, email, or both).

In-person real estate classes can be beneficial if you prefer a traditional learning atmosphere and have an incredibly flexible schedule. But for anyone pursuing a real estate license who has to juggle a full-time job, family, and other obligations, a school offering 100% online real estate classes is a much more convenient option.

Now that you know what the industry-leading online real estate schools have to offer, you can make the most informed decision to launch a new career. Once you have obtained your license, you’ll be ready to complete any post-licensing requirements, continuing education requirements, or pursue your broker’s license. HONG KONG, Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Ruko is excited to announce the launch of its latest drone, the F11PRO 2 Plus (RC4), now available on Amazon. Designed to deliver an upgraded aerial photography experience, the new drone features an integrated 5.5-inch touchscreen remote controller, advanced 8K imaging, enhanced flight stabilization, and intelligent flight capabilities. Enhanced Imaging for More Detailed Aerial Photography

#5342. 8 best Florida real estate schools for 2026

Our editors independently review the products we recommend. When you buy through our links, we may earn a commission. Learn more

Are you ready to begin a fulfilling real estate career in the Sunshine State? To get started, you have to complete 63 hours of prelicensing coursework through a state-approved real estate school before you’re allowed to take the licensing exam. Most schools offer this online now, which makes it easier to work through the material without putting your life on hold.

Not all online Florida real estate schools are the same. Some are better if you want structure and support while others work well if you just want to get through the coursework at your own pace. We’ve broken down the best online Florida real estate schools for 2026, comparing course formats, pricing, study tools and exam prep so you can choose the option that actually fits how you learn and fits your budget.

The CE Shop earns our top spot for one simple reason – it combines strong course content with tools that actually help students pass the exam. Features like a five-day free trial, a pass guarantee and its Exam Prep Edge study tools are all included with higher-tier packages, making it easier to prepare without having to guess what you’ll need to pass the exam.

Their platform is easy to use and includes short, self-paced lessons that allow you to fit lessons into your busy schedule without losing your place. Exam Prep Edge includes quizzes, flashcards, matching exercises and practice tests that reinforce key concepts as you go. For students thinking beyond licensing, the Premium Package also includes first-time renewal coursework and access to the Kickstarter Professional Development Program, which covers business planning, lead generation and negotiation basics.

The CE Shop offers four prelicensing course packages, plus Florida real estate continuing education and broker licensing courses in Florida. All three top-tier prelicensing packages include Exam Prep Edge to help you retain information and ace the exam.

Aceable Agent takes an innovative approach to online learning, with classes offered through its website, unique mobile app and podcast-style audio courses. Its self-paced and cost-effective Florida real estate courses help you learn on the go, so your study schedule can fit your busy life. Courses include engaging videos, interactive games, infographics and knowledge checks that use straightforward language and real-life scenarios inside bite-sized lessons to keep you engaged with the material.

Designed by learning science experts using proven instructional principles, Aceable Agent’s easy-to-understand courses have frequent practice tests, so you’ll go into the state exam feeling confident. Mastery Tracking helps you focus your energy on your weakest areas when studying for your course final and state licensing exams.

Aceable Agent offers three self-paced prelicensing course packages that include audio and video lessons and practice questions. Their Deluxe and Premium packages incorporate additional features like instructor support, exam prep, AI tools and live webinars.

Colibri Real Estate is a great option for students who want structure and help staying on track to meet their learning goals. With hundreds of thousands of agents trained by Colibri, their focus is on providing structured coursework with support from local real estate experts. The online platform is built around accountability by tracking your study time, setting weekly goals and clearly showing your progress, which can be helpful if you do better with defined milestones.

Colibri offers courses with interactive lessons and practice exams designed to reinforce key concepts as you move through the material. The courses also offer exam prep options, even in the lower-priced packages. The standard package includes practice tests and live Q&A sessions. Higher-tier packages include CompuCram Exam Prep with flashcards, audio reviews, readiness assessments and simulated exams. The Ultimate Learning package includes career resources such as how-to videos, checklists and a customizable business plan.

Colibri Real Estate offers four Florida prelicensing course packages, along with options for continuing education and broker licensing. Higher-tier packages include additional exam prep tools and study resources.

Casa Academy is an innovative real estate school in Florida that focuses on audio and AI to make learning easy. While they do offer self-paced courses from your laptop, Casa also has all of their course available on Spotify so you can learn on the go. Each class is structured as an informative discussion, so you’ll get real-world knowledge from experts that you will apply to your future career.

In addition, the integrated AI, built with ChatGPT, is there to enhance your educational experience. The AI tutor remembers your weaknesses and helps you review them until they become strengths. It will prompt you with explanations, quick reviews and drills to keep your knowledge sharp so you’re ready to pass the real estate exam.

Casa Academy provides basic packages with all the course hours you need:

Kaplan Real Estate Education has several packages to help students get ready for the Florida licensing exam. The courses are structured and detailed, with clear explanations that make it easier to understand some of the tougher concepts that Florida requires to pass the exam. Students like having different ways to study, whether that’s watching an instructor online, working through printed materials or using practice tests to see where they stand.

Kaplan’s exam prep tools and student support are what set this school apart. The study guide is detailed, and the practice questions are worded the same way you’ll see them on the exam. If you want a course that keeps you focused and gives you plenty of practice before exam day, Kaplan should be at the top of your list. Even though it comes with a higher price tag, the detailed content is well worth the investment.

Gold Coast Schools is a good option for students who want live instruction and a more hands-on learning experience. While its online courses are powered by Colibri’s learning platform, Gold Coast operates as its own Florida-based school with a strong focus on instructor access and student support.

Although the school doesn’t offer a mobile app, it does stand out for its personalized guidance. Students can speak directly with career counselors when deciding which course to take. Gold Coast also offers classroom, livestream and online options, with courses available in both English and Spanish.

In addition to prelicensing, Gold Coast offers post-licensing, continuing education and broker licensing education. Prelicensing education is offered in three different packages outlined below.

RealEstateU offers a straightforward, courses-only package that saves you money. If you feel confident taking exams and preparing for them, this low-cost real estate course may be right for you. If not, RealEstateU also offers two premium course bundles that go beyond just passing the real estate exam. They provide real-world strategies for success in your new career, like negotiation strategies, how to convert leads and how to choose the right brokerage. You’ll also learn the business of practicing real estate, including expenses, earning potential, commission structures and more.

RealEstateU’s exam study guide is included in their two top-tier packages. It offers practice questions and four practice exams to test your knowledge. If you prefer, audio lessons are available or you can download lessons and study materials to access them offline – providing flexibility if you can’t access wifi or the internet.

RealEstateU’s Florida prelicensing course starts at $99, making it the most affordable option on our list. Exam prep and additional study resources may cost extra, so make sure you factor that into your total budget if you need extra support.

VanEd stands out for how clear it is about what students are signing up for. You get a five-day free trial with full course access, which makes it easier to decide if the format works for you before committing. VanEd has been developing real estate courses for more than 17 years, with content built by instructors who understand both the licensing process and what Florida students need to know to pass the exam.

The courses use a mix of videos, infographics, flashcards and interactive exercises to keep the material moving. VanEd also includes virtual field trips that connect concepts to real-world scenarios, which can help with retaining what you learn. Everything works across all devices, so you can study from your laptop, tablet or phone and pick up where you left off.

VanEd offers three course packages at an affordable price. The five-day free trial is included in every package.

To determine the very best Florida real estate schools, we conducted extensive research, rating each school based on the following:

Finally, we considered the schools with unique features and professional development opportunities that can have significant value for real estate agents. We do the research so you don’t have to, bringing it all together in this guide to the best real estate schools in Florida. All that’s left for you to do is choose one and launch your new career.

The cost to get your real estate license in Florida depends mostly on the school and course package you choose. The biggest expense is the required 63-hour prelicensing course, which can range from lower-cost, self-paced options to more expensive packages that include exam prep, instructor access, or career resources. On top of that, Florida charges separate fees for the license application and the state exam.

When you add everything up, most people can expect to spend somewhere between $180 and $600 to get licensed. If you stick with a basic course, you’ll be closer to the lower end – and vice versa.

How long it takes to become a Florida real estate agent depends on how quickly you complete the required steps. The state requires 63 hours of prelicensing coursework, which some people finish in a few weeks if they move quickly, while others take a couple of months studying part-time. Once you complete the course, you’ll need to pass the state exam and submit your license application.

For most people, the process can take anywhere from one to three months. It depends on whether you’re studying full-time or part-time and what other commitments you may be juggling at the same time.

Once you have passed the real estate licensing exam, you can apply for a Florida real estate sales associate license online. In fact, Florida prioritizes flexibility, allowing licensees to take the prelicensing course, submit their license application and even take the state exam online through Pearson VUE proctoring.

The Florida Real Estate License Exam tends to be one of the more difficult to pass. There are 100 multiple-choice questions on the Florida real estate licensing exam, and the required passing score is 75%. According to the data available on Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR), as well as other reputable digital resources and news sites, there is a 40-50% pass rate for those taking the Florida real estate exam for the first time. This makes it all the more important to make sure you choose the best real estate school to help you pass the exam on the first try.

According to Indeed, the average Florida real estate agent earns $101,676 annually (as of this writing), which is actually the same as the national average.

Getting your real estate license in Florida starts with choosing the right school helping you feel prepared on exam day and beyond. Some people need structure and guidance. Others just want a straightforward way to finish the coursework and move on. The schools in this guide give you options either way.

#5341. Dance Experts Serge and Yana Nelyubov Explain What Happens at Your First Ballroom Lesson

Serge and Yana Nelyubov outline what beginners can expect during their first ballroom dance lesson and how instructors help build confidence from the start.

WILLIAMSVILLE, N.Y., Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What happens at your first ballroom lesson? A new HelloNation article featuring insights from Dance Experts Serge and Yana Nelyubov of Fred Astaire Buffalo in Williamsville, New York, explains what beginners can expect during their first visit to a dance studio and how ballroom dance lessons are designed to create a relaxed, welcoming learning experience.

The article explains that many first-time students arrive with questions about what they will be asked to do and whether previous experience is required. According to the feature, beginner ballroom dancing is designed with new dancers in mind, allowing students to learn at a comfortable pace without feeling pressured to keep up with anyone else.

Readers learn that a first ballroom lesson typically begins with a conversation between the student and the dance instructor. This discussion helps the instructor understand each student's goals, whether they are preparing for a wedding, looking for a new hobby, or simply interested in learning ballroom dance lessons for fun. The article notes that understanding these goals allows instruction to be tailored to each student's comfort level.

The feature also emphasizes that no prior dance experience is necessary. Many students arrive for their first ballroom lesson without knowing any dance steps, and instructors expect beginners to start from the basics. According to the article, lessons are structured to introduce simple movements one at a time, helping students develop confidence as each new skill builds naturally on the last.

The article explains that early instruction often focuses on fundamental skills such as footwork, rhythm, posture, balance, and partner connection. These concepts provide the foundation for future ballroom dance lessons while remaining approachable for new students. By introducing these basics gradually, instructors help students feel successful from the very beginning.

Readers also learn that students can participate whether they arrive with a partner or attend alone. The article explains that many dance studios provide instructors or practice partners when needed, allowing anyone interested in beginner ballroom dancing to participate comfortably. This flexibility helps make ballroom dancing accessible to a wide range of students.

Another point highlighted in the article is that making mistakes is an expected part of learning. The dance instructor encourages questions, provides corrections, and allows students time to practice without feeling rushed. Rather than viewing mistakes as setbacks, the article describes them as valuable opportunities that help students improve with each lesson.

The feature also discusses the pace of instruction during a first ballroom lesson. Instead of introducing numerous dances at once, instructors typically focus on mastering a few basic movements correctly before moving forward. This steady approach helps students retain what they have learned while building confidence through consistent progress.

The article also offers practical guidance about preparing for the lesson itself. Comfortable clothing that allows easy movement and secure shoes are generally all that is needed for a first visit to a dance studio. Special dance attire is rarely necessary, allowing beginners to focus on learning rather than worrying about what to wear.

As the lesson concludes, many students discover they have learned more than they expected in a single session. The article notes that initial nervousness often gives way to confidence as basic movements become more familiar. Regular ballroom dance lessons continue to build on that foundation, helping students develop new skills while enjoying the movement, social connection, and satisfaction that come with steady improvement.

#5340. Why biodiversity belongs in the master plan

Biodiversity can improve how parks, drainage and open space perform in master-planned communities. Studies cited show native plantings can lift pollinator abundance two to three times, and monitoring at Baseline recorded a 500% increase in macropollinators.   AI Summary

Master-planned communities have always been exercises in long-term thinking. Decisions about infrastructure, open space, water, landscaping and mobility made early in the planning process shape how a community functions decades later.

Parks, drainage areas and open spaces require substantial investment. But there’s growing evidence that designing those landscapes to support biodiversity can help that investment do more. Planned early as part of the infrastructure conversation, biodiversity can help a community better manage water, withstand environmental stress and create stronger connections between residents and the natural environment.

Pollinator habitats offer one of the most practical places to begin. Bees, butterflies and other pollinators help many flowering plants reproduce, sustaining vegetation that supports broader ecosystems.

Development decisions can remove or fragment the food sources and nesting areas those species need. At the scale of a master-planned community, developers have an opportunity to connect habitat across parks, drainage corridors and neighborhoods, making conservation part of the places people use every day.

Developers already expect infrastructure to serve a defined purpose and perform over time. Landscape systems deserve the same scrutiny.

A stormwater basin can manage runoff while also providing habitat. A trail corridor can connect residents to destinations while connecting pollinators to food and nesting resources. Plant selection can account for seasonal habitat needs alongside appearance and maintenance.

These decisions are much more than aesthetic considerations. A 2024 npj Urban Sustainability review examining research across stormwater management, water purification, heat mitigation, infrastructure resilience and maintenance costs found that biodiversity can meaningfully influence how blue-green infrastructure performs. More diverse ecological systems were associated with benefits ranging from improved stormwater retention and water purification to greater resilience under changing environmental conditions.

For developers, the implication is practical: Ecological and engineering performance do not necessarily need to be treated as separate objectives. Incorporating habitat into drainage or open-space plans creates opportunities to serve multiple purposes within the same land area. It also brings stewardship into the budget early, when responsibilities can be assigned, and maintenance requirements can inform design.

The value of parks, trails and public spaces extends beyond a direct line-item return. Planning those landscapes to support biodiversity adds another dimension to that investment, allowing them to contribute to ecological health while serving the needs of the community.

Pollinators depend on more than a patch of flowers. They need plants that provide resources throughout the growing season, places to nest and landscapes they can move through. An isolated garden may offer some of those resources, but a coordinated network can support them across a larger area.

Research shows how much landscape design can matter. A 2026 study published in Urban Ecosystems compared two newly developed residential neighborhoods and found that pollinator abundance and diversity were two to three times higher in the neighborhood dominated by native plants than in one with conventional landscaping. Despite similar numbers of flowers, the difference suggests that what developers plant can matter as much as how much they plant.

Master-planned communities have an unusual ability to create that network. Developers overseeing hundreds or thousands of acres can coordinate planting and habitat connections across property lines and development phases.

Rather than treating pollinator-friendly landscaping as a one-time intervention, the strategy needs to evolve alongside the community. Establishing baseline ecological conditions before construction and continuing monitoring as development progresses creates a reference point to evaluate changes over time.

That approach also requires considering habitat connectivity throughout the development process. Native plantings, open spaces and landscape corridors can be incorporated into the broader plan, rather than treated as isolated conservation features.

As developers, we routinely track home sales, water use, construction costs and other indicators of a community’s performance. Tracking ecological outcomes brings that same discipline to landscape investments.

At Baseline, a 1,100-acre master-planned community in Broomfield, Colorado, Butterfly Pavilion introduced its Pollinator District model in 2019, integrating conservation into development and ongoing operations. With monitoring in place before construction, researchers recorded 3,805 macropollinators in developed areas in 2025, up from 587 in 2023, an increase of more than 500%.

But numbers alone don’t tell the full story. Much of the increase came from nonnative western honeybees, making pollinator diversity an equally important measure of progress. The findings also highlight opportunities for additional native plantings to better support native bees.

The broader lesson is that ecological performance can be measured, and those findings can inform future decisions. Pollinator counts alone cannot establish the impact of every landscape intervention, but monitoring provides a way to identify changes, evaluate habitat strategies and adjust as development progresses.

That same principle can apply beyond pollinators. Whether evaluating stormwater systems, native landscaping or habitat corridors, establishing meaningful measures of performance can help developers better understand the long-term outcomes of their investments.

Integrating biodiversity also creates an ongoing opportunity to learn. Working with ecological specialists helps developers understand the starting landscape, set meaningful goals and see how it responds. That work needs to carry into everyday landscape care, from what gets planted to how areas are mowed and pests are managed, with resources and responsibility for stewardship established for the years ahead.

Monitoring can guide future plant selections and help identify gaps in habitat connections as new neighborhoods take shape. It also requires consistency and an understanding that ecological conditions vary with weather, seasonal timing and other factors.

Protected lands and conservation areas remain essential to ecological health, but developed communities can contribute, too. Places designed for people can also provide meaningful habitat when ecological considerations are incorporated into planning and long-term operations.

For developers, this is part of the longer commitment that comes with creating a master-planned community. These are places people will call home for decades, and caring for their ecological health is another part of planning for how they perform and evolve over that same horizon.
