#5313. Amazon threatens to leave NYC again, this time over delivery bill, as it rallies customers to fight it

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:51 pm

Amazon and New York City are fighting again.

The Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to New Yorkers’ doors. It’s also asking its customers to help fight the bill.

The legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city. Amazon is the main target, but FedEx and several regional couriers would also be covered.

Companies would need a license from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which would also investigate complaints. The bill was introduced in February.

On Thursday, Amazon began showing New York City customers pop-up messages and a homepage banner that reads, “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The notices link to a form and a pre-written letter customers can send to their council members to oppose the bill, Bloomberg reported. Amazon pointed GeekWire to a study by consulting firm AKRF estimating the bill would raise consumer costs by $409 to $664 a year, but didn’t detail how it arrived at the per-order figure.

In a blog post, Amazon said it relies on a network of small delivery businesses in the city. “If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city,” the company wrote. “That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.”

Amazon launched its Delivery Service Partners program in 2018, letting entrepreneurs start their own companies to deliver Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans and uniforms. The companies hire their own drivers, while Amazon pays them to deliver and offers discounts on vehicles, fuel and insurance. The model lets Amazon expand its delivery network without directly employing drivers.

In a statement to GeekWire, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the bill “as written” would threaten more than 40 small delivery businesses the company works with in the city and the more than 5,000 New Yorkers they employ. More than 2,000 Amazon employees also work at its delivery facilities in the city, the company said.

“We’re hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written,” Nantel said. “But so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations.” Amazon said neither Council Member Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, nor Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accepted its offer to visit a delivery facility. The company also said customers sent about 20,000 emails to council members within six hours of the campaign’s launch Thursday morning.

The standoff echoes Amazon’s 2019 reversal on its second headquarters. That February, the company abruptly canceled plans to build a 25,000-person “HQ2” office in Long Island City, Queens, after more than a year of competition among cities to host it. Amazon blamed “a number of state and local politicians” who opposed the project, which drew fierce criticism over roughly $3 billion in government incentives.

Amazon stuck with its plans for Arlington, Va., and Nashville and didn’t reopen its search. Polls at the time showed most New Yorkers supported the deal, but Queens officials, labor leaders and activists fought it. State Sen. Michael Gianaris, who led the opposition, accused Amazon of trying to shake down governments to get its way.

It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections.We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.If… https://t.co/UWXVTJhRL6

City leaders backing the delivery bill see a familiar pattern. “Amazon is once again making spurious attacks against this commonsense legislation that would make workers and our streets safer,” said Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, who called Amazon’s warning a “dishonest scare tactic.”

City Council Speaker Julie Menin questioned Amazon’s cost claims in a post on X.

“It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections,” she wrote, adding that the council is “crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.”

Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon’s subcontractor model “leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets,” CNBC reported.

Supporters, including the Teamsters union, which has sought to organize Amazon drivers and warehouse workers, say the bill would make the work safer and make it harder for Amazon to distance itself from driver injuries.

Amazon disputes that the bill would improve safety. The company said it has invested more than $2.5 billion in driver safety since 2019, that the serious crash rate for its drivers in New York City fell 35.7% from 2024 to 2025, and that drivers there have averaged nearly $24 an hour since January 2025, with required health coverage and paid time off.

Meanwhile, business groups have run ads against the bill and warned they may sue the city if it passes, according to CNBC. The measure is awaiting review by Menin.

Redmond, Wash.-based RBC Signals has announced a $10 million strategic growth investment aimed at accelerating the company’s expansion into government satellite data services and the commercialization of emerging space technologies.

RBC Signals supports satellite operators by arranging access to a global network of ground stations, including its own assets and antenna facilities operated by partners.

Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners, highlighted RBC Signals’ role in addressing the growing demand for space connectivity. “We see tremendous potential in the company’s ability to deliver mission-critical capabilities, and we’re excited to support the team as they enter this next phase of growth,” Faltas said.

#5310. Report links Alice Huang to Chinese firms with smuggled Nvidia chips

An investigation has linked Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the Nvidia Corp. controversy, to Chinese firms that reportedly possess smuggled chips.

Bloomberg researched the firms in question by reviewing regulatory documents from China. The paper published the results of its analysis today.

In October, the New York Times revealed that Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang had an affair with Alice Huang. Some U.S. officials reportedly believe she is a spy, while others see her ties to China’s intelligence service as “more circumstantial.” Nvidia’s board ousted Jensen Huang over the affair and reinstated him about two weeks later.

Bloomberg’s investigation focused on the Yangtze River Delta Project, a data center campus in China. The paper found links between the project and Megaspeed, a Singaporean cloud provider that Alice Huang headed until last year. According to the report, Megaspeed at one point described the campus as its largest data center.

The investigation also determined that the Yangtze River Delta Project’s president is a businessman called Kang Wei. Earlier reports identified him as Alice Huang’s husband.

Bloomberg looked into a Chinese company called Shanghai Kezhan that has ties to the Yangtze River Delta Project. The company is reportedly a unit of a Japanese firm that is controlled by Alice Huang. Kezhan stated in a filing that it uses the data center to host 32 servers equipped with Nvidia’s H200 chips, which can’t be legally exported to China.

The company also uses the facility to host a GB200 rack. GB200 systems include 72 of Nvidia’s Blackwell B200 graphics cards, which are significantly more capable than the H200. They too are subject to U.S. export restrictions.

A second Chinese company, Shanghai Shuoyao, has reportedly deployed a GB300 rack at the data center. Such systems are based on the Blackwell Ultra, an upgraded version of the B200 that features significantly more memory. It’s Nvidia’s second fastest graphics card behind its latest Rubin accelerator.

Both Kezhan and Shuoyao described the servers in loan documents. They used the systems as collateral for millions of dollars in debt financing. According to Bloomberg, it’s possible the companies possess additional Nvidia systems but didn’t mention them in the documents because they weren’t used as collateral.

The report raises fresh questions about the effectiveness of Nvidia’s regulatory compliance efforts days before Jensen Huang is scheduled to appear before Congress. According to CNBC, he will testify before three House committees on Sunday and the Senate Banking Committee next Thursday.

#5309. Binance Secures In-Principle Approval in Gelephu Mindfulness City, Plans Asia Hub in Bhutan

The regulatory milestone marks a major step toward Binance establishing an Asia hub in Gelephu Mindfulness City, alongside commitments to create jobs and strengthen Bhutan's digital-asset capabilities

BANGKOK, Nov. 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Binance, the leading global financial platform powered by blockchain, has received in-principle approval (IPA) from the Gelephu Central Bank (GCB) to establish regulated digital-asset operations in Gelephu Mindfulness City (GMC), Bhutan.

The milestone was marked at Binance Blockchain Week 2026, where Binance and GMC signed a cooperation agreement setting out their broader partnership and plans for GMC to become an Asia hub for Binance users. The IPA is an important milestone in a broader, ongoing effort to expand access and build out the ecosystem locally. Binance has been deepening its presence in Bhutan since launching a national crypto-powered tourism payment system in 2025. As the partnership progresses, Binance will continue building out the local digital-asset ecosystem.

Binance will now work with GCB to fulfil the conditions attached to the IPA and complete the remaining regulatory requirements before receiving its full licence.

The partnership goes beyond licensing. Binance plans to establish a substantive operational presence in Bhutan, creating employment opportunities while investing in the development of talent and digital-asset capabilities.

As part of the partnership, Binance will work with GMC to build capabilities and upskill the talent pool, including through employment, training, knowledge sharing and collaboration across areas such as digital assets, compliance and operations. The parties also intend to explore opportunities to develop GMC as a regional centre of excellence, supporting Binance's broader operations in Asia while building expertise and capabilities within GMC.

Speaking on this milestone, Jigdrel Singay, Board Director of Gelephu Mindfulness City, said "Binance choosing Gelephu Mindfulness City as a base for its Asia operations is an important milestone for what we are building in Bhutan. Our ambition is not simply to attract global companies to establish an entity here. We want them to build real operations, create meaningful jobs, develop talent and transfer capabilities that remain in the country over the long term.

"The in-principle approval is an important first step, and we look forward to working closely with Binance and GCB as Binance completes the remaining regulatory requirements and builds its presence in GMC," Singay added.

SB Seker Head of APAC, Binance said, "Establishing an Asia hub in Gelephu Mindfulness City is a strategic decision that reflects Binance's commitment to operating within clear, progressive regulatory frameworks. The IPA from GCB is an important validation of GMC's approach to digital asset regulation, one that protects users while enabling innovation."

"GMC's vision of combining traditional values with cutting-edge technology, powered by renewable energy, makes it an ideal location for Binance's regional center of excellence. We are committed to making this partnership a model for responsible growth in the digital asset sector," added Seker.

The partnership forms part of GMC's broader ambition to establish Bhutan as a trusted and internationally connected hub for digital assets and financial innovation, combining a clear regulatory framework with a long-term focus on developing local talent and institutional capabilities.

The granting of the IPA does not constitute a full licence. Binance must satisfy the conditions specified by GCB and complete the remaining regulatory requirements before the relevant regulated activities may commence.

For more information, visit www.gmc.bt.

#5308. John Deere acquires Orchard Robotics, an AI farming startup with Seattle ties

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 7:52 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:14 am

Orchard Robotics, an agtech company using artificial intelligence to help growers monitor crops and make farming decisions, has been acquired by John Deere. The deal was announced Thursday and the terms were not disclosed.

The startup has developed a system of cameras mounted on tractors and other equipment that gather images as the machines traverse a farm. Orchard’s AI analyzes the images to generate data on vines, trees and crops, which is then used to track growth, yield and health.

“This acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field,” Tim Marquis, John Deere’s director of farm systems innovation, said in a statement.

That includes helping farmers target treatments and make better-timed decisions about thinning, spraying and harvesting.

Orchard was founded by CEO Charlie Wu, a Thiel Fellow who dropped out of Cornell University to launch his business in 2022.

“Over these next few years, our goal is to bring the power of Orchard’s industry-leading technology and AI Farming capabilities to every farmer out there,” Wu said in a LinkedIn post. “This is only the beginning of a long and awesome journey ahead.”

The startup is based in San Francisco and has an office in Seattle. Wu splits his time between the two cities and was a finalist for Young Entrepreneur of the Year at the 2026 GeekWire Awards.

Orchard has raised more than $25 million from investors, including a $22 million Series A round announced in September 2025. The startup has 45 employees, according to PitchBook.

The Pacific Northwest is home to numerous agtech startups. That includes other companies that collect and analyze data, such as Loftus Labs and innov8.ag, as well as IUNU and Koidra, which are focused on greenhouse crops. Businesses tackling field operations include weed destroyers Carbon Robotics and Aigen; rock-removing TerraClear; and irrigation startups FarmHQ and Verdi.

#5307. Binance Pay, DK Bank and Tether Sign MOU to Expand Stablecoin Payments to Merchants Across Bhutan, Starting with USD₮

Signed at Binance Blockchain Week 2026, the initiative builds on Bhutan's national crypto payment network and plans incentives to help merchants adopt stablecoin payments

BANGKOK, Nov. 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Binance Pay, DK Bank, Gelephu Mindfulness City's official bank, and Tether today signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to bring stablecoin payments to merchants across Bhutan, starting with USDâ®. The MOU was signed at Binance Blockchain Week Bangkok 2026 by Thomas Gregory, Vice President of Payments & Fiat at Binance; Ugyen Tenzin, Chief Executive Officer of DK Bank; and Tether.

The MOU builds on the payment network Binance Pay and DK Bank launched in May 2025, when Bhutan became the first country to introduce a national-level crypto payment system for tourism. Subject to eligibility requirements, users can pay participating merchants with supported digital assets, and merchants receive Bhutanese ngultrum. More than 3,700 merchants now accept payments through the system, from hotels and airlines to roadside vendors.

Under the MOU, the parties will work to promote stablecoin payments for merchants on this network.

To encourage participation, eligible users can receive a 5% rebate on qualifying transactions, capped at US$5 per transaction. Eligibility criteria and final terms are subject to agreement.

"Bhutan has shown that crypto payments can work at a national level," said Thomas Gregory, VP of Payments & Fiat, Binance. "With Tether and DK Bank, we want to make stablecoins and crypto the easier way to pay in Bhutan, and make accepting it worth it for every merchant."

"Since 2025, Bhutanese merchants have shown growing interest in accepting digital payments," said Ugyen Tenzin, CEO of DK Bank. "This initiative further enhances their ability to accept payments from international customers, and merchants can benefit from the reach of digital payment networks while continuing to receive their payments entirely in local currency."

The MOU is non-binding. Implementation, including the launch date and rebate terms, remains subject to final agreement between the parties.

About Binance Pay: Binance Pay is a secure, seamless, and borderless payment feature on Binance. It enables users and merchants to pay with fiat or crypto, and send and receive cryptocurrencies worldwide, all without gas fees. Supporting more than 300 cryptocurrencies and accepted by over 21 million merchants globally, Binance Pay helps connect digital assets with everyday commerce. Since its launch in 2021, Binance Pay has processed more than $321 billion in transaction volume.

About DK Bank:  Established in 2021, DK Bank is Gelephu Mindfulness City's official bank, serving individuals and corporations within the Gelephu Mindfulness City (GMC) and across the Kingdom. With a focus on innovation, cross-border payments, and emerging financial technologies, DK Bank is building an integrated financial ecosystem that bridges traditional banking with Web3 finance. For more information, visit https://www.dk.bt.

About Tether and USDâ®:  Tether is a pioneer in stablecoin technology. It aims to revolutionize the global financial landscape and provide accessible, secure, and efficient financial, communication, and energy infrastructure that helps enhance security and efficiency. Tether enables greater financial inclusion and communication resilience, fosters economic growth, and empowers individuals and businesses.

As the creator of the industry's largest, most transparent, and liquid stablecoin, Tether is dedicated to building a sustainable and resilient infrastructure for the benefit of underserved communities. By leveraging cutting-edge blockchain and peer-to-peer technology, it is committed to bridging the gap between traditional financial systems and the potential of decentralized finance.

#5306. StepSecurity, led by two Microsoft vets, raises $20M to defend developers’ tools from hackers

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am

StepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft. This week, as their startup announced a new round of funding, its researchers were also investigating a hacked Microsoft software package.

Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.

StepSecurity, a Seattle-area cybersecurity startup, raised a $20 million Series A round led by Elephant, with participation from existing investors Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital and SaaS Ventures. The company has now raised $23 million, including a $3 million seed round in 2024. Axios Pro first reported the latest round.

The startup protects the systems used to build software: developers’ laptops, code repositories, package downloads and CI/CD pipelines, the automated systems that assemble and ship code.

The problem is that attackers increasingly slip malicious code into open-source software that developers download. That code can do damage as soon as it runs on a developer’s laptop or build system, stealing the passwords and keys that unlock other systems.

“A supply chain attack used to take a skilled team,” CEO Varun Sharma wrote in a blog post announcing the funding. “Now one person can vibe code it.”

Sharma spent about 15 years at Microsoft, where he led a team in Azure Security focused on making security easier for developers. CTO Ashish Kurmi spent nearly eight years at Microsoft before leading cloud security at Uber and infrastructure security at Plaid.

The two met at Microsoft and started StepSecurity in 2021, after working through the fallout from the SolarWinds and Codecov supply chain attacks at their respective employers.

A busy week: The Microsoft package, agent-framework, is the Python version of Microsoft’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

It gets roughly 190,000 downloads a month. Two malicious versions published on Nov. 17 to PyPI, the main public repository for Python software, included code designed to steal cloud and CI/CD credentials as soon as Python started up, SecurityWeek reported. PyPI quarantined both versions, and a Microsoft maintainer said an investigation was underway.

That’s one entry in a long list. StepSecurity’s announcement also cites the $6.3 billion Binance breach in October, which the FBI attributed to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Binance has said the attack started with a compromised employee laptop.

It also points to a tampered copy of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension that sat in Cursor’s extension marketplace for about 11 hours last month. Cursor said up to 5,000 users may have received the malicious version.

StepSecurity says it documented 56 confirmed compromises of trusted software components between August 2025 and August 2026, and roughly one every three days from March 2026 through the August report.

How it works: StepSecurity got its start with its own tool, Harden-Runner, which is free for open-source projects. It watches automated builds on GitHub and flags anything unexpected in the processes they run, the network connections they make or the files they change.

More than 20,000 open-source projects use it, the company says, up from about 3,000 at the time of the seed round. Unusual behavior spotted in those public builds has helped StepSecurity catch attacks early, the company says, including the March 2025 compromise of tj-actions, a widely used add-on for GitHub’s build automation.

StepSecurity’s paid products also protect developers’ laptops and check code repositories. Its Secure Registry service screens software packages before a company’s builds download them from public sources such as npm, the main public repository for JavaScript packages. It blocks versions known to be compromised and holds brand-new releases for a waiting period, giving researchers time to catch malicious ones before anyone installs them.

Along with the funding, StepSecurity is making Secure Registry free for public GitHub projects that use Harden-Runner and run their builds on GitHub’s servers. The free version defaults to a two-day waiting period and supports JavaScript packages, with Python, Java, Ruby and Rust planned.

StepSecurity has plenty of competition. Socket, a San Francisco startup that screens open-source packages for malicious code, raised $60 million at a $1 billion valuation in May. Sonatype, JFrog and Endor Labs also sell tools that can block risky packages before they’re installed.

Growth spurt: StepSecurity says its annual recurring revenue grew fivefold in 2024, fivefold again in 2025 and more than fivefold so far this year. It didn’t disclose dollar figures.

Named customers include Circle, Dexcom, Kong, Mercari, Chainguard and XBOW.

The company has 27 employees, up from four, including the founders, at the time of the seed round. Sharma is based in Sammamish and Kurmi in Kirkland, and the rest of the remote-first team is spread across the U.S., Canada and India.

What’s next: StepSecurity plans to extend its protections to agent sandboxes, the isolated environments where AI agents run code. Its argument is that anyone who asks an AI agent for a spreadsheet may be downloading and running open-source packages.

The company says it also plans to double its team over the next 12 months, mostly in security research, engineering and sales and marketing.

#5304. Vitalik Buterin Is Designing Chips: Could Ethereum Become a Hardware Company and Overtake Nvidia?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Vitalik Buterin is taking Ethereum’s decentralization philosophy down to the silicon level. The Ethereum co-founder published a deep dive into open-source chip design today, covering everything from transistor architecture and manufacturing to hardware security. His central argument? It could have implications far beyond Ethereum, and computing hardware shouldn’t remain a proprietary black box.

Could Ethereum eventually move beyond blockchain infrastructure and build its own hardware ecosystem? Vitalik’s latest exploration makes that prospect an interesting thought experiment, particularly as Nvidia dominates the computing industry.

Vitalik’s argument starts with a familiar problem in crypto: trust. Software can be audited, code can be published, and blockchain transactions can be independently verified. Hardware, however, remains considerably harder to inspect.

A chip can contain hidden vulnerabilities or malicious modifications that users cannot easily detect. Even a secure wallet application cannot guarantee safety if the hardware underneath it has been compromised. This has happened recently with Ledger, and Ledger is not the only one, with Trezor and other hardware wallets being recently compromised.

“Not your silicon, not your keys.” – Vitalik put the problem bluntly.

The phrase extends crypto’s self-custody mantra into the physical computing layer. Owning private keys might not mean much if users cannot trust the hardware handling them.

This is why Vitalik argues that “the hardware layer must be open for participation and tinkering too.” He wants hardware designs to become accessible to developers, researchers, and independent auditors, allowing them to examine and modify components rather than blindly trusting manufacturers.

This could eventually create opportunities for Ethereum hardware focused on security, cryptographic computing, and decentralized infrastructure. Ethereum validators, hardware wallets, and zero-knowledge proof systems all depend on computing components that users need to trust.

Nvidia built its dominance by turning GPUs into the backbone of artificial intelligence. Its hardware, software ecosystem, and CUDA platform have made competition increasingly difficult.

But Vitalik’s vision displays a different approach. Instead of chasing the fastest processors, Ethereum hardware could prioritize openness, verifiability, and security.

Vitalik acknowledges that open-source hardware faces performance limitations. Advanced chip manufacturing remains expensive and tightly controlled, leaving open designs behind the industry’s most sophisticated commercial processors.

Yet that trade-off might not matter for every workload. Vitalik writes that “Secure hardware may be 10x less efficient or more” while still being sufficient for many computing needs. That’s a striking contrast to an industry obsessed with squeezing more performance from increasingly expensive chips.

Ethereum already has an extensive developer community experimenting with cryptography and distributed computing. Extending that culture into silicon could give the ecosystem a foothold in hardware without immediately challenging Nvidia’s AI infrastructure.

The ambition could be less about building another GPU giant and more about creating a competing hardware philosophy.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Vitalik’s argument reaches beyond blockchain. He sees open hardware as a broader computing movement, where users can inspect, verify, and modify the machines they depend on.

That could eventually extend into personal computers, servers, IoT devices, and secure computing infrastructure. Hardware designed around transparency could become valuable as AI, financial services, and sensitive personal data move into increasingly powerful machines.

Nvidia’s dominance isn’t going to disappear overnight. But Ethereum has never needed to follow the traditional technology industry’s playbook.

Its greatest strength has been building infrastructure around open participation rather than centralized ownership. If that philosophy eventually reaches the silicon powering modern computing, Ethereum could find itself competing in an industry few would have expected.

Vitalik’s latest deep dive into chip design raises a question: What happens when crypto’s decentralization movement stops at software and starts building the hardware, too?

#5303. How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am

It has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do. This has nothing to do with the willingness of defenders to try. It has everything to do with the ancient truth that to succeed, defenders have to get it right every time but adversaries only have to get it right occasionally.

Now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI. Do you like that math? Does anyone?

The disastrous update that broke Teams, Outlook, SharePoint and other packages was not a direct attack by AI-wielding bad guys. Nor was the FAA outage. Nor were most of the outage events of the past few weeks, though who can say what’s up with those European Union refrigerators.

No. The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated for several months now not on powerful new AI-honed attacks, but on an absolute deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and other defenders with a formal patch process aren’t built to process.

The question is whether traditional patch programs can adapt their processes to handle the deluge. Microsoft’s is MAPP (Microsoft Active Protections Program), to which the company has been committed for nearly two decades. If the industry-spanning events of the past few weeks are any indication, these programs can’t.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said Wednesday at the New York Times DealBook Summit that last week’s Microsoft 365 outage came from a latent bug and wasn’t directly tied to AI, but he warned that AI-driven patching could bring more instability.

He elaborated in a separate appearance on CNBC the same day, saying the flood of patches being applied to older infrastructure is making systems less stable.

AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” Nadella said, when asked by Jim Cramer about a string of recent outages at United, Schwab, Chase and other organizations.

Some context: MAPP turned 18 this year. The program, run by the MSRC (Microsoft Security Response Center), handles outreach to partner companies that gain early access to information on the bugs in advance of each month’s Patch Tuesday release. In-house, it coordinates the patch release process, just as the larger MSRC organization helps coordinate the handling of bug reports from external finders.

MSRC also runs point on prioritizing patches of the worst bugs through its SSIRP (Software and Services Incident Response Plan) program, itself dating to 2004. In its time, it was an industry leader in how companies can efficiently get their arms around bad bugs.

MAPP in its own way is similarly remarkable. It has undergone a few traumas over the years, usually when a partner breaks confidence and leaks the advance details it receives. In 2025, after attacks on SharePoint raised suspicions of a leak from the program, Microsoft stopped giving Chinese companies early access. But MAPP continues to tick along in a way that would make any program manager proud. Other companies have their own version of MAPP / MSRC, as do community efforts such as those supporting Linux.

Full disclosure: I’m a former MSRC employee who learned about MAPP at the knee of the program’s principals. I subsequently tracked patch releases at a company partnered with MAPP at its highest (Validate) level, which means I was privy to the 14-day multi-stage run-up to each month’s release. I admire and respect the program… and I’m afraid that in the AI-finder era, it’s in big, big trouble.

Since January 2021, Microsoft has issued patches for an estimated 10,319 CVEs. (I use estimated numbers throughout this analysis because there are various ways of counting such things, including whether or not the patch accrues to an application such as Edge, which actually relies on the Chromium project for its fixes. Other analysts arrive at larger or smaller counts.)

Over half of those — 5,383 CVEs — are 2026 releases, 5,128 of which were addressed since April. In comparison, 2025’s full-year CVE total was 1,180.

What happened in April? As nearly as analysis can determine, the floodgates opened and finders (security researchers) started barraging the company with reports.

The first quarter of 2026 saw 255 CVEs addressed over three months. April had 163, May 132; in June the number jumped to 209. In July it was off to the races with 575 CVEs. In October, the monthly count topped 1,400.

Most of these bugs aren’t coming from the usual security stalwarts. They’re coming from new finders, they’re coming in with multiple simultaneous finders not believed to be working together, and they’re coming in relatively weak.

Though the overall volume has skyrocketed, the number per month of bugs under active exploit in the wild — the notorious “zero-days” — hasn’t increased proportionally.

Moreover, average bug severity has in fact decreased. Until 2026, the average CVSS severity score for all bugs tended to hover around 7.8 (out of 10) each month. In 2026, that’s dropped to approximately 7.4 as of September — not garbage finds, but the sort of thing that doesn’t scramble the jets.

No surge in zero-days and a drop in severity — that’s good news. The problem is the volume.

Once bugs are received by Microsoft, each goes through a MAPP-helmed, multi-team process of investigation and patch development.

The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated not on powerful new AI-honed attacks, but on a deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and others aren’t built to process.

Since many products have several versions still in support, that often means that multiple teams within each product group are asked to ingest a bug report, replicate the problem, devise and test a fix, ensure the fix doesn’t trigger other problems or inadvertently point to a similar bug elsewhere in the product and ready it for mass consumption. Even AI slop has to be taken seriously, just in case.

Meanwhile, MAPP is the traffic cop for the entire release, working with each team to ascertain patches are ready, understand the nature of the bugs and what can be safely communicated to partners and the public, and ready the processes that make the second Tuesday of each month a festival of downloads and reboots. From where we stand right now, it’s all fairly… hand-crafted.

In theory the process is automatable to some extent, though the success of that effort so far in light of recent events is debatable. But high volume also leads to other problems, such as exposing information on incomplete patching.

For instance, Microsoft has recently patched Office bugs that apply to both Windows and Mac, but patches have initially only been available for Windows versions.

Microsoft’s release-day information about such bugs — patching Windows versions while asking Apple users to monitor Microsoft communications for news of their own patch — alerts the world, including eager adversaries, that the flaw exists. Apple customers just have to hope no adversaries exploit it while their patch is pending.

More broadly, many of the steps in the current patching process involve judgment calls, not processes that scale well or that can reliably be handled by existing AI-driven systems. In Microsoft’s case, MAPP is a remarkably small team of humans and, being security folk at Microsoft, they’re not always the loudest or most popular voice in Redmond.

Add the mercurial nature of finders, who may or may not provide full details on their bugs (ask any MSRC person how often they receive a crash dump and a demand for payment) and may or may not disclose their finds publicly if they don’t feel they’re getting sufficient response.

Do not add the kind of defender staffing needed to handle a massive increase in volume — either in MAPP or in the individual product groups building the actual patches — because in the AI era, it’s likely the companies won’t add it either.

The cracks are showing. Microsoft has been compelled to issue OOB (out-of-band) releases and servicing updates monthly since July, often within just a few days of the original release.

OOBs are important enough to merit release outside the usual patch cadence, often because there’s a security issue involved, but they’re tough on administrators already wading through a slew of regularly scheduled patching. With volumes high, patch testers may rush or elide certain steps, such as checking that a fix doesn’t break something deeper in the system.

Nadella told the DealBook audience this week that a patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week. Now, he said, the patch “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create instability.”

Think of MAPP as Mariners catcher Dan Wilson in 2001: a pro handling a staff of skilled human pitchers, one pitch at a time. Now it’s 2026, and the pitchers have been swapped for a bank of mediocre pitching machines all slinging fastballs at … 2026-era Dan Wilson.

Here, again, AI can’t fix a system that requires defenders to catch every pitch. Secondary lines of defense that have worked in the past — for instance, the requirement by various regulatory programs that enterprises ascertain that patches are safe for their own systems — rely heavily on companies sending out the soundest possible patches.

Managed service providers might at least make sure that patches are flagged to customers as available, relevant and urgent. But they’re in no position to do much more than trust that what’s shipped is safe to deploy and react when things go wrong.

Even that gets harder when a bug kneecaps the security tools they depend on. Last week’s Microsoft 365 outage affected parts of Microsoft Defender that interact with Exchange Online.

It’s not just Microsoft, of course. The Linux community is seriously suffering, and both Apple and (especially) Google have struggled with patch-release quality in 2026 as evidenced by their own emergency updates and post-release device instability reports. Industry-wide, ecosystems built around reliable, transparent patch cadences and patch-development processes have never seemed more in danger of being overwhelmed.

What needs to happen? Sure, build those AI systems; the marketing people will be pleased. It’ll speed up some parts of the process. But a system capable of replicating, every time, the human judgment calls that go into the patch-release process isn’t going to magically create itself; people have to create it.

Is there some chance that the deluge will ebb — that researchers and their tools will at some point finally find all the bugs in all the world’s products?

It’s a pretty thought, and some relief may eventually come. When more and more unrelated finders turn up the same bug, it gives one hope that the set is finite. But no one knows when relief will come, and most folk in tech suspect that really, no, there is no bottom to the bug barrel. Nor, for the foreseeable future, any rest for the weary.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

#5302. Predictions 2027 and beyond: Amazon’s Werner Vogels on the human advantage in AI

BREAKING ANALYSIS by Dave Vellante

The next phase of artificial intelligence will be judged by how much useful capability it puts in the hands of people, and whether organizations can afford, secure and control that capability over time. Model intelligence is one part of that equation. The architecture surrounding it will determine how much of the promise becomes productive work.

That is our central takeaway from a private discussion with Werner Vogels, Amazon.com Inc.’s chief technology officer, about his technology predictions for 2027 and beyond. His outlook spans biological computing, autonomous defense, sovereignty, personalized medicine and interfaces that decode human intent. Together, these predictions describe a future in which technology extends human capability while placing new demands on the people who design and operate it.

In our discussion, Vogels mixed immediate priorities with longer research horizons. As we’ve put forth in our research, security and sovereignty are already central in enterprise architecture decisions. Living neural systems and everyday brain interfaces have much further to mature. We believe separating those timelines is key to understanding Vogels’ prognostications.

Early in our conversation, Vogels pointed to Cambridge Dictionary’s choice of “human” as its word of the year for 2026.⁠ He likened the growing appeal of human authorship to the way consumers look for organic products. In his words, “human becomes sort of the new organic.”

That narrative became the central thread in our discussion. We pressed him on whether current AI truly learns through experience, how autonomous security can be tested safely, whether sovereignty survives failover and where quantum computing fits. We closed by observing that the conversation had returned to enhancing humanity through technology.

In this Special Breaking Analysis, we examine the five predictions and their implications for the economics and operating model of enterprise AI.

Prediction themes are drawn from our interview; the enterprise implications are our analysis.

Vogels’ first prediction addresses a problem that is central to the AI infrastructure debate, specifically the resources required to produce useful intelligence. In our discussion, he emphasized the expense of operating AI systems for five or 10 years. That shines a light on the lifetime value and costs of the capability that is delivered.

The brain is Vogel’s reference point. It combines memory, processing and adaptation in ways that inspire several distinct approaches to computing. He described three as follows: 1) Using living neurons as computational material; 2) Building hardware that emulates useful features of neural behavior; and 3) Designing software memory that reinforces valuable information while de-emphasizing less useful information.

Notably, biological computing uses living cells. Neuromorphic hardware takes ideas from biology. Agent memory borrows principles about what to retain and what to forget. Each has a different learning path, and progress in one does not necessarily have a direct impact on the others.

In typical Amazon style, Vogels reached into his customer bag of examples and used Australian-based Cortical Labs as a reference. Its CL1 system cultivates living neurons on silicon and connects them to a simulated environment through electrical signals. The company has reported computational benchmark work running at approximately 30 watts. Vogels cited demonstrations involving navigation tasks, including a version of the video game “Doom.” Though these are early demonstrations, the power consumption alone is encouraging.

We asked Vogels if he sees contemporary or future AI systems are autodidactic in the same sense as the biological systems he described. He said: “not like these systems, not like our own brains.”

That question is relevant to enterprise buying decisions. What changes after a system completes a task? Does it retain a record that can be consistently retrieved at a later time? Does it update properly? Does the underlying system learn and adapt? Buyers should expect vendors to explain how and if the system improves through experience, how that is measured, and how incorrect results can be identified and corrected.

The infrastructure implication is that useful work per watt and per dollar continue to be key metrics. A credible benchmark needs to account for accuracy, performance, repeatability and fit with operating requirements. For biological systems, it must also include the realistic demands of maintaining the “living” system.

Vogels sees particular potential where electricity and connectivity are in short supply. Our take is that more efficient learning could expand the range of places where intelligence makes sense. A remote industrial site, for example, would benefit from local capabilities that do not require connectivity all the time to a distant centralized data center. Whether a particular architecture can deliver that benefit remains a question.

For enterprises building agents today, the most relevant implication may be the software memory layer. We believe designers should be precise regarding which experiences an agent retains, which records represent the true corporate knowledge, and when older information should be deleted. As we learned from the big-data days of Hadoop, accumulating more history is useful only if the system can turn that history into better decisions and ultimately action. The same concepts that govern enterprise data should extend to what agents learn from it.

Vogels’ second prediction is that every system will defend itself. His jumping-off point was the falling cost of investigating software for exposures. If an attacker can let loose large numbers of agents, a defender cannot realistically protect its systems without automation.

The economics are becoming notable. Microsoft Corp.’s David Weston, in his Black Hat keynote, reported that generating proofs of concept for 182 confirmed Linux kernel crash incidents averaged $3.61 in model cost per successful case. That figure demonstrates the low cost of a particular validation step, with important work still required around it to account for other factors like initial screening or human validation or patch readiness.

Regardless, Vogels argues that defenders should use the same capacity proactively. He described Amazon’s use of opposing groups of agents where one is searching for attack paths, and another is testing defenses. The analogy he used was Toyota’s andon cord, which allows a production problem to stop the line. In software, he wants known vulnerabilities to trigger action before a release reaches customers. This type of “infinite loop” is becoming more common in security circles.

We asked whether this testing could take place in a digital twin of the environment. Vogels agreed that a replicated execution environment is one way to do it. We believe that is an important architectural concept. Testing an application in isolation can miss the permissions, dependencies or interactions that make a failure more serious. A representative digital environment provides a stronger basis for monitoring those effects and learning from system behavior.

The next piece of the puzzle is remediation. Mozilla reported fixing 423 security bugs across its April 2026 releases, compared with roughly 20 to 30 a month during 2025. Its engineering account shows the work involved in handling the findings and shipping fixes. Greater discovery capacity creates an associated obligation to validate and repair what has been found.

Vogels said the following about the role of expertise: “These tools are there to help the security experts.”⁠ We completely agree. An automated fix can change system behavior in ways that matter to customers. A defensible operating model must establish what the agent can change, how the change is tested, who authorizes consequential actions, and how the organization recovers if the correction causes another problem.

This connects directly with our view of AI cyber resilience. As agents gain permission to take action, a security incident can involve business state as well as infrastructure state. An agent might execute an incorrect transaction or initiate a workflow that continues after the agent itself has been stopped. As such, recovery requires understanding what happened and restoring the affected process to an acceptable state.

We believe the most useful security measures will connect discovery to outcomes. In other words, confirmed exposures are removed, harmful actions can be contained, changes are validated and business operations safely resumed.

The Toyota andon analogy also needs further understanding. Passing a set of automated attacks gives evidence about the tests performed; it doesn’t necessarily prove that a system has no weak points. Continuous testing should strengthen engineering accountability. As Vogels put it, “Without security, you don’t have a business.”

Sovereignty was the most immediate point of connection with our recent work at theCUBE Research. Vogels said the dominant customer conversation had shifted from controlling cost toward questions of dependence and control. His prescribed response is to apply the architectural discipline behind his Frugal Architect framework to sovereignty.

The phrase “non-functional requirement” can muddy the significance for a business audience. It describes a property the system must satisfy in operation. Availability and security are examples. Applying the same treatment to sovereignty means specifying the control requirements before choosing the design, then maintaining proof that the system satisfies them.

AWS’ published Digital Sovereignty Lens reflects that approach. It addresses workload location, access, continuity, portability and evidence of control. It also recognizes that residency requirements can constrain disaster recovery choices.

Vogels cautioned against applying the most restrictive operating model to every workload. “Isolation is not necessarily the same as control,” he told us. We agree that buyers should classify workloads according to the requirements and risks that actually apply. An overly restrictive design can add cost, handcuff the business or limit recovery options without resolving the concerns that prompted it.

Our take is that hard sovereignty requirements should inform which designs are viable. A requirement imposed by law cannot simply be exchanged for a better price (unless the consequences are more valuable than the fine). Preferences and risk tolerances can be weighed within the set of designs that meet those requirements.

We raised this directly in the context of failover. A recovery process can restore technical service while moving data or operations into an unsanctioned location. The design therefore needs to account for the recovery destination and the people who can administer it must be in the proper jurisdiction.

We also pressed on a more demanding requirement. We specifically asked if that means Amazon must offer a customer-operated, air-gapped stack that does not depend on vendor management – a capability our research indicates Amazon doesn’t possess. Vogels responded by emphasizing customer risk assessment and architectural choices, drawing a parallel with longstanding dependencies on database and enterprise software suppliers. He did not give a definitive answer to the specific operating capability we described and essentially dodged the question.

That leaves an important requirement for buyers to resolve with any supplier. If continued operation without vendor management is necessary, the proposed solution should demonstrate it. The evaluation needs to establish who controls administration, updates, identity, keys and recovery, including what happens when a required external service becomes unavailable.

The same discipline applies to model choice. Vogels sees open-weight models as a route to greater control. Our view is that access to weights can expand customer optionality, while practical control also depends on the surrounding software, data, licenses and operating model. Buyers should test the actual substitution they expect to deploy.

His advice on exit was: “Keep the exits open, make sure that you exercise that.” We believe a credible exit strategy is a tested operation, end-to-end. The organization should know what must move, how long it takes, what changes in behavior, what expense is incurred, and which dependencies remain in place. This applies to models, infrastructure, software and contracted services.

The broader implication is that sovereignty has to survive change. A system can meet its requirements at deployment and veer from them as configurations change. We believe control should be demonstrated through the operating lifecycle, including recovery and exit. This is how sovereignty becomes an architectural requirement with teeth.

Vogels’ fourth prediction is rooted in a personal interest in medicine. He described his earlier work in radiology and radiotherapy and the realization that technology could help him contribute to patient outcomes. His emphasis was on how individual a treatment for a disease can be, even if several patients share the same diagnosis.

The challenge is searching an enormous corpus of possible interventions and identifying those worth pursuing for a particular biological problem. Vogels compared it with finding the right key among a billion candidates. Agents can help scientists examine evidence and narrow that search, while scientists can direct the work and verify the results.

We described the destination as “N of 1.” Vogels called it “medicine for one.” We believe the economic opportunity lies in reducing the cost of investigating highly specific problems. If a team can evaluate more possibilities with a given research budget, it may be able to pursue conditions or individual variations that were previously too costly to investigate.

Stanford Medicine reported a virtual research organization using approximately 37,000 AI agents to analyze about 50,000 clinical trials. The work illustrates the scale of evidence synthesis that agents can support.

There is also progress in individualized treatment. In August 2026, Merck and Moderna announced positive topline Phase 3 results for an investigational personalized mRNA therapy combined with pembrolizumab in melanoma. The companies reported meeting recurrence-free and distant-metastasis-free survival endpoints. Though the firms were criticized for potentially profiting from taxpayer-funded research, these findings support the potential of individualized treatment.

The broader movement toward individualized treatment also includes the case of KJ Muldoon, which Vogels highlighted. Researchers at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia and Penn Medicine developed a personalized CRISPR-based therapy for the child. CHOP subsequently reported meaningful clinical improvements, while emphasizing that the treatment was not a cure and that long-term monitoring would continue. The case illustrates how individualized and specific a therapy can become.

Our interpretation is that AI could make the economics of precision treatments much more attractive. The opportunity exists beyond accelerating an existing research task. It could change which questions researchers can afford to ask and which patient groups receive attention.

Despite the technological promise, Vogels consistently placed scientists in the process. That human responsibility is integral to the prediction. The role of agents is to expand the evidence and possibilities available to experts; the experts remain accountable for deciding what to test and how to interpret the result.

We asked whether quantum computing would change the medical opportunity within Vogels’ forecast timeframe. He did not see it as an immediate prerequisite. He expects more capable quantum systems to help in the future, while emphasizing a security issue that organizations should address now.

That issue is the possibility of attackers collecting encrypted information today and decrypting it when capable quantum computers become available. NIST describes this “harvest now, decrypt later” risk and recommends that organizations inventory their cryptographic dependencies and begin planning migration to post-quantum protection.

The practical decision depends on how long information must remain confidential and how long migration will take. Organizations can act on those requirements while the hardware timeline remains uncertain. The same architectural principle applies here as in sovereignty in that future risk can create a design requirement today.

Vogels’ final prediction moves from machines inspired by the brain to interfaces that interpret signals from it. He described the possibility of non-invasive systems translating deliberate intent into actions, reducing the physical steps required to interact with technology.

He was careful, saying: “It’s not mind reading, it’s really trained to decode deliberate intent.”

That clarification should guide how this prediction is discussed. Meta Platforms Inc. and its research collaborators have demonstrated decoding language-related signals recorded while participants typed sentences. The work uses non-invasive measurements of brain activity, but the researchers also identify practical constraints, including imperfect performance and the requirements of the recording equipment. We see this laboratory result as a step toward a practical and usable interface.

We also believe accessibility gives a compelling reason to go after this work. A dependable way to translate intended communication or movement into action could expand independence for people who face substantial barriers with conventional interfaces. The proof will be the performance of those systems with the people and in the environments they are intended to serve.

Vogels’ ambition goes a bit further. He is interested in interfaces that help people retain a fleeting idea, recover a difficult-to-access memory, or express their creativity more effectively. Those are longer-term aspirations.

Our thinking brings another question: How does the person retain control? A useful system should make clear when it is active, what it retains and how the user can stop or correct an action. If neural information becomes part of an interface, consent and control should be part of the design from the beginning.

This brings the discussion back to sovereignty at an individual level. The objective is to give a person greater ability to communicate and act. We believe the system should preserve that person’s control over the capability and the information it generates.

Vogels’ closing thoughts were around creativity, judgment and wisdom. These were the human qualities he wants technology to amplify, not replace. That is why we ended our conversation by connecting its human-centered opening to the possibility of technology that helps people exercise more of their distinctive abilities.

We believe Vogels’ outlook gives enterprise leaders two kinds of work. The near-term opportunity is architectural – ways to improve operating economics, make adversarial testing continuous, establish sovereignty requirements and prepare for changes in cryptography. The longer-term work is to track emerging capabilities mapped to useful applications.

For infrastructure suppliers, our interpretation is that success will depend increasingly on the cost and reliability of the outcome their systems support. For software suppliers, the opportunity includes memory, identity and access, testing and recovery capabilities that make agents dependable. For buyers, the mandate is demand demonstrations that reflect the conditions under which the system will actually operate.

Human responsibility is a recurring theme across all five predictions. Security experts must assess consequential changes. Enterprise leaders must decide which dependencies are acceptable. Scientists must validate candidate treatments. People using new interfaces must retain authority over their actions and information. Increased machine capability makes these responsibilities more serious.

Vogel’s predictions also suggest a good way to evaluate AI investment. We should ask which blockers are being removed, what new bottleneck arises, and whether the complete process produces a better outcome.

“Whatever we can do to amplify our unique skills will be very important in the future,” Vogels told us.

We enthusiastically share that view. The opportunity is to make useful intelligence accessible to more people and more organizations, with the economics and controls required to make it viable. That is the human advantage we see running through these predictions, and the standard against which we believe the next phase of AI should be judged.

Thanks to Werner Vogels for sharing his year-end predictions with us and good luck at AWS re:Invent 2026. John Furrier and theCUBE team will be broadcasting and SiliconANGLE will have the news. You can catch all the action on thecube.net and siliconangle.com.

#5301. Bitcoin News: Swiss ETF Debut Meets $7B Options Expiry and US Strategic Reserve Push

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin is facing a crowded weekend as bearish options positioning collides with a new Swiss spot ETF and news on the US Strategic Bitcoin Reserve. Nearly $7 billion in Bitcoin options expire November 27, while traders have shifted heavily toward downside protection. Meanwhile, Switzerland’s first spot Bitcoin ETF begins trading, and Washington is moving legislation that could lock government-held BTC away for 20 years.

Bitcoin hasn’t found much footing near $60,000, and Friday’s massive options expiry could make matters worse. But the bearish mood contrasts with developments in institutional access and US crypto policy, creating a market that could swing sharply with sentiment changes.

Around $7 billion in Bitcoin options expire Friday on Deribit, with another $600 million in Ethereum contracts expiring alongside them. Bitcoin options positioning has shifted rather sharply since October, when traders were betting more heavily on a recovery toward $90,000 and $100,000.

The put-call open interest ratio has climbed to 0.81 across all expiries, compared with 0.55 ahead of October’s settlement. Friday’s contracts show a ratio of 0.89, reflecting growing demand for downside protection as Bitcoin trades around $59,000.

Deribit Chief Commercial Officer Jean-David Pequignot said positioning had changed considerably since October, with puts now concentrated at $60,000 and lower. He pointed to major defensive clusters around $60,000, $58,000, $50,000 and $40,000.

Implied volatility has also climbed. Deribit’s Bitcoin DVOL index, which measures expected volatility over the next 30 days, rose to around 55 from 38 in October. Near-term options are now commanding a higher premium than longer-dated contracts, suggesting traders expect turbulence in the coming weeks.

History, however, offers no clear bearish signal from expiry alone. Bitcoin finished higher in the week following seven of the past 12 monthly expiries, lower after four, and unchanged after one. The median absolute move was 2.15%, compared with 3.1% for ordinary seven-day periods.

Bitcoin’s institutional access is expanding even as traders brace for another volatile session. The Bitcoin Fund ETF, ticker BBIT, began trading on the SIX Swiss Exchange today, giving Swiss investors direct Bitcoin exposure through a regulated investment fund.

The fund launched with 350 BTC and charges a 0.19% annual expense ratio. Bitcoin is held in cold storage at Swiss bank AMINA, with the fund available in Swiss francs and US dollars through traditional securities accounts.

🇨🇭 Today, Bitcoin Fund ETF (BBIT) will list on SIX Swiss Exchange: Switzerland’s first and only FINMA-approved Bitcoin ETF.🕘 Trading opens at 9:00 CET (8:00 UTC)News announcement: https://t.co/N112jUZiUP*Switzerland only. Not for US persons. Capital at risk. pic.twitter.com/CJa7lkh3uT

This launch is unlikely to reverse Bitcoin’s price weakness overnight. But it shows institutional infrastructure continuing to grow while prices fall, potentially widening the investor base when market sentiment eventually improves.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

🇺🇸JUST IN: The US Strategic Bitcoin Reserve bill is now eligible for a full House vote, banning any $BTC sales for 20 YEARS.Under the bill, Reserve Bitcoin can't be "sold, swapped, auctioned, encumbered, or otherwise disposed of" for at least 20 years.The bill does not allow… pic.twitter.com/qJmsgFtpWX

The House Financial Services Committee advanced the American Reserve Modernization Act, H.R. 8957, which would establish the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve in federal law. The bill would prohibit reserve Bitcoin from being sold, swapped, auctioned, or otherwise disposed of for at least 20 years. It also requires federal agencies to provide the Treasury with an accounting of their Bitcoin and other digital asset holdings.

The legislation has now been formally reported to the House and placed on the Union Calendar, making it eligible for a floor vote. It has not yet passed Congress, but it is good news for Bitcoin holders nevertheless.

Bitcoin now has a near-term derivatives test and two longer-term developments running in its favor. Friday could expose just how pessimistic the market has become.

#5300. Startup Spotlight: An engineer’s search for better, safer baby products led him to launch Birch

Startup Spotlight profiles tech startups in the Pacific Northwest.

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:41 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:41 am

A new baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night? What if nursing is a challenge. What is that rash?! Given the countless unknowns, the last thing a parent needs are worries about the quality of the baby’s crib or the chemicals in a pacifier.

But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.

“We struggled a lot,” Gangiredla said. “We did a lot of research on what was safe, what’s not.”

An engineer with roughly 20 years of experience in supply chains and logistics, including roles at Amazon, Flexport and TikTok, Gangiredla found himself on the consumer side of the retail equation, scrutinizing strollers and bottles.

To spare other parents the same headache, he turned that research into Birch, an online marketplace that offers baby product buying guides and assigns each item a TrustScore. Its scoring system draws on certifications, lab reports and recall databases to help parents assess goods ranging from baby wipes to teething toys.

The site provides information on more than 10,000 items across 110 brands, including manufacturing locations, suppliers, certificate numbers and test reports.

Birch has contracts with brands it has checked out, and serves as their merchant of record, meaning if a customer has issues with a product or wants to return it, Birch handles those steps. It operates fulfillment centers in Los Angeles and New Jersey.

Gangiredla said the startup flips the e-commerce approach of retail giants, focusing on the shoppers’ needs, not those of the merchant. It does not accept ads or sponsored rankings.

If you took away the ad revenue for Amazon or TikTok, “the business wouldn’t exist,” Gangiredla said. “So it’s very difficult for them to approach the problem in a different way.”

The platform also offers a gift registry and tools for tracking fetal development during pregnancy, an infant’s nursing and sleep schedules, and other developmental steps. The tools are free for users.

We caught up with Gangiredla, Birch’s CEO and founder, for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.

In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch

Birch is the trust-first platform for baby and kids products and parenting resources. We research and score products across 50+ safety and quality signals before listing — and stock only what clears the bar — so parents skip the endless research and buy with confidence, from pregnancy through the toddler years.

What problem are you obsessed with solving?

The impossible research burden on new parents. Every purchase feels like a safety decision, the information is scattered and often unverified, and the stakes feel enormous. We’re obsessed with moving the work of figuring out what’s trustworthy off the parent and onto a system that does it rigorously — and then showing our work.

What surprised you after talking to customers?

How universal the trust problem is. We assumed it would track with income or with first-time parents, but our customers span all 50 states and every kind of household — big metros to small towns. And what they consistently want isn’t more options or a lower price; it’s someone to tell them, credibly, what’s actually worth buying.

How has AI changed the way you build your company?

It’s core, not a feature. Our TrustScore engine evaluates thousands of products across dozens of safety and quality signals in ways a human team our size never could, and the same intelligence powers discovery and personalization. It also lets a very lean team operate like a much larger one — and we now license that engine to other baby and kids brands as a product called Juno.

What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

That “curated” means limited or expensive. Curation isn’t about carrying less for its own sake, or about selling premium — it’s about removing the untrustworthy. In our own data, price and trustworthiness barely correlate; some of the highest-scoring products are among the most affordable. Fewer and better, not fewer and pricier.

What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Turning away brands and revenue. When you’re early, every dollar is tempting — but our entire promise is that everything on Birch has earned its place. Saying no to products and partners that didn’t clear the bar, even when the revenue was real, was hard. It’s also the decision that defines what we are.

What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Earn trust before you try to scale it. It’s slower and less glamorous than chasing growth, but trust compounds and shortcuts don’t. And talk to your customers far earlier, and far more often, than feels comfortable.

…a parent’s first instinct, the moment they find out they’re expecting, is to come to Birch — and “did you check the TrustScore?” is just how families talk about buying for their kids.

#5299. Hinge’s founder once bribed students with chocolate bars to get the $691 million-a-year dating app off the ground: ‘I had to beg and borrow a lot’

Today, Hinge has more than 30 million users, with a date being set up every two seconds. But in 2011, when it launched, its founder Justin McLeod was just a young Harvard Business School student—and he was so desperate for people to sign up for his app that the fresh-faced, twenty-something entrepreneur even bribed them with chocolate.

At the time, online dating largely took place on desktops and required real effort. The idea of swiping to find the love of your life (or a one-night stand) on your mobile phone seemed alien.

So persuading fellow students (who had no shortage of opportunities to meet people in class and dorms and at parties) to sign up for Hinge was challenging, McLeod told Fortune.

“I remember the days of running around the college library in Washington, D.C., at this college, Georgetown, and bribing kids with Kit Kats to come try my app,” he said, laughing. “We would get dozens of users a day—maybe, if that.”

Financing Hinge also required a lot of scrappiness, with McLeod adding he had to “beg and borrow a lot” to get the app off the ground.

“I was out there networking and talking to as many people as I could and taking money from anyone who would give it to me. That’s just what it takes sometimes,” he said. “I was collecting—me—literally like, $5,000 checks and $10,000 checks to come and start Hinge.”

These days, it’s hard enough landing an internship while studying—let alone walking straight into a full-time job right after graduation. But for McLeod, that wasn’t the case: He hadn’t even finished his second year of business school when McKinsey offered him a spot in its coveted grad program.

A career in consulting would have set McLeod on a path to a six-figure salary, with Glassdoor estimating that the average consultant earns between $173,000 to $233,000 a year. McLeod’s sign-on bonus alone was $12,000.

It turned out to be the big break he needed—to finally get Hinge off the ground.

“I was able to keep putting off my offer for, like, a couple of years,” he said, while adding that he “borrowed” the money to build his app.

“Once Hinge started to become successful, and they saw I was the founder of it, they were like, ‘You’re probably not coming to be an analyst here, are you?’ And, of course, by that time I had to pay it back.”

Why did McLeod choose the highly risky path of entrepreneurship when he could have had a comfortable career at McKinsey?

“I turned down my offer and started to work on Hinge, really because I was just so passionate about the idea. Once I started thinking about it, it was hard for me to stop. I really knew this was what I was meant to work on,” McLeod added.

Of course, it paid off: By 2015, Hinge had raised $26.35 million and had an estimated valuation of $75.5 million, before [hotlink]Match Group[/hotlink] bought the company from McLeod for an undisclosed amount.

The founder treated himself and his family to a nearly $13 million apartment in New York soon after. Meanwhile, Hinge brought in around $691 million last year, according to its parent company Match Group. And after more than a decade shaping modern romance, McLeod left Hinge behind last year to launch his next venture: another dating app, with an AI twist, called Overtone.

Like McLeod, young people today aren’t dreaming of holding down a nine-to-five gig after college or climbing the corporate ladder. Research consistently shows they want to be their own boss.

And they’re already making those dreams a reality: In fact, the second fastest-growing job title among Gen Z grads right now is “founder,” according to LinkedIn.

His advice for young entrepreneurs: “You have to be hopelessly idealistic and ruthlessly practical at the same time—that’s how you create something big and successful.

“Some people who are, like, too in the hopelessly idealistic camp, dream but never make something a reality, and people who are too in the ruthlessly practical camp do things but nothing that big or game-changing,” McLeod explained.

Instead, he said, successful founders like himself constantly balance the two: Essentially dream big, but “pay attention to the very practical day-to-day realities in order to make that come to life.”

Meanwhile, for Gen Zers who don’t know what they want to do career-wise after school, his advice is to stop overthinking it—just give work a go, whether that’s starting your own business or dipping your toes in the rat race.

“I think people who get too self-involved in, like, ‘What’s my career going to be? What am I going to do?’ They miss the opportunity to cultivate that passion, that interest for something out there in the world,” he said.

“I would never have figured out what I wanted if I just sat around, like, meditating about it. I had to work a summer in health care and realize, ‘That’s not it.’ I worked on a few other startup ideas before Hinge came to me, and it was a lot of figuring out what I didn’t like or what didn’t resonate with me. But each time, I got a little bit smarter and a little bit closer.”

A version of this story originally published at Fortune.com on Sept. 22, 2024.
