#5298. Microsoft ‘To Do’ users make a big to-do over popular task app’s pending retirement

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 2:06 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 2:07 pm

Microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal users that Microsoft To Do would be their new home. Now they’re being asked to pack up again.

Microsoft plans to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app. Microsoft disclosed the change Wednesday in a long Planner blog post amid the company’s Ignite announcements, and Windows Latest flagged the change later that day.

The reaction was swift and mostly unhappy. Tom Warren of The Verge summed it up on X: “Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app.”

That’s not entirely fair to Planner, which is built for a different job. But it captures the gripe: To Do was simple, free and worked across Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and the web, and nothing Microsoft is offering replaces all of that.

For work and school accounts, Microsoft says Planner “will be the destination for managing personal work tasks,” but “existing To Do tasks and lists will not migrate to Planner.” It says it will offer a way to export To Do data before the app shuts down.

Tony Redmond of Office365itpros, who tracks Microsoft 365 closely, cataloged the gaps: no file attachments on private Planner tasks, no equivalent for To Do’s list groups, no transfer of shared-list membership, assignments or permissions, and no native Planner apps for Windows or Mac.

He also noted the irony that Outlook’s old Exchange-based tasks will outlive To Do.

Why Microsoft is doing it: The company said putting individual and shared work on the same foundation lets it deliver more consistent features, and lets people connect their own tasks to Copilot and other AI agents. A new Planner agent, available with a Copilot add-on license, can take on tasks and generate status reports.

The Register’s Richard Speed put it less charitably, saying Microsoft had slipped the news into “this week’s Ignite AI puffery.”

Users weigh in: Brad Silverberg, the former Microsoft executive who led Windows 95 development and later became a Seattle venture investor, posted on X that he has used To Do daily, and Wunderlist before it.

“Very disappointed now,” he wrote, adding that he’s looking at TickTick and Todoist.

Similar posts piled up on LinkedIn from Microsoft 365 consultants and everyday users, some of them describing Planner as clunky by comparison.

Patrick Husting, a Seattle-area entrepreneur and software developer whose Ghostwriter add-in brought AI to Microsoft Office before Microsoft announced Microsoft 365 Copilot, offered on LinkedIn to maintain To Do for Microsoft for free.

Rivals smell an opportunity: Competitors wasted no time. TickTick posted a migration guide for To Do refugees. Todoist CEO Amir Salihefendic wrote on LinkedIn that the shutdown was “pretty unexpected” and pointed out that his app has outlasted competitors for 20 years.

The most pointed pitch came from Superlist, which called itself “the natural successor” and said it already has a tool for importing To Do lists. Wunderlist founder Christian Reber started the company in 2020.

Reber and his co-founders sold Wunderlist’s parent company, 6Wunderkinder, to Microsoft in 2015 for a reported $100 million to $200 million. In 2019, as Microsoft prepared to shut the app down, he publicly asked Satya Nadella to sell it back. Microsoft kept it, then retired it in favor of To Do.

Now some of those former Wunderlist users may end up back with the people who built it.

#5297. High earners are feeling the pain of wealth creep—and it’s leading to a new tradeoff in their spending

Some of investing’s top voices have always warned against lifestyle creep. You have Warren Buffett still driving a beat-up car and living in his modest Nebraska home; Sheraton Hotels and Purdue Farms heiress Mitzi Perdue flying economy and wearing hand-me-downs; actress Keke Palmer keeping her rent below $1,500; and the 30-year-old billionaire founder Lucy Guo shopping at Shein and driving a Honda Civic.

But what you’re starting to see is the other side of this: High earners (who, albeit, may not be billionaires or millionaires) opting to forgo the small things and splurge on the big stuff.

Walmart’s latest quarter shows who is hunting for deals: upper-income households drove the retailer’s market-share gains across categories in the three months ended Oct. 31, the company said Thursday. Walmart ended the quarter with about 7,700 price rollbacks, many of them on food.

But the same shoppers filling carts with discounted pantry staples aren’t necessarily cutting back across the board. A growing number of affluent consumers appear to be making a new kind of financial tradeoff: skimping on everyday purchases while preserving room in their budgets for travel, concerts, restaurants, and other experiences. Call it selective spending: bargain hunting for groceries or household goods, then paying up for a five-star hotel or a Michelin restaurant.

Erin O’Connor-Bell, director of financial planning and client experience at Aprio Wealth Management, said she sees that behavior as part of a broader shift in how consumers think about value. O’Connor-Bell, who specializes in shifting behavior and mindsets around finances, leads Aprio’s financial planning department and focuses on helping clients align their financial lives with their goals and values.

“Individuals with disposable income may look for lower prices amid rising costs, but are also more likely to spend money on experiences,” O’Connor-Bell told Fortune. “So they are okay with spending money on special trips or concerts or meals. And I think that suggests that this group may make financial tradeoffs in certain areas, but value those experience-based expenditures.”

The high earner buying discount groceries may be the same person booking a five-star hotel, not because they’re financially confused, but because they’ve decided what they value in their spending.

For some consumers, a grocery store is just a grocery store. If the same pasta, cheese, paper towels, or pantry staples can be found at a lower price, the savings feel rational. (After all, it’s one banana, why should it cost $10?) But a birthday dinner, a long-awaited trip, or a concert with friends may offer something harder for these consumers to put a price tag on: social connection, pleasure, or a sense of well-being.

“Those experiences, those tradeoffs, are still worth it to them,” O’Connor-Bell said. “So they’re still willing to go out for an expensive meal, if it’s fostering social connection and giving them that sense of well-being that maybe they don’t get from the grocery store that they choose.”

However, the ability to treat thrift as a strategy is not universal. Terrance Williams of TruStage, a mutual insurance company geared toward middle-market consumers (defined as households making between $55,000 to $160,000), said the insurer is seeing middle-market consumers make harder tradeoffs as grocery, gas, housing, and other costs squeeze household budgets. Some customers, he said, are calling to lower premiums, restructure coverage, or cancel policies altogether.

“What we’re seeing is that consumers are now having to make tough decisions,” Williams told Fortune. “They’re tightening their budgets and having to make decisions about what do I keep and what do I continue to lean into?” For some households, he added, the choice can come down to essentials: “Do I pay for my cell phone because I have to have that? Or do I pay for my life insurance policy?”

For high earners, buying cheaper groceries may be less about financial stress and more about redirecting money toward the experiences or comforts they value most. A person may drive an aging car, comparison-shop for groceries, or brew coffee at home while still spending thousands on travel. But O’Connor-Bell said those decisions often reflect personal priorities rather than strict budgeting.

“You could still be spending money on that special trip and be driving a 20-year-old vehicle,” she said. “It kind of leads back to individual preferences and what they value.”

Rising prices have made even comfortable households more aware of costs. Inflation rose a staggering 1%, hitting grocery items the hardest: coffee, nonalcoholic beverages, and other food items were among the most affected. But some of these financial decisions, O’Connor-Bell said, are often shaped by one’s upbringing and emotions.

“This is about personal experiences and your history, your feelings toward money,” she said. “It’s definitely much deeper than just running the numbers.”

That can be especially true for people whose current income differs sharply from the household they grew up in. (As referenced above, Keke Palmer is a prime example: Her parents were making $40,000 when she got her first big TV role.) Some may find it hard to spend even when they can afford to. Others may need help understanding where their money is going and whether their spending lines up with their long-term goals.

O’Connor-Bell said her role is not to tell clients which purchases are worthy, but to help them understand the tradeoffs.

“It is my job to help people understand what their choices impact long-term or short-term,” she said. “I have clients that are just like you who say, ‘I’m going to save that money. I’m not going to buy coffee anymore. I can get my own beans and make my own coffee in the morning.’ And that is a tradeoff that they’re consciously making. The next question is, what is that money then going toward?”

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on April 30, 2026.

Catherina covers markets, the economy, energy, tech, and AI.

#5296. After years of missteps, Nike is racing to repair its relationship with runners

When Swedish track star Andreas Almgren won the men’s 2026 New York City Marathon in his marathon debut earlier this month in the Nike Apex racing shoe that hits the market in January, he gave the struggling sportswear giant a dream opportunity to bolster its credibility with serious runners. Nike has put Almgren front and center; he even discussed the merits of the Nike shoe at its investor day last week. Nike also paid for the insert the New York Times traditionally publishes the morning after the marathon that includes the names and times of most race participants. And last week, Nike renewed its sponsorship deal with the Chicago Marathon, the only top tier marathon for which it is the main gear sponsor, through 2036. It’s also re-upped its sponsorship of a Portland marathon and last month announced a deal with the San Antonio marathon.

Taken together, the moves show how Nike is trying to repair a broken relationship with the running community that’s contributed to its sputtering comeback, and Nike is likely to apply the strategy to other sports it’s been accused of neglecting, like training, soccer, basketball, and outdoor activities.

“We went back to building deep relationships and running communities through our ground game and through our running experts,” CEO Elliott Hill told Wall Street analysts last week. “Our running business was the first proof point that our model works.”

Nike’s running business had logged a few difficult years before Hill was hired as CEO in 2024 to try to stop the sneaker giant’s decline. Nike had shifted its focus away from big wholesalers to build sales at its own stores and web site, but in so doing, lost much of its influence at independent running stores that are key to reaching more serious runners. That proved to be a disastrous decision: between 2016 and 2025, Nike’s share of the $9 billion U.S. sports footwear market dropped from 40% to 30%, according to Euromonitor. The misstep coincided with a running boom that Nike largely missed out on; it focused on limited-edition and lifestyle sneakers over innovative running footwear, allowing rivals like Hoka and On to steal market share.

“We were reminded that to lead a sport, we had to live inside it. Start with the athlete and the problem that we’re solving,” said Hill. Nike running has now reported nine straight quarters of growth, the last six of which were double-digit growth. (Nike does not disclose the business’s sales separately.) The running business has recovered enough that it’s climbed from fifth place among brands to third in the last 12 months, Nike president Amy Montagne told investor analysts last week.

“We have to serve every runner, the elite runner chasing a record and the person training for our first 5K,” said Montagne.

The post-marathon New York Times insert reflected that inclusive tone; it included a tribute to the course and the runners from Nike, concluding with the quote, “I can make it across the finish line anywhere.” It stood in contrast to an ad Nike ran ahead of the Boston marathon in April that seemed to mock slower runners and came off as out of touch and slightly mean.

Hill and Montagne told investors last week that they want to use running as a model to update its approach to other sports, but their audience wasn’t convinced. Shares fell 6% on its investor day, compared to the S&P 500’s 1% decline, as company executives said Nike’s revenue would return to growth in fiscal 2029 and that it was looking at $5 billion in new annual revenue by the end of fiscal 2031. (In its last fiscal year, which ended in May, Nike reported $46.4 billion in revenue, down 2% from the previous year, excluding currency fluctuations.) Company shares have fallen 60% since Hill became CEO two years ago.

The changes at Nike have gone beyond marketing. Hill said that running shoe and clothing design has focused on maximum cushioning, new materials, and more support and stability.

Those kinds of updates may be more of what investors want to hear. As Robert Drbul, managing director and consumer retail analyst at BTIG, wrote in a research note: “Product innovation remains one of the most important catalysts for Nike’s recovery.”

Phil Wahba is a senior writer at Fortune primarily focused on leadership coverage, with a prior focus on retail.

#5295. Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am

The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the company acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

Testing that more closely replicates the company’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company says it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

What set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software update that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

The bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows update used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

So what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

The final report doesn’t say what the July update was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report says.

First, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

Third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

How it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report says.

The preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate issue.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”

Once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft says it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft says it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

It also plans to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

Some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

Microsoft says its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it plans to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

The report also confirms what Microsoft said the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it says. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”

The new testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the company says, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

#5294. Jensen Huang’s reported affairs rattled Nvidia, echoing scandals that hit Bill Gates and Jeff Bezos

Mark Zuckerberg is becoming something of a rarity among the world’s wealthiest tech founders: a billionaire whose marriage hasn’t been publicly linked to an affair.

The Meta cofounder and CEO has been married to his college sweetheart, Priscilla Chan, since 2012. Several peers at the Magnificent Seven companies have instead made headlines for reported affairs, relationship scandals, and divorces.

The latest case is the most consequential. This month, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang resigned as CEO over reported affairs, including one with a woman U.S. officials reportedly suspect works for Chinese intelligence, and was reinstated 11 days later.

At companies built around a founder, a private life can quickly become a governance question. It can trigger a board investigation, move a stock, and, in a divorce, change ownership.

Nvidia cofounder and CEO Jensen Huang told employees in a Nov. 8 memo that he had been unfaithful to Lori Huang, his wife since 1985, as I previously reported for Fortune. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” he wrote. “My actions hurt her and our children.”

The admission followed The New York Times’ reporting that U.S. intelligence agencies suspected Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, of gathering information for Beijing and that she had a close relationship with Huang. Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation into whether Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, and the company said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised.

Two more relationships were reported within days. The New York Times reported that Huang had been romantically involved with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, citing five former employees, CNBC reported. Reuters later reported an intimate relationship with another Nvidia employee, who was not named. Huang has not publicly confirmed either relationship.

On Nov. 12, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned as president, CEO, and board member, and named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO. Nvidia, No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500 and the first company on the list to pass $4 trillion in market value, slipped below that mark as news of the affairs and his resignation spread.

On Nov. 23, the board unanimously reinstated him, saying it had received input from senior U.S. government officials and was confident his return posed no national security risk. President Donald Trump said afterward that he had been “represented” at the board meeting.

The board says its own investigation will proceed to conclusion, and Nvidia says it will keep cooperating with government investigations and inquiries. Huang remains married to Lori Huang, who is president of the couple’s $9 billion foundation and co-trustee of the trusts holding most of their Nvidia stake.

Amazon founder Jeff Bezos announced in January 2019 that he and MacKenzie Scott were divorcing after 25 years of marriage. The same day, The National Enquirer published details of his relationship with Lauren Sánchez, including text messages and photographs.

The Wall Street Journal later reported that the tabloid’s publisher had paid Sánchez’s brother, Michael Sánchez, $200,000 for the texts, a report he disputed. Bezos and Lauren Sánchez went on to date publicly, became engaged in May 2023, and married in June 2025.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk has been married three times to two women and has 14 publicly known children with four women, according to People.

In 2022, The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk had a brief affair with Nicole Shanahan, then the wife of Google cofounder Sergey Brin, and that it prompted Brin to file for divorce. Musk called the report “total BS,” Shanahan denied it through her lawyer, and the Journal said it stood by its reporting.

Musk has also faced an accusation of workplace sexual misconduct. Business Insider reported that SpaceX paid $250,000 to settle a flight attendant’s claim stemming from an alleged 2016 incident. Musk denied the claim.

Brin has faced infidelity allegations of his own. His marriage to 23andMe cofounder Anne Wojcicki ended in divorce in 2015 after eight years, and Vanity Fair reported that he had been involved with Amanda Rosenberg, a Google Glass marketing manager, while still married.

Microsoft cofounder Bill Gates has acknowledged extramarital affairs during his marriage to Melinda French Gates. In February 2026, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing a recording of a Gates Foundation town hall, that Gates apologized to staff for his ties to Jeffrey Epstein and acknowledged two affairs, which he said did not involve Epstein’s victims.

In a closed-door interview with the House Oversight Committee on June 10, Gates acknowledged three extramarital affairs, according to the official transcript. He told lawmakers that Epstein had learned of two of them and appeared to be moving toward using them as leverage, though Gates said he was never blackmailed.

The couple married in 1994 and announced their divorce in May 2021, finalizing it that August after 27 years of marriage.

Divorce gets especially complicated when billions of dollars in assets are involved. The division of marital property depends on state law, the nature of the assets, and whether a prenuptial or postnuptial agreement exists, which is why Fortune examined what California divorce law could mean for the Huangs’ Nvidia fortune. For the richest executives, a split can also raise questions about company shares, liquidity, and control of a major business.

None of these cases show that wealth causes infidelity or divorce. They do show how quickly a founder’s marriage can become a matter for boards, regulators, and shareholders.

Nvidia’s board says its inquiry into whether a foreign intelligence effort targeted Huang will run to the end. Its findings will test a decision the board made in 11 days: that Nvidia is better off with Huang than without him.

#5293. After the Outlook outage: Mary Jo Foley on Ignite, Microsoft’s AI pitch, and a new approach to the press

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 10:09 amNovember 21, 2026 at 10:13 am

This week on the GeekWire Podcast, longtime Microsoft beat reporter Mary Jo Foley, a GeekWire contributing writer, sizes up where the company stands after one of its most eventful weeks in years.

#5292. Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am

In less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down. Sen. Josh Hawley said that if this was all a coincidence, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Yet intelligence and law enforcement officials told Congress they’ve found no evidence that anyone was attacking us.

Attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you. Terrorists claim credit. Criminals issue ransom notes and often brag as well: the hackers who crippled MGM’s casino systems in 2023 told TechCrunch within days. None of this month’s outages came with any of that.

Could a state actor be flexing its cyber capabilities to warn us? China’s Volt Typhoon hackers kept access to U.S. critical infrastructure for at least five years before anyone made it public, positioning themselves to disrupt it in a future crisis. However, hackers who are that patient don’t blow their cover by knocking out the world’s email. A warning shot also works only if the target knows who fired it, and we don’t have a credible suspect for a shooter here.

Each outage has a separate origin tracing back to the organization’s own systems: a new router a contractor was installing for the FAA, a bug Microsoft shipped in July, a software bug at Chase, an internal update at Apple, a patch at the NSA. To stage that, a single attacker would have to break into three companies and two federal agencies, disguise every intrusion as a routine mistake and leave nothing for investigators to find.

A far more credible root cause is the patch treadmill set at too high a speed: AI is finding security holes faster than anyone can safely fix them, and the rush to patch and upgrade is making everything more fragile. Think of an immune system in overdrive. It fights off infection, and sometimes it attacks healthy tissue. This month’s outages were a flare-up.

On Nov. 17, the startup Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical flaw in Java, the software platform used by government agencies and about 90% of Fortune 500 companies. Calif found it with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model. Oracle shipped a patch the same day, and a federal alert urged organizations to “immediately patch.”

Last month the same startup used OpenAI models to find a flaw in PHP, the programming language behind an estimated 70% of websites, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tied the NSA’s outage to the patching that followed. Microsoft alone fixed 1,413 vulnerabilities in October, more than its previous record for an entire year.

AI is forcing faster fixes. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says his company’s outage came from a dormant bug, but he warned this week that AI-driven patching could bring more instability. AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” he told CNBC.

A patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week, he said at the New York Times DealBook Summit. Now it “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”

The FBI warned on Nov. 13 that criminals and state-backed hackers are already using ARTEX, an open-source AI tool built for testing a company’s own defenses, with some intrusions going from first targeting to administrator-level access in under three hours. So the patching can’t slow down. Nobody would give up their immune system to avoid a flare-up.

It will get worse before it gets better. Calif’s CEO, Thai Duong, expects Java4Shell to threaten systems that don’t update for the next five to 10 years.

Meanwhile, the AI that finds flaws like this one is spreading. Open-weight models, which anyone can download and run without safeguards, trail the most advanced models on cyber tasks by only four to seven months, according to the UK AI Security Institute. Every month will bring more bugs, more emergency patches and more flare-ups.

There’s a finite amount of code in Windows, iOS and Chrome, and every bug AI finds and fixes there is one an attacker can’t use. Partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, a program to secure critical software before AI can be turned against it, found more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity bugs in its first month.

Former Microsoft security staffer Angela Gunn sees a hopeful sign: more and more unrelated researchers are turning up the same bugs, which suggests the supply is finite. Fixing still lags finding, but the giants have the money and people to catch up. Within a year or two, I expect Windows, iOS and Chrome to be more secure than they’ve ever been.

#5291. Inside Anthropic’s culture clash: Effective Altruists, IPO hopefuls, and an acrimonious breakup with the AI safety movement that helped create it

“Anthropic is an unusual company. Some might say weird—and in fact, many have,” Daniela Amodei, Anthropic’s cofounder and president, joked from the stage at the Nasdaq MarketSite in Times Square, just hours before the company’s blockbuster IPO earlier this month. In her speech, Amodei stressed that the company was not like other technology companies, largely because of its  “safety-first” culture.

Anthropic has long positioned itself as the most responsible AI lab. The company had an AI safety team before it even had a product. Its founders and employees have been vocal about AI risk, and even its IPO prospectus warned investors that advanced AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

For this reason, over the majority of its five-year history, Anthropic has counted the community of people focused on  AI safety—both technical researchers and policy experts—among its closest allies. But in the run-up to the company’s IPO, some prominent figures in that once-sympathetic field openly broke with the company and now see it as a threat instead of an ally.

“Anthropic is absolutely not the voice of the AI safety community,” said Steven Adler, a former OpenAI safety researcher who co-founded Guidelight AI Standards, which sets safety benchmarks for AI companies. “Many researchers I know believe that Anthropic is the most likely company to get everyone killed.”

These divisions were on full display the day Anthropic made its market debut. Outside the company’s headquarters in San Francisco, more than 100 protesters gathered to demand a ban on “recursive self-improvement,” or RSI, a term for using AI systems to autonomously build yet more powerful AI. Among them was Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic researcher who made headlines around the globe when he quit in September over safety concerns.

Inside the company, Anthropic has, at times, struggled to keep hold of its safety-conscious culture as it has grown, according to three former employees and two people familiar with the company who spoke to Fortune. From its origins as a group of researchers primarily concerned with AI safety, Anthropic’s headcount has swelled to more than 5,000 employees, and its market value closed its first day of trading at about $1.76 trillion. (Since then, it has slipped closer to a $1 trillion market cap.) Now some are questioning whether Anthropic’s safety-first culture can survive life as a public company, and whether the company has already betrayed its founding principles.

“Anthropic has sought to create a race to the top on safety: to show that it’s possible to build AI carefully and succeed commercially, and to make safety something on which AI companies compete,” an Anthropic spokesperson said. “We remain true to our vision to build AI systems that put safety and humans at the center, while maximizing the benefits for humanity.”

Anthropic was founded in 2021 by seven former OpenAI employees, led by the siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei. The group split off primarily because they felt OpenAI’s leadership was not taking AI safety seriously enough and was not trustworthy enough to control such a powerful technology, several former employees said. (Personal conflicts between OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Dario Amodei also played a role, some said.)

Because of that founding mission, most of the company’s early employees came from the AI safety community. Many also hailed from the world of effective altruism—a philanthropic movement that uses evidence and reason to try to do the most good and whose adherents came to rank AI as one of humanity’s most neglected risks. To this day, Anthropic has more people who are adherents of effective altruism, or share many of its values, than rival labs, two former employees who spoke to Fortune said.

Much of Anthropic’s early money also came from EA-aligned investors. Skype cofounder Jaan Tallinn, who has backed a number of EA-affiliated organizations, led Anthropic’s $124 million Series A in May 2021, with Facebook cofounder Dustin Moskovitz, another major funder of EA-related philanthropies, and the Center for Emerging Risk Research also investing. A year later, Anthropic’s $580 million Series B was led by the disgraced crypto kingpin Sam Bankman-Fried, then the movement’s best-known donor.

In the early days, one of Anthropic’s principles was that it would not push the frontier of AI research, according to one former Anthropic engineer, who asked for anonymity to discuss sensitive information about their former employer. Leadership said explicitly that it did not want to start or worsen an AI arms race, and described the lab’s aim as being “a close second,” the person said. Most employees also believed strongly that advanced AI posed an existential risk to humanity.

The company continues to weigh safety concerns heavily, funds its safety teams generously, and holds onto its safety talent, former employees say. But some in Anthropic’s organization also have deep qualms about what the world looks like following the development of the kind of superintelligent AI Anthropic wants to build.

David Duvenaud, a University of Toronto professor who led Anthropic’s Alignment Evaluations team from 2023 to 2024, says many early Anthropic employees believed AI presented a chance of destroying or enslaving humanity. (Duvenaud himself has put the odds of AI destroying much of what humanity values at 70% to 80% by the year 2100).

As a result, Anthropic initially didn’t want to release a product, former employees said. In the summer of 2022, months before OpenAI debuted ChatGPT, launching the AI boom, Anthropic had developed a working chatbot but chose not to release it. Dario Amodei later called that incident a “one-time overhang.”

As Anthropic has grown, its commitment to some of these early principles seems to have eroded. In March 2024, Anthropic released Claude 3, which by some measures beat OpenAI’s GPT-4. It no longer seemed to be playing just for second place.

Then came Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding agent, released in 2025. The tool’s wild popularity kicked off a race between the leading AI labs to perfect AI’s coding abilities. But because AI models are themselves code, advancing AI’s coding capabilities inherently pushes the entire field toward recursive self-improvement. Most AI safety advocates see RSI as inherently dangerous, since an AI model that can autonomously improve itself with little to no human oversight could quickly evolve beyond human control.

Some of Anthropic’s critics argue that the lab pushed the rest of the industry toward that dangerous threshold by loudly demonstrating how good Claude Code was. One former employee pointed to Google DeepMind’s recent increased investment in developing AI coding abilities, in part to keep pace with Anthropic, and OpenAI’s retreat from side projects like video generator Sora, in part in order to free up resources to work on its coding agent Codex, as examples of Anthropic pushing rival labs to the frontier.

For years, the former employee said, colleagues at Anthropic would argue that their competitors were already racing as hard as they could, so Anthropic’s choices didn’t matter. In truth, they said, the rest of the industry was racing harder every year because of Anthropic.

“We’ve been clear that Anthropic may at times go slower than we could to make our systems safer, even at a competitive disadvantage,” an Anthropic spokesperson said. “As our founders have written, we are committed to standing up for our values at critical points, even when it is costly for us commercially.”

Anthropic’s leaders have made culture a priority to a level that former employees say is unusual even by standards of Silicon Valley, which frequently pays lip service to the importance of “mission-driven” companies. Dario Amodei has said publicly he spends “a third, maybe 40%” of his time attending to Anthropic’s culture. In interviews, candidates have been asked unusual culture questions, such as how they would feel if Anthropic abandoned its business ambitions for safety reasons and the stock went to zero.

Anthropic famously went to mat with the Pentagon over its “red lines,” refusing to give in to demands that its models be used by the government for “any lawful use.” The company also takes seriously the philosophical position that very powerful AI models might deserve moral consideration, two former employees said.

Anthropic apparently sees the possibility of a shift in this culture as a potential financial risk. In the company’s IPO prospectus, Anthropic warns investors that employees who joined for its safety commitments “may experience a decline in morale, disillusionment, a loss of trust in leadership, or reduced productivity” if they believe the company is not living up to its values. But keeping that highly-prized culture intact got harder as the company scaled, multiple former employees told Fortune.

For the past 12 months, it’s been clear that an IPO was looming—a liquidity event that might attract people more interested in a financial payoff than in saving the world from dangerous AI.

Coxon, the 27-year-old researcher who resigned in September, has since criticized Anthropic’s broader workforce, claiming many of its employees were just in it for the money. “There were so many non-EA guys at Anthropic who snuck through the interview,” he said. “Just silently praying for the IPO of a lifetime while their whole company crashes out and declares imminent apocalypse.”

Duvenaud said the company “spend[s] a ton of time worrying about culture and who they’re bringing in. But I think it’s almost like trying to hold back the tide.”

“If you build this thing that’s super powerful and going to make everyone rich … you’re in an awkward position if you want to only select for people with really good motivations,” he added.

Anthropic has so far been successful in keeping talent from leaving. The company’s IPO filing reports “regrettable attrition” of just 1% in the 12 months through September, amid a talent war where rivals offer individual researchers hundreds of millions of dollars. The company says its culture is a big reason why.

By the time Anthropic’s cofounders rang the Nasdaq bell, prominent AI safety figures were calling the company a danger.

On the day Anthropic priced its shares, the Center for AI Safety and a coalition of scientists, legal scholars, and tech figures published the “MisAnthropic Statement.” It declared that “Anthropic is not a safe AI company” and launched with 89 signatories, including cognitive psychologist Steven Pinker, president of the Future of Life Institute, Max Tegmark, and xAI cofounder Igor Babuschkin.

“People in this coalition disagree on almost everything, yet we all recognize the danger of a company that convinces itself its own dominance is the greater good,” said Dan Hendrycks, CAIS’s executive director, in the announcement.

According to Adler, Coxon’s resignation was a missed opportunity for Anthropic and the start of its rift with the wider safety community. “Jacob Coxon’s resignation could have been a moment for Dario to speak candidly,” he said. “He ought to have said in no uncertain terms that he is concerned about human extinction, as I know him to be. Instead, Dario mostly dodges questions like these now that Anthropic is in the spotlight.”

Amodei has pushed back on some of this criticism. In October, after Nathan Calvin, chief strategy officer of the AI safety advocacy group Encode AI, published a long post accusing Anthropic of racing toward superintelligence, Amodei replied on X with a roughly 2,000-word defense. “Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the ‘race to the top’—by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry,” he wrote. “The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier.”

“Anthropic’s leadership is open and candid about the risks of powerful AI, including those of AI-automated research, and has led the call for pacing with governments and the industry,” an Anthropic spokesperson said. “And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control.“

But a recent report from METR, an outside evaluator, widened the growing rift between the company and AI safety advocates. From August to October this year, METR had unprecedented access to Anthropic’s internal data and was tasked with assessing whether AI was speeding up Anthropic’s own research—an important safety concern.

The evaluators concluded that the pace of AI research at Anthropic had almost doubled in the past year and that use of AI to automate research was a key reason. However, Anthropic eventually “redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative for these conclusions,” METR wrote in a blog post about the report. METR’s disclosure about the redactions, and other comments METR made about how Anthropic had limited the scope of its evaluation, earned Anthropic derision from AI safety experts.

“We determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster,” Anthropic co-founder Sam McCandlish said in an X post responding to the criticism. “We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work.”

The company has tried to build in protections against market pressure and to guard the culture it values so highly. For example, it remains a public benefit corporation, legally required to weigh its mission alongside shareholder returns, and its Long-Term Benefit Trust helps choose its board. Its prospectus warns investors that this structure could lead to decisions that “may conflict with short-, medium-, or long-term financial interests.” But governance experts have questioned whether those safeguards will hold when profits are on the line.

While some say Anthropic’s life as a public company will make it more difficult to prioritize safety, two former employees said the IPO itself doesn’t change much. The company has always been conflicted, Duvenaud said: building a technology while telling everyone it is “so insanely dangerous” that it could kill everyone.

“I’m not sure being public actually changes the calculus all that much,” he added.

For a long time, the AI safety community was willing to believe that Anthropic cared more about making the world safe than making money. They believed the company could avoid the “god complex” that has driven other AI labs to keep pushing the frontier. But now, many in the AI safety community have come to doubt that is true. Indeed, some now think Anthropic has become exactly the kind of company it was founded to stop.

Beatrice Nolan is a tech reporter on Fortune’s AI team, covering artificial intelligence and emerging technologies and their impact on work, industry, and culture. She's based in Fortune's London office and holds a bachelor’s degree in English from the University of York. You can reach her securely via Signal at beatricenolan.08

#5289. Zillow says mortgage rates will stay above 7% until at least mid-2027

For would-be homebuyers hoping for a reprieve in mortgage rates next year, the outlook isn’t good as borrowing costs are expected to remain high.

According to Freddie Mac, the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.21% as of Wednesday, down from last week’s average of 7.28% as the stock market selloff pushed investors to safe haven Treasuries, lowering bond yields. But at this same time last year, the 30-year rate was 6.23%.

The rate spike in recent months has frozen the housing market. Sales of existing homes plunged 5.5% in October from the prior month and 8.8% from a year ago to an annualized pace of just 3.75 million units, the lowest in 16 years. Pending sales, an indicator of future closings, hit a second consecutive record low in October, down 4.7% month over month and 16.7% year over year.

Americans are also physically stuck. The housing turnover rate, which is how often homes get new owners, is just 3.8% a year, well below the 5% rate before the financial crisis. And the rate at which people move from region to region has been falling for two years.

Zillow expects mortgage rates to remain above 7% for the rest of this year and through mid-2027 with sales falling 3.5%, potentially dampening the spring selling season and weighing further on the housing market next year.

The problem is that inflation is accelerating, so the Federal Reserve is widely expected to keep hiking rates, which will push up borrowing costs across the economy.

To be sure, oil prices have eased as the Iran war continues to simmer without re-escalating, but the latest consumer price index came in hotter than expected with inflationary pressure spreading beyond energy categories.

Ironically, the frozen housing market is also stoking inflation, keeping the Fed hawkish, as discouraged buyers turn to the rental market and push up rents.

“New-lease rents are growing at their fastest pace in 2025-2026, so they’re no longer pulling down housing inflation measures, and forecasts for on-market rents have been revised upward in recent months,” Zillow Senior Economist Kara Ng wrote earlier this month. “In other words, while oil-related developments could ease some inflation pressure, firmer rent growth means the Fed may get less help from shelter in 2027.”

The U.S. economy is also booming as AI hyperscalers pour hundreds of billions of dollars into data centers and other infrastructure. Their capital expenditures are expected to top $1 trillion in 2027. Third-quarter GDP jumped 4.3%, and the fourth quarter is on pace to see still-robust growth of 2.9%.

That continues to support strong wages and resilient consumer demand, allowing businesses to pass on higher costs and add further to inflation.

“However, a slowdown elsewhere in the economy or faster progress on inflation would pull mortgage rates down sooner,” Ng pointed out. “With inventory forecast to rise about 11% next year, there should be enough supply to meet demand if buyers return.”

For now, the housing market is still reeling from the mortgage rate shock. The 30-year fixed mortgage had been around 6.60% in July, then soared to 7.61% by the start of October, and has stayed above 7% since then.

Zillow CEO Jeremy Wacksman told CNBC earlier this month that the full-percentage-point surge was one of the fastest three-month increases seen in decades. That has sent the purchase mortgage market down 4% year over year, and he expects it to be down 10%-15% in the fourth quarter. Meanwhile, rents in the third quarter were up nearly 20%.

“That is buyers just not being able to afford the homes they were looking at,” Wacksman explained. “They were thinking about a mortgage and then they couldn’t pull the trigger, and so now they’re renting longer.”

Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune, where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing.

#5288. Beyond Nvidia: Convoy co-founder and former Microsoft leader raise $277M to rethink AI infrastructure

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm

Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.

The outsized seed funding for their new startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on. As AI shifts from training models to running them in everyday products, Marlowe designs and operates computing systems for that work. It’s starting with chips from AMD and Etched, expanding beyond the Nvidia GPUs that have fueled the AI boom.

They say tuning the chips, networking and software for specific AI workloads and applications will maximize performance and efficiency, lowering costs as a result.

The new funding values Marlowe at $1.15 billion, according to the company, making it a unicorn out of the gate. Accel led the latest round, joined by a long list of big names in tech and finance, from KKR co-founder Henry Kravis to Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi.

Lewis, Marlowe’s CEO, previously co-founded the trucking startup Convoy and later was an enterprise AI leader at Microsoft, where Srinivasan, now Marlowe’s CTO, was a corporate vice president and the company-wide technical lead for AI infrastructure.

“The demand for intelligence and AI is very high,” Lewis said in an interview, when asked how a former freight marketplace CEO ended up in AI computing. “It’s something that should be accessible and affordable for everyone.”

Marlowe, founded in May, is based in both Bellevue, Wash., and Redwood City, Calif., and is approaching 30 employees. Lewis said the two home bases reflect where its customers, partners and talent are concentrated, pointing to Bellevue as an emerging AI hub.

Lewis, a former Amazon general manager, joined Flexport as a technical advisor when the freight company acquired Convoy’s technology after the startup’s abrupt shutdown in 2023. In February 2025, he returned to Microsoft, where he had also worked previously, as a chief product officer focused on enterprise AI, later becoming a corporate vice president.

GeekWire first reported in June that he had left Microsoft to launch a new startup, but he wasn’t ready to share details at the time.

From Microsoft to Marlowe: The founders said the idea for Marlowe grew out of what they saw at Microsoft: demand was surging for inference, running AI models in products and services, but data centers were still being built mainly for training those models in the first place.

“We were always oversold, effectively sold out,” Lewis said.

Since then, demand for inference has grown faster than supply, pushing up costs at the same time that power shortages, permitting and financing are making new data centers harder to build. The company cites a 40% increase in data center construction costs since 2020, which makes every watt more valuable.

The company isn’t using Nvidia chips for now, but it hasn’t ruled them out.

Its first site, built around Etched’s chips, is scheduled to go live in December, the founders said. A second, larger site using AMD’s new Helios systems is on track for the second quarter of 2027.

Both sites are under contract, and a third is under a letter of intent. The company says it has signed three customer agreements but isn’t yet naming the customers or the locations.

Srinivasan said that at the big tech companies where he has worked, chips from vendors other than Nvidia made up a small slice of the fleet. When a new AI model came out, the top engineers focused on getting it running on the Nvidia chips, and the rest got left behind.

“There were literally times when a significant portion of our non-Nvidia fleet was either idle or grossly underused or didn’t support the latest models and workloads,” he said.

That’s the gap Marlowe is trying to close. Its engineers work directly on customers’ workloads to get other chips performing at their full potential, giving those companies a way to reduce their dependence on a single supplier.

Marlowe says gains of 10% to 20% at each layer of the system, from chips and networking to power management and software, add up to two to three times more output per watt and per dollar than conventional GPU clouds, measured in tokens, the chunks of text that AI models process and generate.

Competition and funding: Marlowe isn’t alone in the bet. Gimlet Labs, which raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation in September, and General Compute, which raised $100 million in October, are also building inference clouds that run on a mix of chips.

CoreWeave, the largest of the so-called neoclouds, rents out computing power built almost entirely on Nvidia chips. Nvidia held about 47 million CoreWeave shares as of Sept. 30, and CoreWeave has taken on about $47 billion in debt to build out its data centers.

Marlowe’s launch also comes during a turbulent stretch for Nvidia. The company’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after his resignation.

Much of Marlowe’s funding will go toward chips, networking equipment and the support needed to run the sites, along with hiring, the founders said. By the standards of AI infrastructure, $277 million doesn’t go far.

Rather than chasing giant facilities, Marlowe plans to prove its approach at sites of tens of megawatts and then finance more capacity site by site, Lewis said. He noted that some startups have raised four to five times as much and will deploy a little less computing power on a similar timeline.

The $277 million includes a smaller initial round led by Eclipse, Lewis said. Eclipse founder and CEO Lior Susan is Marlowe’s executive chairman, and Ido Susan, founder and CEO of the data center networking company DriveNets, is on the board. Other backers include Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides, Journey and Valor.

Angel investors also include Box CEO Aaron Levie and former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky. Mark Okerstrom, the former Expedia CFO and CEO who later served as Convoy’s president, is also an investor.

Past lives: Srinivasan’s career runs from video games to AI infrastructure. In an earlier stint at Microsoft, he worked on DirectX and games including Halo 3, then spent eight years at Valve, where he led the team that built the first Steam mobile app.

He later served as the lead architect for machine learning training infrastructure at Facebook, and as a technical fellow at LinkedIn before moving to Microsoft’s CoreAI group in 2025.

Marlowe is a very different business from Convoy, the digital freight marketplace Lewis co-founded to match truckers with shippers. Convoy reached a $3.8 billion valuation before shutting down in 2023, amid a freight recession and a pullback in venture funding.

Asked how Marlowe would avoid getting similarly squeezed by forces outside its control in a capital-intensive business, Lewis said the industry is at “the very beginning” of a long-term shift in how people use AI and data.

He also pointed to a mix of long- and short-term contracts and multiple customers, rather than one big customer that could pull out.

Ultimately, Lewis said he believes Marlowe’s edge will come down to having the engineering skills to get the most out of new chips. “You can’t just take a new chip that comes out and plug it in and expect it to produce tokens,” he said. “You have to go do the work.”

Updated at 6:20 a.m. PT with Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO.

#5287. For banks, a breach is now a matter of when, not if, says OCBC’s tech head—and reaction time matters as much as prevention

Since September, South Korea’s financial sector has been hit by a rolling wave of cyberattacks, with regulators counting 40 incidents at 37 financial firms, including banks, brokerages, insurers and crypto exchanges. Researchers traced the September attacks to Artex, an AI-powered tool that automated the intrusions.

“With the velocity that cyberattacks are happening, it is a matter of when rather than if,” Praveen Raina, head of group operations and technology at Singapore’s Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp. (OCBC), tells Fortune.

For banks, trust may now come not from preventing any and all attacks, but from detecting, closing and repairing them faster. “I wish I could prevent them—and we’ll try—but what we can control is having the right processes so that we can react quickly to whatever happens,” Raina says.

His strategy consists of two elements: cybersecurity and resilience. “We’re leveraging AI for cybersecurity,” he explains. “With agentic AI attacking organizations, humans cannot keep up with it… it’s the nature of the beast. So, we’re building a defensive AI wrapper around the bank to protect it.”

His team also regularly conducts red-teaming exercises: structured simulations in which a group acts like a real-world attacker to improve their ability to react in the event of a hack. “We practice a lot among ourselves and with other industry players,” Raina says. “We also have a bug bounty program for white hackers to identify [security] issues in exchange for a reward.”

Raina joined OCBC in 2008 as its SVP in group operations and technology, after spending the early years of his career as an IT consultant to telcos and enterprise software firms in Canada. (OCBC was founded in 1932; Today, it is Singapore’s second-largest bank, and ranks No. 13 on Fortune’s Southeast Asia 500 list.)

In his first year at OCBC, while spending the holidays away from home, Raina amassed a small team to build an iPhone-native banking app. “The tech team was a lot smaller then,” he says. “We didn’t have a deep expertise in building things, and instead mostly bought [our tech solutions] from vendors and implemented them. As the world changed around us, we made it a point [to develop in-house expertise].” (The final product, launched in 2008, was the first digital banking app debuted by one of Singapore’s three local banks: OCBC, DBS and UOB.)

From then on, Raina’s team—which today consists of roughly 600 to 700 employees—started building almost everything in-house. “It gives us better control of things, and we can do more and faster releases,” he explains, adding that failing “over and over again” adds to the joy of creation.

In July, OCBC launched its Avatar Banking app, which allows clients round-the-clock access to AI-enabled virtual relationship managers. The entire process from ideation to release took four to six weeks, Raina says. “It was an unplanned pregnancy,” he says. “We just happily stumbled upon the idea, and worked every day to generate ideas to see what we could do [to bring it to life].”

The new app was initially launched as a beta version to just fifty customers, but Raina says he’s preparing to onboard all the bank’s private wealth clients onto the platform by the first quarter of 2027. (On the app, users can pick between two virtual wealth managers: a man named Wayne and a woman named Wendy.)

“The white glove service is always important, and we are not taking that away,” says Raina, who also heads up the tech division at the Bank of Singapore, OCBC’s private banking subsidiary. “The point is, if I wake up at 3 a.m. and want to look at what’s happening with my portfolio, who do I go to? At that time, even if you call your relationship manager, they will likely not pick up.”

Experts estimate that “Q-Day”, the day quantum computers will be able to crack traditional encryption, will happen around the year 2030. Raina expects a Y2K-style crunch, with every institution competing for the same vendors at the last minute. OCBC is trying to get ahead by training over 100 quantum-literate staff, and running pilots with universities and ST Engineering.

“When we go into our mobile banking app, our phone sends a signal to the OCBC data center, and there’s a handshake happening and a key is exchanged to verify our identity,” Raina explains. “The issue with quantum computing is that it’s so powerful that it can break those keys… so the security layer is gone.”

Raina compares quantum technology today to AI in the pre-ChatGPT era. “It’s a theoretical field, which we aren’t experts in, so we partner with universities to get a better understanding of the technology stack,” he says. “We are building [quantum security] for the future; we don’t need it today, but when the technology comes to life on Q-Day, we will be ready.”

Ultimately, banking is a trust-based business, and Raina sees it as his role to upkeep the faith that users have in OCBC. “People work and they put their life savings with the organization—there’s no bigger trust than that,” he concludes. “We as an organization have to do our part to ensure that everything is protected.”

Angelica Ang is a Singapore-based journalist who covers the Asia-Pacific region.

#5286. Microsoft’s Brad Smith on Trump’s data center tax threat: ‘You can’t support Helsinki from New Jersey’

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 5:49 amNovember 23, 2026 at 6:01 am

Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S. companies that build data centers abroad: most of them have to be where their customers are.

Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith said the president is “making an important point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.

But he said most data centers run everyday cloud services, such as streaming video, video games and business software, and need to be close to the people using them.

“You can’t support Helsinki from New Jersey any more than you can keep the lights on in Helsinki from an electricity power plant in New Jersey,” he said.

A tax on foreign data centers could have significant financial implications for Microsoft, which says it has more than 600 data centers in 34 countries.

Trump made the statement Friday at a White House press conference, saying companies would face a “tremendous tax” if they build data centers outside the U.S.

His reason: “We’re not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”

.@POTUS: "Whoever wins SI, wins… We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries — because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." pic.twitter.com/FiH1LfAQDu

He gave no rate or timeline and acknowledged that he hadn’t told his own staff. “That’s a breaking story,” he said. “I haven’t even said that to my people. But I’m telling them now — they’re here.”

Trump had just returned from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

His one example was an unnamed company that wants to build in Finland. Google announced a €13 billion investment in Finland in September, covering data centers and clean energy projects. Margaret Brennan, host of the CBS program, said he might have meant a Chinese project.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who appeared earlier in the same CBS broadcast, said he hadn’t spoken with the president about the proposal, but added that Trump is “very concerned that we don’t do a big technology transfer offshore.”

Smith also fielded questions on other topics in his “Face the Nation” appearance.

TikTok’s owner: Brennan asked about TikTok’s Chinese owner, ByteDance, which is in advanced talks to spend about $500 million more on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, mostly to use OpenAI’s models, The Information reported last week.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chair of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, said Microsoft should not sell AI tools to ByteDance, called it unacceptable for a Pentagon contractor, and asked the company for a briefing.

Smith noted that TikTok’s U.S. business is now a separate company, and said Microsoft expects to answer the committee’s questions on Capitol Hill.

White House ballroom: Microsoft committed $10 million to Trump’s ballroom project, according to an internal donor list reported by the Washington Post. Brennan asked why, and whether Microsoft is worried about scrutiny from a Democratic-controlled Congress.

Smith said Microsoft takes the same approach with every administration, regardless of party. “We partner where we can. We stand apart when we should,” he said.

He put the ballroom donation in the first category, and said the company “didn’t know, obviously,” that the project would involve tearing down the East Wing. In the second category, he pointed to lawsuits Microsoft has filed against the current administration, as it has against previous ones, to stand up for issues it considered important.

Outlook outage: Smith reiterated Microsoft’s apology for the Nov. 12 global Microsoft 365 and Outlook outage. He said the outage wasn’t caused by AI or a cyberattack.

Speaking more broadly, he said much of the recent wave of tech failures can be seen as “AI ripple effects” — the result of AI making software bugs easier to find, which has companies racing to patch systems faster than they can test the fixes.

(GeekWire has covered that angle in depth, including the surge in AI-discovered bugs, Microsoft’s final outage report and Oren Etzioni’s column on the conspiracy theories.)

Smith said the patching race won’t be finished anytime soon. “The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now,” he said.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

#5284. Lauren C. Templeton’s 3 rules for ‘maximum pessimism’ investing

The hedge fund manager treats a market crash as an opportunity for a “shopping spree.”

The investor Lauren C. Templeton is not a pessimist—though she’s happiest when everyone around her is.

The Tennessee-based author and fund manager has taken up the creed of “maximum pessimism” espoused by her legendary great-uncle, Sir John Templeton, whom many view as the greatest stock picker of the 20th century. Sir John famously said that every bull market is born in pessimism, which creates an environment where bargains abound—if you know where to look for them.

Templeton, who began her career working alongside her renowned great-uncle, has likewise made a name for herself by placing bets in bad times. Those bets have included buying airline stocks after 9/11 and scooping up Amazon shares at the outset of the pandemic. She and her husband run the hedge fund Templeton and Phillips Capital Management, with $325 million in assets.

Templeton inherited her contrarian investment style from her great-uncle, but also from her stockbroker father. She recalls the time he returned home from work on Black Monday in 1987—a day when the Dow Jones plunged 23%—and told her mother he was the only broker in his branch to put in a buy order.

As a child, Templeton says, she was passionate about stocks because purchasing even a single share made her feel like a part owner of the company. She once even wrote a letter of disappointment to Walmart founder Sam Walton about a filthy restroom she encountered at a store. (Walton wrote back promising to tighten things up.)

Today, Templeton’s investment thesis reflects Warren Buffett’s famous maxim to “be greedy when others are fearful.” It’s a sound strategy, but that doesn’t mean it’s easy. Here are three rules she follows.

“There are only three sources of alpha available in the markets: You can have a better model; you can have better information; or you can have better behavior,” says Templeton.

“Behavior” in this case means discipline, which can be hard to maintain in times of volatility. The undoing of many retail investors, says Templeton, comes from selling when the market is diving—a decision that can lead to unloading good assets and, even worse, missing out on the big bounce backs that often follow selloffs. Indeed, there is sobering research that shows that, over the past 30 years, 78% of the stock market’s best days occurred during bear markets and in the first two months of a bull market—and that missing the market’s 10 best days during that period would have reduced your portfolio by half.

Templeton stresses that it’s crucial for investors to know how to wait. She says her fund’s approach can be unsettling for younger employees, who may be itching to trade. “I always tell them, ‘We’re just sitting around reading. It’s not going to be an eventful day-to-day environment, because we don’t overtrade.’”

This premium on patience is something Templeton also conveys to potential investors. While they may appreciate her “maximum pessimism” philosophy, not all have the stomach for it. “If clients hire and fire managers based on their own personal cycles of fear and greed, the strategy breaks,” she says. “A major part of our responsibility isn’t just managing the asset allocation, but actively managing our investors’ emotions.”

The investing success of Sir John Templeton, who as a student at Yale paid for his tuition in part by playing poker, was based on a clever trick of psychology: He kept a wish list of stocks at the ready for the next downturn, which helped anchor his thinking when opportunity arose. His grandniece uses the same strategy.

“The psychological pressure of a market crash is immense. When prices tank, human nature forces you to obsess over your losses and fear opening your financial statements,” she says. “But if you can actively shift your mindset by pulling out a preapproved list of elite companies that you’ve always wanted to own but found too expensive, the script completely flips. Suddenly, a market crash becomes an exciting shopping spree.”

She and her partner and spouse, Scott Phillips, use this strategy not only to buy quality stocks on the cheap when the market dives, but also to turn their portfolio over. To do this, they typically use a dollar-cost averaging approach to take large positions in new stocks while divesting other ones they hold.

The couple employed this strategy during the financial crisis of late 2008 and early 2009. Templeton recalls this period, which brought about the collapse of numerous major banks, with happy nostalgia. “At that point, asset prices were so detached from reality that it felt like shooting fish in a barrel,” she says.

It’s easy enough to understand the idea of waiting to buy at the bottom of the market. The problem, of course, is that no one—including Templeton—can be sure exactly when the bottom is in.

“The simple answer is that you don’t ever truly know,” she says. “We might be getting a little uncomfortable or excited as prices plummet, but we don’t have a crystal ball. You simply observe that a massive cluster of high-quality bargains has emerged, and you want to get your hands on them.”

Such moments don’t come along all the time. Indeed, the current bull market in U.S. equities recently entered its fifth year. But that doesn’t mean there aren’t opportunities to find elsewhere.

Templeton recalls that her great-uncle realized this in the late 1950s and 1960s when he looked at publicly traded companies in Japan. He understood that investors had significantly undervalued these firms because of lingering anti-Japanese sentiment from World War II as well as quirks in the companies’ accounting that didn’t properly account for subsidiary profits. Sir John bought shares—and profited handsomely.

Lauren Templeton says she has never forgotten this lesson, and that it leads her to scour the globe for regions where investors are undervaluing the shares of companies that are performing well. It’s a playbook she has run repeatedly—and is ready to do so again.

“Right now, we have our eyes firmly on India,” she says. “It all goes back to that global perspective: Why wouldn’t you look across the globe for the absolute best bargains available? We believe some of the greatest bargains today are in India.”

This aritcle appears in the December 2026/January 2027 issue of Fortune.

Jeff John Roberts is the Finance and Crypto editor at Fortune, overseeing coverage of the blockchain and how technology is changing finance.
